(p-164)Surat al-A'raf

Section on its revelation

Al-'Awfi, Ibn Abi Talha, and Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that Surat al-A'raf is Meccan. This is also the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatada. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada that it is Meccan except for five verses, the first of which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And ask them about the town﴾. Muqatil said: all of it is Meccan except His saying, ﴿And ask them about the town﴾, up to His saying, ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring﴾ [al-A'raf: 163-172], for these are Medinan.

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾

As for the tafsir: regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾, we have already mentioned in the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah a general discussion of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a, the isolated letters at the beginnings of surahs), and it applies to this as well. As for what is specific to this verse, there are seven opinions.

The first: its meaning is "I am Allah, the All-Knowing, the One who explains." This was narrated by Abu al-Duha from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-165) The second: it is an oath which Allah swore by it. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is one of the names of Allah, Exalted is He. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that the alif is a key whose name is "Allah," the lam is a key whose name is "Latif" (the Subtle), the mim is a key whose name is "Majid" (the Glorious), and the sad is a key whose name is "Sadiq" (the Truthful). This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fifth: that ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾ is the name of the surah. This was said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. This was said by Qatada.

The seventh: that it is part of a word. There are then two opinions regarding that word.

One of them: al-Musawwir (the Fashioner). This was said by al-Suddi. The second: al-Musayyir ila kitab undhila ilayk (the one who leads to a Book sent down to you). This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 2:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A Book that has been sent down to you﴾. Al-Akhfash said: "al-Kitab" (the Book) is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). The view of al-Farra' is that Allah, at the beginning of the surahs, suffices with some of the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-mu'jam) rather than all of them, just as a speaker says "alif, ba', ta', tha'" meaning twenty-eight letters. So the meaning is: the letters of the alphabet, (this is) a Book which We have sent down to you. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is also permissible for "al-Kitab" to be nominative by an implied "this is the Book" (hadha al-kitab). Regarding "haraj" (constriction), there are two opinions.

The first: it is doubt (shakk). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: it is constriction/tightness (dayq). This was said by al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj. Regarding the pronoun in "minhu" (from it), there are two opinions.

The first: it refers back to the Book. On this view, there are two meanings of the statement. One: let not your chest be constricted in conveying (the message), and do not fear, as said by al-Zajjaj. The second: do not doubt that it is from Allah. (p-166) The second opinion: it refers to an implied antecedent, which is indicated by the warning (al-injar), namely denial (al-takdhib), as mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Al-Farra' said: The meaning of the verse is: let not your chest be constricted if they deny you. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿that you may warn thereby﴾ is placed first; the meaning is: It was sent down to you so that you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers, so let there be no constriction in your chest because of it. "Dhikra" (a reminder) may be in the place of nominative, accusative or genitive. As for the accusative, it is based on His saying: "sent down to you that you may warn thereby, and as a reminder for the believers," meaning: and that you may remind thereby with a reminder, because warning carries the sense of reminding. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning: and it is a reminder, as in your saying: "and it is a reminder for the believers." As for the genitive, it is based on the sense of "li-tundhira": the particle "li" governs the verb "an tundhira" (that you warn), so the meaning is: for warning and reminder, and it is in the genitive position.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. If it is said: How did He address him in the singular in the first verse, then say in the plural with His words ﴿Follow﴾? There are three answers to this.

The first: when He knew that the address was to him and to his community, the plural was fitting for that meaning.

The second: the first address is specific to him; the second is understood as a warning (infar), and warning takes the form of speech, so it is as if He said: say to them, as a warner: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both of these.

The third: the second address is to the polytheists. A group of the exegetes mentioned this, saying: "and what was sent down to them is the Qur'an." Al-Zajjaj said: "What was sent down" is the Qur'an and what came from the Prophet (ﷺ), because it is among what was sent down to him, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. ﴿And do not follow, apart from Him, allies﴾, meaning: do not take as allies those who have turned away from the religion of truth; and everyone who adopts a school of thought is an ally of the people of that school. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little do you remember﴾, "ma" is an emphasizing extra particle (ma za'ida mu'akkida), and the meaning is: you remember a little.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "tadhakkarun" with the dhal and the kaf both doubled (tashdid). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "tadhakkarun" with the dhal light and the kaf doubled. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads "tudhakkarun" with tashdid intends "tatadhakkarun" and assimilates the ta' into the dhal; this assimilation is good, because the ta' is voiceless (mahmusa) and the dhal is voiced (majhura); the voiced sound is louder and stronger than the voiceless, so assimilating the weaker into the stronger is good. As for Hamza and those who agree with him, they omitted the ta' that these readers assimilated, and this is good because of the meeting of three close consonants. Ibn 'Amir read "yatadhakkarun" with a ya' and a ta', addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ); the meaning is: little do these people remember who were admonished by this address.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 4:**

Allah's words: ﴿How many a town We destroyed﴾. *Kam* indicates multitude, while *rubba* is used for fewness. al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "How many a people of a town," so he omitted "the people," because the context gives evidence of it.

Allah's words: ﴿Then Our punishment came upon it﴾ are understood according to the wording "the town." The meaning is: Our punishment came upon them heedlessly, while they did not expect it, either at night while they were sleeping, or by day while they were taking their midday rest. Ibn Qutayba said: *Ba'sana* means "Our punishment." *Bayatan* means "at night." *Qa'ilun* comes from *al-qa'ila*, which is the midday rest. If it is said: The punishment came upon them before the destruction, so how does the destruction come first? There are three answers to this.

The first: the destruction and the punishment occurred together, as you say, "You gave me and I did well," where the doing well was neither after the giving nor before it, but both happened together. This was said by al-Farra'.

The second: the verb "to be" (*al-kawn*) is implied in the verse. Its estimated form is: "We destroyed it, and Our punishment had come upon it," so the verb "to be" was left implicit, as it is implied in Allah's words: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited﴾ [al-Baqara 2:102], meaning "what the devils had been reciting." And Allah's words: ﴿If he steals﴾ [Yusuf 12:77] mean "If he has stolen."

The third: the verse contains inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*). Its estimated form is: "How many a town, Our punishment came upon it at night, or while they were taking their midday rest, so We destroyed it," like Allah's words: ﴿Indeed I will take you and raise you to Me﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:55], meaning "I will raise you and take you." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both of these.

Allah's words: ﴿or while they were taking their midday rest﴾. al-Farra' said: In it there is an implied *waw* (the conjunction "and"). The meaning is: "Our punishment came upon them at night, or and while they were taking their midday rest," because they disliked stringing one coordination upon another.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their only plea was﴾ [the translation of "فَما كانَ دَعْواهُمْ"]. The philologists (lughawiyyun) said: "Here, ad-da'wa (claim, plea) means ad-du'a' (calling out) and qawl (speech). The meaning is: their speech and their calling out to one another, when the punishment came upon them, was nothing but the confession of wrongdoing." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The word ad-da'wa in speech has two usages.

The first is ad-di'a' (claiming). The second is al-qawl and ad-du'a' (speaking and calling out)." (p-169) The poet said:

When my leg goes numb, I call on you, seeking relief through your calling, from the numbness in it, and so it becomes easy.

Allah's saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾, meaning: the nations will be questioned: "Did the messengers convey to you, and what did you answer?" And the messengers will be questioned: "Did you convey, and what did you receive as answer?" ﴿Then We will surely relate to them﴾, meaning: We will inform them of what they did, with knowledge from Us, ﴿and We were not absent﴾ from the messengers and the nations. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Book will be placed, and it will speak of what they used to do.

Allah's saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾, meaning: the nations will be questioned: "Did the messengers convey to you, and what did you answer?" And the messengers will be questioned: "Did you convey, and what did you receive as answer?" ﴿Then We will surely relate to them﴾, meaning: We will inform them of what they did, with knowledge from Us, ﴿and We were not absent﴾ from the messengers and the nations. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Book will be placed, and it will speak of what they used to do.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 8–9:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the weighing on that Day will be the truth﴾, meaning: the justice. He said ﴿its scales﴾ because "man" (man) carries the sense of the plural (jami'), as indicated by His saying: ﴿then those﴾. Regarding the meaning of ﴿they wronged﴾ there are two opinions.

One of them: they deny (yajhadun). The second: they disbelieve (yakfurun).

Al-Farra' said: What is meant by ﴿its scales﴾ is its weighing. The Arabs say: "Would you like a dirham for the weight (mizan) of your dirham," and "the weight (wazn) of your dirham," and they say: "My house is by the mizan of your house, and the wazn of your house," and they mean: opposite your house. A poet said:

"Before meeting you, I was once
With you, a contender over his mizan (scale/measure)"

meaning: like his speech and his wording.

Section

The doctrine of the scale (mizan) is well known in the hadith, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an speaks of it. The Mu'tazilah denied this and said: deeds are accidents (a'rad), so how can they be weighed? The answer: the weighing returns to the records (sahifah), by the evidence of the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will single out a man from my community before the people on the Day of Resurrection, and will spread out before him ninety-nine registers (sijill), each register as far as the eye can see. Then He will say to him: 'Do you deny any of this? Have my recording scribes wronged you?' He will say: 'No, my Lord.' He will say: 'Do you have an excuse, or a good deed?' The man will be confounded, and he will say: 'No, my Lord.' He will say: 'Yes, indeed, you have one good deed with Us, and there is no injustice upon you today.' Then a card (bitaqah) will be brought out for him in which is: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger.' The registers will be placed in one pan and the card in another pan. He said: The registers will be outweighed, and the card will be heavier." Related by Ahmad in his Musnad, and al-Tirmidhi. And Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A tall, heavy-eating, heavy-drinking man will be brought, and he will not weigh the wing of a mosquito." On this basis, the human being is weighed.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The good deeds and the evil deeds are weighed in a scale which has a tongue and two pans. As for the believer, his deed will be brought to him in its most beautiful form, and it will be placed in the pan of the scale, and his good deeds will outweigh his evil deeds. As for the disbeliever, his deed will be brought to him in its ugliest form, and it will be placed in the pan of the scale, and his weight will be light.

Al-Hasan said: The scale has a tongue and two pans.

There came in the hadith: "Dawud, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to show him the scale, and He showed it to him. He said: 'O my God, who can fill its two pans with good deeds?' He said: 'O Dawud, when I am pleased with My servant, I fill it with a date.'"

Hudhayfah said: Jibril is the holder of the scale on the Day of Resurrection, and his Lord says to him: "Weigh between them, and return from some of them to others." So he returns to the wronged from the wrongdoer whatever good deed he has. If he has no good deed, something is taken from the wronged one's evil deeds and added to the evil deeds of the wrongdoer, and he returns with the weight of mountains upon him.

If it is said: Does Allah not know the measures of deeds? So what is the wisdom in weighing them? The answer: in it there are five wisdoms.

The first: testing the creation with belief in this in the world. The second: displaying the sign of happiness and misery in the Hereafter. The third: making the servants know what good and evil they have. The fourth: establishing the proof against them. The fifth: informing that Allah is just and does not wrong. A parallel to this is that He recorded the deeds in a book and copied them, without the possibility of forgetfulness upon Him.

(p-172) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly established you upon the earth﴾, concerning which there are two opinions.

One of them: We made you firmly settled in it. The second: We made it easy for you to dispose of it (its affairs).

And concerning "ma'ayish" (means of livelihood) there are two opinions.

One of them: what you live by of food and drink.

The second: what you use to reach livelihoods, such as farming, work, and earning. Most of the readers leave out the hamza in "ma'ayish," though Kharijah narrated it from Nafi' with the hamza. Al-Zajjaj said: All the Basran grammarians hold that hamzing it is an error, because the hamza occurs only on an added (extra) yā', as in ṣaḥīfah and ṣaḥā'if; ṣaḥīfah comes from ṣuḥuf, and the yā' is added. As for ma'ayish, it comes from 'aysh (life), so the yā' is original (radical).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾, meaning: your thanks is little. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means that you are not thankful.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ — concerning it there are eight opinions.

The first: "And We created you" in the loins of Adam, "then We fashioned you" in the wombs. This was related by ʿAbdullah ibn al-Harith from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "And We created you" in the loins of men, and "We fashioned you" in the wombs of women. This was related by Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah also said it. (p-173)

The third: ﴿And We created you﴾, meaning Adam, ﴿then We fashioned you﴾, meaning his offspring after him. This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: ﴿And We created you﴾, meaning Adam, ﴿then We fashioned you﴾ in his back. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: We created you as drops (nutfah) in the loins of men and the ribs (tara'ib) of women, and ﴿then We fashioned you﴾ when the drops came together in the wombs. This was said by Ibn al-Saʾib.

The sixth: ﴿We created you﴾ in the bellies of your mothers, ﴿then We fashioned you﴾ after the creation, by the splitting of the hearing and the sight. This was said by Maʿmar.

The seventh: ﴿We created you﴾, meaning Adam, We created him from dust, ﴿then We fashioned you﴾, that is, We fashioned him. This was said by al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn Qutaybah said: He attributed the creation to them since they came from him; so whoever said it refers by "We created you" to Adam, its meaning is: We created your origin; and whoever said: "We fashioned his offspring in his back," meant bringing them out on the Day of the Covenant like the particles (dharr).

The eighth: ﴿And We created you﴾, meaning the spirits, ﴿then We fashioned you﴾, meaning the bodies. This was reported by al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla in "al-Muʿtamad." Regarding the word "then" (thumma) mentioned twice, there are two views.

One: that it means "and" (waw), said by al-Akhfash. The second: that it indicates sequence (tartib), said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 12:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ "Ma" (what) is an interrogative, and its meaning is reproach (al-inkar). Al-Kisa'i said: "la" (not) here is superfluous (za'ida). The meaning is: What prevented you from prostrating? Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "ma" is nominative (raf'). The meaning is: What thing prevented you from prostrating? And "la" is superfluous (za'ida) and emphasizing (mu'akkida); a similar example is: ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29]. Ibn Qutayba said: "la" may be added in speech. Its meaning is that it is dropped out of refusal (iba') in speech, or denial (jahd), as in this verse. It was added because he did not prostrate. A similar example is: ﴿that when it comes, they will not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 109] according to the reading of the one who vocalized "anna" with a fatha, so "la" was added because they did not believe. A similar example is: ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya: 95]. Al-Farra' said: "la" here is pure denial (jahd mahd), not superfluous, and the prevention (al-man') refers back to an interpretation of speech; the interpretation is: whoever said to you, "Do not prostrate"; so he placed the prevention in the position of speech, and "an" (that) entered after it to indicate the interpretation of the speech whose wording was not stated explicitly. Ibn Jarir said: there is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: What prevented you from prostrating, so that you were compelled that you did not prostrate? Al-Zajjaj said: God the Exalted's question to Iblis, "What prevented you?", is a rebuke to him, and to show that he is obstinate, and for this reason he did not repent. He gave an answer that has the meaning of a reply but whose wording is not a reply, because his saying, ﴿I am better than him﴾, is in fact an answer to "Which of you is better?" But the meaning is: my superiority over him prevented me from prostrating. A similar example is your saying to a man, "How are you?", and he says, "I am well"; the actual answer should be "I was well," but he answers with what he needs and more. The scholars said: the error occurred from Iblis when he analogized in the presence of an explicit text, and the superiority of clay over fire was hidden from him; and its superiority is in several respects.

The first of them: that the nature of fire is haste, blazing and rashness, while the nature of clay is calm and gravity.

The second: that clay is the cause of growth and existence, while fire is the cause of destruction and annihilation.

The third: that clay is the cause of gathering things together, while fire is the cause of scattering them.

Firstly: that it refers to the heaven, because he was in it. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Secondly: that it refers to Paradise. This is the view of al-Suddi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾. If it is said: Is it then permissible for anyone to be arrogant elsewhere? The answer: the meaning is that it is not fitting for the arrogant to be in it, whereas arrogance belongs to other places. As for al-Sagir (ṣāghir), he is the humiliated one, and al-saghar (ṣaghār) is humiliation. Al-Zajjaj said: Iblis was arrogant by refusing to prostrate, so Allah informed him that he was humiliated because of that.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 14–15:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: "Give me respite"﴾, that is, grant me delay and postpone me, ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾. He wanted to cross the bridge of death, and he asked for immortality, but He did not answer him to that, and granted him respite until the first blast, when all creation dies. The duration of his respite has been made clear in (al-Hijr) by His saying: ﴿until the Day of the appointed time﴾ [al-Hijr 15:38]. Regarding what he asked to be respited for, there are two opinions.

One of them: death. The second: the punishment. If it is said: how was it said to him, ﴿Indeed, you are of those given respite﴾, when there is no one more granted respite than him? The answer: those upon whom the Hour is established are given respite until that time by their terms, so he is one of them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Because You have led me astray﴾, regarding the meaning of this "leading astray" (al-ighwa') there are two opinions.

One of them: that it means misguidance (al-idlal), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the majority (al-jumhur).

The second: that it means destruction (al-ihlak), and from it is His saying: ﴿So they will meet with error (ghayya)﴾ [Maryam: 59], that is, destruction. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Regarding the meaning of "fa-bima" (so because of what) there are two opinions. (p-176) One of them: that it carries the sense of an oath, meaning: by Your leading me astray.

The second: that it carries the sense of a conditional (al-jaza'), meaning: because You led me astray, and for the sake of the fact that You led me astray, ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: meaning, on Your path. A similar usage is their saying: "Zayd struck the back and the belly" (i.e., struck on the back and the belly). Regarding what is meant by "the path" (al-sirat) here, there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the road to Makkah, said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr; as if the intent is to bar them from the Hajj.

The second: that it is Islam, said by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, and Muqatil.

The third: that it is the truth (al-haqq), said by Mujahid.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 17:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and on their right and on their left﴾. Concerning this there are seven opinions.

The first: "from before them" means I will cast doubt upon them regarding their Hereafter; "and from behind them" means I will make them desire their worldly life; "and on their right" means from the direction of their good deeds; "and on their left" means from the direction of their evil deeds. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is like the first, except that they made "from before them" the World (al-Dunya) and "from behind them" the Hereafter. This was said by al-Nakha'i and al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba.

The third: it is like the second, except that they made "on their right" from the direction of the Truth, whom I will turn away from it, and "on their left" from the direction of falsehood, to which I will drive them. This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The fourth: "from before them" from the path of the Truth, and "from behind them" from the path of falsehood; "on their right" from the direction of their Hereafter; "on their left" from the matter of this world. This was said by Abu Salih.

The fifth: "from before them" and "on their right" are from where they can see, and "from behind them" and "on their left" are from where they cannot see. This was also transmitted from Mujahid.

The sixth: the meaning is that I will act toward them in misguidance from all their directions. This was said by al-Zajjaj and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Accordingly, the mention of these directions is for emphasis and intensification.

The seventh: "from before them" refers to what remains of their lifespans, so they do not hasten to obedience in it; "and from behind them" refers to what has passed of their lifespans, so they do not repent of disobedience in it; "and on their right" from the direction of wealth, so they do not spend it in what is praiseworthy; "and on their left" from the direction of poverty, so they do not refrain in it from what is forbidden. This was said by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: "grateful" means monotheists (muwahhidin). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "grateful for Your blessing." This was said by Muqatil.

If it is said: From where did Iblis know this? We have already given the answer to this in surah (al-Nisa').

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 18–19:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Go out from it, reviled and expelled.﴾ Al-A'mash recited "مَذُومًا" (madhuman), with a ḍammah on the dhal (p-178), without a hamzah. Al-Farra' said: al-dha'm (الذَّأْم) is blame (al-dhamm). It is said: dha'amtu al-rajul, o'dha'uhu dha'man; and dhammamtuhu, udhimmuhu dhamman; and dhimtuhu, adhimuhu dhaiman. It is said: rajulun madhu'um, and madhmum, and madhim, with one meaning. Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"They remained until they all perished, in one place, and all of them were reviled."

Ibn Qutaybah said: al-madhu'um is one who is blamed with the most emphatic blame. And al-madhur (المَدْحُور) is one who is pushed away and distanced. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of al-madhu'um is the same as the meaning of al-madhmum, and al-madhur is one distanced from the mercy of Allah. As for the lam in "la-amla'anna" (لأمْلَأنَّ), it is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam); and the speech carries the sense of a conditional and its response, as if it were said to him: whoever follows you, I will punish him; so the lam entered for emphasis and affirmation. Thus the lam in "la-amla'anna" is the lam of oath, and the lam in ﴿for whoever follows you﴾ is a preparatory lam (lam al-tawti'ah) for it. As for his saying "minhum" (مِنهم), Ibn al-Anbari said: the ha' and the mim refer to the children of Adam, because when He said: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11], He was addressing the children of Adam; then He turned to them and said: ﴿whoever follows you from among them﴾, making them absent, because addressing them in this place would cause confusion; and the Arabs shift from address to the third person, and from the third person to address. And whoever holds that ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ is addressed to Adam said: the ha' and the mim return to his offspring, because mention of him suffices for mention of them; and the Arabs suffice with mentioning the father instead of the children when the meaning is clear and confusion is removed. The poet said:

"I see al-Khaṭafī surpassing al-Farazdaq in his poetry, but Khayr is better than Kulayb, Mujashi'."

He meant: I see the son of al-Khaṭafī, and he sufficed with al-Khaṭafī for his son.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾ means the disobedient children of Adam and their companions from the devils.

(p-179) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them﴾. It has been said: the whisper (waswasah) is the concealing of a sound. Ibn Faris said: al-waswas is the sound of ornaments, and from it comes the whisper of Satan (waswas al-shaytan). "Lahuma" here means "ilayhima" (to them). ﴿that he might reveal to them﴾, meaning that he might make appear to them (ma wuwiriya 'anhuma), that is, what was concealed (satara) from them. It has also been said that the lam in "liyubdiya" is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), meaning that the outcome of the whispering led to the exposure of their private parts, though the whispering was not done for the sake of that exposure.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except that you become two angels﴾. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "He only forbade you out of dislike that you become two angels." Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is, "except that you not become," and he dispensed with "an" from "la" and omitted it. If it is asked: how did Adam yield to Iblis, aspiring to become an angel, when he had witnessed the angels prostrating to him? There are two answers to this.

The first: he knew their nearness to God and the gathering of most of them around His Throne, so he aspired to that. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: the meaning is, "except that you become long-lived along with the angels," ﴿or that you become of the eternal ones﴾, who never die. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ya'la ibn Hakim narrated from Ibn Kathir: ﴿an takuna malakayn﴾ with a kasra on the lam (malakayni), and this is the reading of al-Zuhri.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 21–25:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he swore to them both﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He swore an oath to them both. ﴿And he brought them down﴾ into disobedience, by deceiving them.

Ibn Abbas said: He deceived them with the oath, and Adam did not think that anyone would swear by Allah falsely.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they tasted the tree﴾, that is, when they tasted the fruit of the tree. Al-Zajjaj said: This indicates that they merely tasted it, a tasting, and did not go to excess in eating. The word "sawʾah" (private parts) is a metaphor for the genitals, and there is no origin for naming it so. The meaning of "ṭafiqa" (they began) is that they set about the action. The more common form is "ṭafiqa yaṭfuqu," though it has also been transmitted as "ṭafiqa yaṭfiqu" with a kasra on the fa'. The meaning of "yakhṣifān" (they began to join together) is that they placed one leaf upon another, and from this comes the term for the one who patches a sandal: "khiṣāf."

In the verse there is evidence that exposing the private parts is ugly from the time of Adam. Do you not see His saying: ﴿to make apparent to them what was concealed from them of their private parts﴾? They hastened to cover themselves because of the ugliness of being uncovered. It was also said: the private parts were called "sawʾah" (that which causes harm) because uncovering them harms their owner. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Their clothing was light over their private parts, so that neither could see the nakedness of the other. When they committed the sin, their private parts became apparent to them.

Al-Hasan recited "sawʾatuhumā" in the singular form. Likewise he recited "yakhṣifān" with a kasra on the ya' and the kha' with the ṣad doubled. Al-Zuhri recited it with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the kha' with the ṣad doubled. Regarding the leaves there are two opinions.

One: the leaves of the fig tree, said by Ibn Abbas. Two: the leaves of the banana plant, mentioned by the exegetes. What follows has already been explained up to His saying: ﴿He said: In it you will live﴾, meaning the earth.

The readers differed concerning the tā' in "takhrujūn." Ibn Kathir, ʿĀṣim, and Abu ʿAmr read it with a damma on the tā' and a fatha on the rā' here; and in al-Rum: ﴿And thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Rum 19]; in al-Zukhruf: ﴿thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Zukhruf 11]; and in al-Jathiyah: ﴿they will not be brought out from it﴾ [al-Jathiyah 35]. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read all of these with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the rā'. Ibn ʿĀmir read the tā' with a fatha only in al-Aʿraf. As for the one in al-Rum: ﴿when you come out﴾ [al-Rum 25], and in ﴿Asaʾa sāʾil﴾: ﴿the Day they come out﴾ [al-Maʿarij 43], they are both with a fatha without any disagreement.

**(p-182)** The first meaning is "We created for you." The second is "We inspired you with the manner of making it." The third is "We sent down the rain, which is the cause of the growth of that which is made into clothing."

Most readers recited *"wa-rīshan"* (وَرِيشًا). Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, Qatādah, al-Mufaḍḍal, and Abān from ʿĀṣim recited *"wa-riyāshan"* (وَرِياشًا), with an alif. Al-Farrāʾ said: "*Al-riyāsh* may be the plural of *al-rīsh*, and it may also mean the same as *al-rīsh*, as they say *lubs* and *libās*." The poet said:

*When they uncovered the garment from him, they wiped him with the fingertips of a child who adorned the gazelle-like, patterned one.*

Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said: *"al-riyāsh"* is wealth. ʿAṭāʾ said: wealth and comfort. Ibn Zayd said: *al-rīsh* is beauty. Maʿbad al-Juhanī said: *al-rīsh* is provision. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-rīsh* and *al-riyāsh* are what appears of clothing. Al-Zajjāj said: *al-rīsh* is clothing and everything that covers a person in his body and his livelihood. It is said: "So-and-so *tarayyasha*," meaning he came to have what he lives on. Sībawayh cited:

*My riyāsh is from you, and my desire is with you, even if your visits are infrequent.*

According to the view of most scholars, *al-rīsh* and *al-riyāsh* have the same meaning. Qutrub said: *al-rīsh* and *al-riyāsh* are one. Sufyān al-Thawrī said: *al-rīsh* is wealth, and *al-riyāsh* is garments.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*And the garment of piety*﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamzah recited *"wa-libāsu al-taqwā"* (وَلِباسُ التَّقْوى) with a *rafʿ* (nominative). Ibn ʿĀmir, Nāfiʿ, and al-Kisāʾī recited it with a *naṣb* (accusative) on *al-libās*. Al-Zajjāj said: whoever puts *al-libās* in the accusative conjoins it to *al-rīsh*. Whoever puts it in the nominative, it may be a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and it may be nominative by an implied "*huwa*" (it). The meaning: "And it is the garment of piety," that is, covering the nakedness is the garment of the pious.

Regarding "the garment of piety," the exegetes have ten opinions.

First: it is good comportment. This was said by ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, and al-Dhayyāl ibn ʿAmr narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās. Second: righteous deeds, narrated by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās. Third: faith, said by Qatādah, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Suddī. On this view, it is called the garment of piety because it protects from punishment. Fourth: fear of God, exalted is He, said by ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr. Fifth: modesty, said by Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ibn al-Anbārī. Sixth: covering the nakedness for prayer, said by Ibn Zayd. Seventh: that it is the coat of mail and all other instruments of war, said by Zayd ibn ʿAlī. Eighth: chastity, said by Ibn al-Sāʾib. Ninth: that it is what one protects oneself with from heat and cold, said by Ibn Baḥr. Tenth: the meaning is that what the pious wear in the Hereafter is better than what the people of this world wear, narrated by ʿUthmān ibn ʿAṭāʾ from his father.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*That is better*﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is that the garment of piety is better than clothing, because the immoral person, even if his garment is fine, is still exposed in his nakedness. "*Dhālika*" (that) is redundant. A poet expressed this meaning:

*I see the one who has no shame and no trustworthiness in the midst of the people as if he were naked.*

Ibn al-Anbārī said: it is also said that "the garment of piety" is the first garment, and He repeated it when He informed that it is better than being naked, since they used to worship in the pre-Islamic period by going naked during the circumambulation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿*That is among the signs of God*﴾. Muqātil said: He means that the garments and the wealth are among the signs of God and His craftsmanship, so that they may remember and take heed in His craftsmanship.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 27:

The first: that it was light. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas; and we have mentioned it from Ibn Munabbih.

The second: that it was like a fingernail (zufr); when they ate, nothing remained on them of it except the fingernail. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd also said this.

The third: that it was taqwa (God-consciousness). This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that it was of the garments of Paradise. This was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿That He might show them their private parts﴾ — meaning, that each of them might show the other his private part. ﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you do not see them﴾. Mujahid said: "His tribe" refers to the jinn and the devils. Ibn 'Abbas said: God made them flow through the sons of Adam like blood, and the chests of the sons of Adam are their dwellings; so they see the sons of Adam, while the sons of Adam do not see them.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made the devils allies to those who do not believe﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: We gave them authority over them, so that they increase them in their error. Abu Sulayman said: We made them supporters of those people.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they commit an abomination﴾, concerning whom this verse refers there are three opinions.

The first: they are those who used to circumambulate the House (the Kaaba) naked. The abomination is the uncovering of the private parts. This was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Suddi also said so.

(p-185) The second: they are those who made the sa'iba (free-roaming camel), the wasila (she-camel given as a gift), and the ham (stallion camel), and that is the abomination. Abu Salih related this meaning from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they are the polytheists, and the abomination is shirk (associating partners with God). This was said by al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Al-Zajjaj said: God, mighty and majestic, informed them that He does not command abomination, because His wisdom indicates that He only does what is deemed good. And al-qist (justice) means 'adl (justice). And 'adl is that whose ugliness is firmly established in souls?!

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And set your faces upright at every place of prostration﴾. On this there are four opinions.

The first: when prayer comes due while you are near a mosque, pray in it, and let none of you say, "I will pray in my own mosque." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak, and Ibn Qutaybah (d. 276 AH) chose it.

The second: face toward the Kaaba wherever you are during prayer. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

The third: make your prostration purely for Allah, exalted is He, to the exclusion of anyone else. This was said by al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas.

The fourth: aim for the mosque at the time of every prayer, as a command to attend congregation for it. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. And concerning His saying, (﴿and call upon Him﴾), there are two opinions.

One: that it means worship. The second: that it means supplication. And concerning His saying, ﴿sincere in religion to Him﴾, there are two opinions.

One: singling Him out in worship. The second: monotheists, not associating partners with Him.

And concerning His saying, ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: just as He originated you as happy and wretched, so you will be resurrected. ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah narrated this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was said by Mujahid, al-Qurazi, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and al-Farra'.

The second: just as you were created by His power, so He will bring you back. al-ʿAwfi narrated this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, and al-Zajjaj, who said: this statement is connected to His saying, ﴿In it you will live, and in it you will die﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 25].

The third: just as He originated you, you possess nothing, so you will return. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 30:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A group He has guided﴾. Al-Farra' said: He put "a group" (farīqan) in the accusative by [governing it by] "you will return" (taʿūdūna). Ibn al-Anbari said: "a group" and "a group" (farīqan wa-farīqan) are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in "you will return" (taʿūdūna). He means: you will return just as He originated your creation, differing, some of you happy (suʿadāʾ) and some of you wretched (ashqiyāʾ).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Misguidance has become due for them﴾. That is: by the ancient decree (al-kalima al-qadīma) and the preceding will (al-irada al-sabiqa).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 31:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment﴾. The occasion of its revelation: some of the Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked, the men by day and the women by night, and a woman would tie strips of cloth around her private parts and say:

"Today some or all of it appears, and what appears of it, I do not make lawful."

Then this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn ʿAbbas. Abu Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said: when they performed Hajj and departed from Mina, it was not fitting for anyone among them, according to the religion they had devised, to circumambulate in his garments; he would take them off until he had completed his circumambulation, so this verse was revealed. Al-Zuhri said: the Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked, except the Hums (the Quraysh and their allies). Whoever came from other than them would take off his clothes and circumambulate in the garments of the Hums. If he could not find anyone from the Hums to lend him clothing, he would cast off his clothes and circumambulate naked. And if he circumambulated in his own clothes, he would make them forbidden to him once he had finished the circumambulation. Therefore this verse came. Regarding this adornment there are two opinions.

The first: it means clothing. Within this there are three views. One: it was revealed concerning covering the private parts during circumambulation; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan along with a group. The second: it was revealed concerning covering the private parts during prayer; this was said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. The third: it was revealed concerning adorning oneself with the finest garments at gatherings and festivals; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The second: the intended meaning of adornment is the comb; this was said by Abu Razin.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And eat and drink﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: the people of the Jahiliyya would not eat fat during the days of their Hajj, and would take from food only sustenance, out of veneration for their pilgrimage. So He revealed: ﴿And eat and drink﴾. Regarding His saying: ﴿And do not be excessive﴾ there are four opinions.

One: do not be excessive by forbidding what Allah has made lawful for you; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: do not eat what is forbidden, for that is excess; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: do not associate partners (with Allah); here excess means association; this was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: do not eat from the lawful beyond need; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

It is related that al-Rashid had a skilled Christian physician, and he said to ʿAli ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid: "There is nothing of the science of medicine in your Book." ʿAli said: "Allah, Exalted is He, has gathered medicine into half a verse of our Book." He asked: "What is it?" He said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And eat and drink and do not be excessive﴾. The Christian said: "Nothing about medicine is transmitted from your Prophet." He said: "Our Messenger has gathered the science of medicine into few words." He asked: "And what are they?" He said: "The stomach is the house of disease, and restraint is the head of medicine, and accustom every body to what it is used to." The Christian said: "Your Book and your Prophet have left nothing of medicine for Galen."

The author (Ibn al-Jawzi) said: This is how this story has been transmitted, except that this hadith attributed in it to the Prophet (ﷺ) is not authentic. Indeed, there have come from him (ﷺ) concerning medicine hadiths which I have mentioned in my book "Laqt al-Manafi fi al-Tibb" (Gleaning of Benefits in Medicine).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 32:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah⁠﻿...﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: The polytheists reproached the Muslims because they wore clothes during the circumambulation (tawaf) and ate good things, so this was revealed. Abu Salih related it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: They used to forbid things that Allah had made lawful, from crops and other things, so this verse was revealed. Ibn Abi Talha related it from Ibn Abbas.

The third: It was revealed concerning their circumambulation of the House naked. This was said by Tawus and Ata. Regarding "the adornment of Allah" there are two opinions.

One of them: It is the covering of the private parts. The meaning is: Who has forbidden you to wear, in your circumambulation, that which covers you?

The second: It is the adornment of clothing. Regarding "the good things" there are two opinions.

One of them: They are the lawful. The second: They are the pleasant. Then, regarding what is meant by them, there are three opinions.

The first: They are the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham, which they had forbidden. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada.

The second: They are ghee, milk and meat, which they had forbidden during the state of ihram. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The third: They are the tilth (crops), the livestock and the milk. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely [for them] on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: "Khalisatan" (purely) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from a concealed lam, its estimation being: "they are for those who believed in the life of this world, shared," and "they are for them in the Hereafter, purely," so the lam was deleted for the clarity of its meaning, as the Arabs delete things whose omission does not cause confusion.

The poet said:

"My daughter says, when she saw me pale: 'As if food were a physician protecting you.'
A succession of calamities falls upon my brothers,
so they have whitened my head, and calamities do whiten."

He meant: So I said to her: "That which has made you see me thus is a succession of calamities," deleting it because the meaning was clear.

The exegetes said: The polytheists shared with the believers in the good things, so they ate, wore and married, but then Allah makes the good things purely for the believers in the Hereafter, and there is nothing of them for the polytheists. It was also said: "Purely" means free from harm or sin. Nafi' read "khalisatun" with a nominative ending. Al-Zajjaj said: He made it nominative as a predicate after a predicate, as you say: "Zayd is wise, discerning." The meaning: "Say: they are established for those who believed in this world, purely on the Day of Resurrection."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus do We detail the verses⁠﻿...﴾ That is: Thus do We clarify them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies﴾. Hamza recited (rabbiya al-fawahisha) with the letter ya' (ي) of "rabbi" sukun (silent). ﴿those of them that are apparent and those that are concealed﴾. On this there are six opinions.

The first: that what is meant by them is fornication (al-zina). "Those that are apparent" is its openness, and "those that are concealed" is its secrecy. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this.

The second: that "those that are apparent" is marrying the mothers (nikah al-ummahat), and "those that are concealed" is fornication. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn also said this.

The third: that "those that are apparent" is marrying the wives of one's sons and fathers, combining two sisters, and marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt; and "those that are concealed" is fornication. This was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that "those that are apparent" is fornication, and "those that are concealed" is coitus interruptus (al-'azl). This was said by Shurayh.

The fifth: that "those that are apparent" is the circumambulation of the Jahiliyya while naked, and "those that are concealed" is fornication. This was said by Mujahid.

(p-191) The sixth: that it is general, encompassing all sins. Then, regarding "those that are apparent and those that are concealed," there are two views.

One of them: that the apparent is the open, and the concealed is the secret. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The second: that "those that are apparent" are the actions of the limbs, and "those that are concealed" are the beliefs of the hearts. This was said by al-Mawardi.

Regarding (al-ithm) there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the sin that does not entail a prescribed punishment (hadd). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Farra'.

The second: that it means all sins. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: that it is wine (al-khamr). This was said by al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Ibn al-Anbari said: A man recited to us in the assembly of Tha'lab, in his presence, and claimed that Abu 'Ubayda had recited to him:

"We drink al-ithm openly from the cup, and we see the wine-jar (al-mutk) lent among us."

Abu al-'Abbas said: I do not know this, nor do I know that al-ithm means wine in the speech of the Arabs. Another man recited to us:

"I drank al-ithm until my reason was lost; likewise al-ithm takes away the minds."

Abu Bakr said: This verse is not known even in the poetry of those whose poetry is cited as evidence, and I have not seen anyone among the scholars of rare vocabulary (ashab al-gharib) include al-ithm among the names of wine, nor did the Arabs name it thus in the Jahiliyya or in Islam.

If it is said: wine falls under al-ithm, that is correct, but not because it is one of its names.

If it is said: how is al-ithm distinguished from the indecencies, when every indecency contains sin? The answer: every indecency is a sin, but not every sin is an indecency; so al-ithm is for every blameworthy act, while the indecency (al-fahisha) is the grievous one. As for al-baghy, al-Farra' said: it is arrogance over people. (p-192)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you associate with Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "an" is in the accusative; so the meaning is: He has forbidden the indecencies, and He has forbidden shirk. And al-sultan is the proof.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾. This is general in forbidding speaking about the religion without certainty.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for every nation there is a term﴾. The occasion of its revelation: they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for the punishment, and it was revealed. This was related by Muqatil. Regarding the term (ajal), there are two opinions.

One of them: it is the term of the punishment. The second: it is the term of life. Al-Zajjaj said: the ajal is the appointed time. ﴿So when their term comes, they will not delay an hour﴾. The meaning: nor by less than an hour. He mentioned the hour (sa'a) only because it is the smallest of the names of time.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 35–37:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among yourselves﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: there is an implied "then obey them" (fa-ati'uhum). The meaning of "in" (imma) has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah (2:38). The rest is clear up to His saying: ﴿their portion of the Book will reach them﴾. Regarding its meaning there are seven opinions.

The first: what has been decreed for them of good and evil. This is narrated by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: their portion of deeds, for which they will be recompensed. This is narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: what He has written for them of misguidance and guidance. This is said by al-Hasan. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: of happiness and wretchedness.

The fourth: what He has written for them of provisions, lifespans and deeds. This is said by al-Rabi', al-Qurazi and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: what He has written for them of punishment. This is said by 'Ikrimah, Abu Salih and al-Suddi.

The sixth: what Allah the Exalted has reported in all the Books: that whoever fabricates a lie against Allah, his face will be blackened. This is said by Muqatil.

The seventh: what He has reported in the Book of their recompense, like His saying: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾ [al-Layl 92:14]. This is said by al-Zajjaj. So, regarding "the Book," there are five opinions.

One: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Two: it is all the Books of Allah. Three: it is the Qur'an. Four: it is the Book of their deeds. Five: it is the decree (al-qada').

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until, when our messengers come to them﴾. Regarding them there are three opinions. One: they are the assistants of the Angel of Death. This is said by al-Nakha'i. Two: it is the Angel of Death alone. This is said by Muqatil. Three: they are the angels of punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

Regarding His saying "yatawaffawnahum" (they take them in death) there are three opinions.

One: they take them in death. This is said by the majority. Two: they take them by gathering them to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. This is said by al-Hasan. Three: they take them into punishment, as you say, "I killed so-and-so with torment," even if he did not die. This is said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Where is what you used to call upon﴾, i.e., worship, ﴿besides Allah?﴾ This is a question of rebuke and reproach. Muqatil said: the meaning is, let them protect you from the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿they have strayed from us﴾ is that they have vanished and gone away, so they will acknowledge at the time of their death that they were disbelievers. Others said: that acknowledgment will occur on the Day of Resurrection.

The fifth: what He has written for them of punishment. This is said by 'Ikrimah, Abu Salih and al-Suddi.

The sixth: what Allah the Exalted has reported in all the Books: that whoever fabricates a lie against Allah, his face will be blackened. This is said by Muqatil.

The seventh: what He has reported in the Book of their recompense, like His saying: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾ [al-Layl 92:14]. This is said by al-Zajjaj. So, regarding "the Book," there are five opinions.

One: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Two: it is all the Books of Allah. Three: it is the Qur'an. Four: it is the Book of their deeds. Five: it is the decree (al-qada').

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until, when our messengers come to them﴾. Regarding them there are three opinions. One: they are the assistants of the Angel of Death. This is said by al-Nakha'i. Two: it is the Angel of Death alone. This is said by Muqatil. Three: they are the angels of punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

Regarding His saying "yatawaffawnahum" (they take them in death) there are three opinions.

One: they take them in death. This is said by the majority. Two: they take them by gathering them to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. This is said by al-Hasan. Three: they take them into punishment, as you say, "I killed so-and-so with torment," even if he did not die. This is said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Where is what you used to call upon﴾, i.e., worship, ﴿besides Allah?﴾ This is a question of rebuke and reproach. Muqatil said: the meaning is, let them protect you from the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿they have strayed from us﴾ is that they have vanished and gone away, so they will acknowledge at the time of their death that they were disbelievers. Others said: that acknowledgment will occur on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 38:

His saying, Most High: ﴿He will say, "Enter"﴾. God Most High says this to them through the angels, because God Most High does not speak to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Qutaybah said: "fi" (in) here has the meaning of "ma'a" (with).

Regarding His saying: ﴿there have passed away before you﴾, there are two views.

One: they passed on to the punishment.

The second: they passed away in time, meaning the disbelievers of the former nations.

His saying, Most High: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾. This is the brotherhood of religion and creed, not the brotherhood of lineage. Ibn 'Abbas said: they curse those who were before them. Muqatil said: whenever a people of one creed enters, they curse the people of their creed; so the Jews curse the Jews, the Christians the Christians, and the polytheists the polytheists, and the followers curse the leaders, and they say: "You are the ones who brought this upon us when we obeyed you." Al-Zajjaj said: they only cursed one another because some of them went astray by following others. (p-195) His saying, Most High: ﴿until, when they have all gathered together therein﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: i.e., "tadaraku" (they overtook one another), so the "ta" was assimilated into the "dal," and the alif was introduced so that the sukun would be preserved for what follows; he means: they followed one another into it and gathered together.

His saying, Most High: ﴿the last of them will say to the first of them﴾. There are three views concerning it.

One: the last nation says to the first nation; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the last people of the era say to their first ones, those who established that religion for them; this is related from al-Suddi. The third: the last of them to enter the Fire, who are the followers, say to the first of them to enter, who are the leaders; this is related from Muqatil.

His saying, Most High: ﴿These have led us astray﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they legislated for us that we should take gods besides You.

His saying, Most High: ﴿so give them a double punishment﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., a punishment that is multiplied.

His saying, Most High: ﴿He will say, "For each there is double, but you do not know"﴾. I.e., a multiplied punishment, but you do not know.

Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "ya'lamun" (they know) with the yā'. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that each group does not know the measure of the punishment of the other group. The rest read "ta'lamun" (you know) with the tā', and in it there are two aspects, which al-Zajjaj mentioned.

One: you, the addressees, do not know what punishment is due to each group.

The second: O people of the world, you do not know the measure of that. It was said: the followers only sought the doubling of the leaders' punishment so that one of the two punishments would be for disbelief and the other for leading them astray. So they were answered: ﴿For each there is double﴾, i.e., just as the leaders have that, you have a punishment for disbelief and a punishment for following.

His saying: ﴿So you had no superiority over us﴾. There are two views concerning it.

One: in disbelief, we and you are alike in it; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: in lightening of the punishment; this is related from Mujahid.
(p-196) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿because of what you used to earn﴾. Muqatil said: [i.e., from polytheism and denial (of the signs of Allah)].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs﴾, meaning: Our proofs and signs that point to the Oneness of God and the prophethood of the prophets, and who were too arrogant to believe in them ﴿the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "tufattahu" with a ta', and they doubled the second ta'. Abu 'Amr read "la taftahu" with a light ta' and a sukun on the fa'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "la yaftahu" with a ya' and a light dhamma. Al-Yazidi, according to his own choice, read "la tuftahu" with an open ta'. ﴿abwabu as-sama'i﴾ with a fatha on the ba', as if pointing to their deeds. Al-Hasan read with an open ya' and the doors in the accusative, as if pointing to God, Mighty and Majestic. There are four opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

The first: the gates of heaven will not be opened for their souls. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and al-Suddi among others, and the hadiths bear witness to it.

The second: it will not be opened for their deeds. Narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it will not be opened for their deeds nor for their supplication. Narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it will not be opened for their souls nor for their deeds. Said by Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil. (p-197) Regarding "as-sama'" there are two views.

One: that it is the well-known heaven, and this is the prevalent view.

The second: that the meaning is: the gates of Paradise will not be opened for them and they will not enter it, because Paradise is in the heaven. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. The "jamal" is the well-known animal. If someone asks: why did He single out the camel over the rest of the beasts, when among them are some greater than it? There are two answers.

One: striking the example with the camel achieves the intended purpose, which is that they will not enter Paradise, just as the camel does not enter the hole of a needle. Had He mentioned something larger or smaller, it would also be permissible. People say: "So-and-so is not worth a dirham," and "This will not avail you a fatil," though we find things smaller than the dirham and the fatil.

Two: the camel is greater in importance among the Arabs than the rest of the beasts, for they place it first in strength over others, since it is loaded and rises with its burden where others do not. For this reason He marvelled them at the creation of camels, saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17], so God preferred mentioning it over others for this meaning. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both answers. He said: Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he read "hatta yalija al-jumulu" with a dhamma on the jim and a doubled mim, and said: it is a thick rope (qals).

The author said: this is the reading of Abu Razin, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn Ya'mur, and Aban from 'Asim. He said: Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "hatta yalija al-jamalu" with a dhamma on the jim, a fatha on the mim, and lightened. (p-198) I say: this is the reading of Qatada, and it has been related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he read "hatta yalija al-jumlu" with a dhamma on the jim and a sukun on the mim. I say: this is the reading of 'Ikrimah.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "al-jumlu" may carry two meanings: it may mean "al-jummal" (a thick rope), and it may mean a group (jumla) of camels; it is said that its plural is "jumal," as one says "hujrah" and "hujar," "zulmah" and "zulim." Likewise, whoever reads "al-jaml" may say "al-jamal," meaning "al-jummal," or "al-jumlu," the plural of "jumlah," like "busrah" and "busr." The adherents of these readings say that "al-habl" and "al-hibal" are more similar to the needle and threads than camels are. Ata' ibn Yasar narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he read "al-jumulu" with dhammas on the jim and the mim, and lightened; this is the reading of al-Dahhak and al-Jahdari. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' read "al-jamalu" with a fatha on the jim and a light sukun on the mim.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿through the eye of the needle﴾. Al-summ in the language means the hole. It has three forms: with a fatha on the sin, which is the reading of most readers; with a dhamma, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Razin, Qatada, Ibn Muhaysin, and Talhah ibn Musarrif; and with a kasra, which is the reading of Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, Abu Nahik, and al-Asma'i from Nafi'. Ibn al-Qasim said: "al-khayyat" is "al-mikhyat," like "al-lihaf" and "al-milhaf," and "al-qiram" and "al-miqram." Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Razin, and Abu Mijlaz read: "fi sammi al-makhit." Al-Zajjaj said: "al-khiyat" is the needle, and its summ is its hole. The meaning is that they will not enter Paradise, ever. Ibn Qutaybah said: this is like saying: "That will not happen until the crow turns white and pitch becomes white."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminals﴾, meaning: in the same way We recompense the disbelievers, that they will not enter Paradise.

(p-199) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them there will be a bed (mihad) of Hell﴾. Al-mihad means al-firash (bedding, a bed).

Regarding the meaning of al-ghawashi (the coverings), there are three opinions.

The first: they are the blankets (al-luhaf). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Qurazi, and Ibn Zayd. The second: it is the smoke that covers them from above, said by 'Ikrima. The third: it is a covering above a covering of fire, said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The wrongdoers (al-zalimun) here are the disbelievers."

(p-199) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them there will be a bed (mihad) of Hell﴾. Al-mihad means al-firash (bedding, a bed).

Regarding the meaning of al-ghawashi (the coverings), there are three opinions.

The first: they are the blankets (al-luhaf). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Qurazi, and Ibn Zayd. The second: it is the smoke that covers them from above, said by 'Ikrima. The third: it is a covering above a covering of fire, said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The wrongdoers (al-zalimun) here are the disbelievers."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 43:

Allah's words: ﴿And We will remove whatever ill will is in their breasts﴾. Regarding who is meant by this verse, there are four opinions.

The first is that they are the people of Badr. Al-Hasan narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "By Allah, it was about us, the people of Badr, that this was revealed: ﴿And We will remove whatever ill will is in their breasts﴾." And Amr ibn al-Sharid narrated from Ali that he said: "I hope that I, Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr are among those of whom Allah said: ﴿And We will remove whatever ill will is in their breasts﴾."

The second is that they are the people of grudges from the time of ignorance (jahiliyya) who became Muslim. Kuthayyir al-Nawwa narrated from Abu Ja'far, who said: "This verse was revealed about Ali, Abu Bakr and Umar." I said to Abu Ja'far: "Which ill will is it?" He said: "The ill will of the Jahiliyya. There had been something between Banu Hashim and Banu Taym and Banu Adi during the Jahiliyya. When these men embraced Islam, they loved one another. Then Abu Bakr was seized by a pain in the side, and Ali began to warm his hand and rub it on Abu Bakr's side, and so this verse was revealed."

The third is that they are ten of the Companions: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Talha, al-Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Sa'id ibn Zayd, and Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. This was said by Abu Salih.

The fourth is that it describes the people of Paradise when they enter it. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The believers will be delivered from the Fire and will be detained on a bridge between Paradise and the Fire. When they have been purified and cleansed, they will be permitted to enter Paradise. By Him in whose hand my soul is, one of them will be more guided to his station in Paradise than he was to his station in this world." Ibn Abbas said: "The first thing the people of Paradise do upon entering Paradise is that two springs are presented to them. They drink from one of the two springs, and Allah removes from their hearts any ill will and whatever else was in them in the world. Then they enter the other spring and wash in it, and their colours become radiant, their faces become clear, and the radiance of bliss appears upon them."

As for al-Naz' (removal), it is uprooting a thing from its place. Al-Ghill (ill will) is the grudge hidden in the breast.

Ibn Qutayba said: al-Ghill is envy and enmity.

Allah's words: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: "He guided us when He brought us to this." Ibn Abbas said: they mean what they reached of Allah's good pleasure and honour. Asim ibn Damra narrated from Ali, may Allah honour his face, that he said: "The young boys (wildan) will meet them as though they were scattered pearls, and they will circle around them as a returning traveller is circled by his close friend. They will give them good news of what Allah has prepared for them, and they will go to their wives and give them good news, and joy will overwhelm them, so they will stand at the threshold of the door and say: 'Did you see him? Did you see him?' He will come to his dwelling and look at its foundation, and behold, it is a rock of pearls. Then he will raise his gaze, and were it not that Allah made it bearable for him, his sight would be taken away. Then he will look below that, and behold, there are couches woven with gold, raised cushions, and scattered carpets. At that point they will say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this. We would never have been guided had Allah not guided us﴾." All of them recited "wa-ma kunna" with the wa (conjunction), except Ibn Amir, who recited "ma kunna li-nahtadiya" without the wa. This is also how it is written in the codices of the people of Syria. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: the reason for dispensing with the wa is that the account is closely linked to what precedes it, and this close connection makes the conjunction unnecessary. A similar example is ﴿their fourth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf 18:22].

Allah's words: ﴿The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth﴾. This is the statement of the people of Paradise when they witnessed directly what the messengers had promised them. ﴿And they will be called out: "This is the Garden"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "tilkum" (this, plural address) because they had been promised it in the world, so it is as if it were said to them: "This is the one you were promised." It is also possible that this was said to them when they saw it before entering it.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Asim and Ibn Amir recited "ūrithtumūhā" without assimilation (idgham, merging of two consonants). Abu Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ūrithtumūhā" with assimilation, and they recited it the same way in [al-Zukhruf 43:72]. Abu Ali said: whoever omits the assimilation does so because the two letters differ in their points of articulation, and whoever assimilates does so because the taa and the thaa are both voiceless and close to each other. There are four opinions on the meaning of "ūrithtumūhā" (you have been given it as an inheritance).

The first is what Abu Hurayra narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "There is no one except that he has a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. As for the disbeliever, he inherits the believer's dwelling in the Fire, and the believer inherits the disbeliever's dwelling in Paradise." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿You have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do﴾. Some said: since Allah called the disbelievers dead by His words ﴿[They are] dead, not alive﴾ [al-Nahl 16:21], and called the believers living by His words ﴿to warn whoever is alive﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:70], He made the living inherit the dead.

The second is that they inherit it because of their deeds, since it was made a reward for their deeds and a recompense for them, as it is their consequence. This was related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The third is that entering Paradise is by Allah's mercy, while the distribution of ranks is according to deeds. Since its attainment is not in exchange for a counter-payment, it was called an inheritance. An inheritance is what you take without any exchange.

The fourth is that the meaning of inheritance here is that their affair returns to it, just as an inheritance returns to the heir.

(p-203) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ That is, of the punishment? This is a question of confirmation and reproach. ﴿They will say, "Yes."﴾ The majority of readers (qira'ah) read the ʿayn with a fatha throughout the Qur'an, but al-Kisa'i used to read it with a kasra. Al-Akhfash said: "They are two dialects."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then a caller will call out among them﴾ That is, a caller will proclaim. ﴿That the curse of Allah is upon﴾ Ibn Kathir, in the narration of Qunbul, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr and ʿAsim read "anna la'nata Allahi" with a light, sukun nun. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "an" with tashdid and "la'nata Allahi" with a fatha. Al-Akhfash said: the "wa-an" in His saying ﴿that this is the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 43], and His saying, "an la'nata Allahi," and His saying, "an ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾" [Yunus: 10], and "an qad wajadna," are all the heavy "anna" that has been lightened.

The poet said:

"In a company of youths
Like swords of India, they have known
That everyone who goes barefoot and shod is doomed."

(p-204) He also recited:

"Are you flattering, while I know that each of us
Is eager against whatever harms his companion?"

Its meaning: that indeed each of us; and "an qad wajadna" may mean "i.e." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The wrongdoers here are the disbelievers."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who bar from the way of Allah﴾ That is, the caller proclaimed that the curse of Allah is upon those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah, which is Islam. ﴿And seek to make it crooked﴾ is explained in [Al 'Imran: 99]. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter﴾ That is, they are disbelievers in the existence of the Hereafter.

(p-203) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ That is, of the punishment? This is a question of confirmation and reproach. ﴿They will say, "Yes."﴾ The majority of readers (qira'ah) read the ʿayn with a fatha throughout the Qur'an, but al-Kisa'i used to read it with a kasra.
