Al-Akhfash said: the "wa-an" in His saying ﴿that this is the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 43], and His saying, "an la'nata Allahi," and His saying, "an ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾" [Yunus: 10], and "an qad wajadna," are all the heavy "anna" that has been lightened.

The poet said:

"In a company of youths
Like swords of India, they have known
That everyone who goes barefoot and shod is doomed."

(p-204) He also recited:

"Are you flattering, while I know that each of us
Is eager against whatever harms his companion?"

Its meaning: that indeed each of us; and "an qad wajadna" may mean "i.e." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The wrongdoers here are the disbelievers."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who bar from the way of Allah﴾ That is, the caller proclaimed that the curse of Allah is upon those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah, which is Islam. ﴿And seek to make it crooked﴾ is explained in [Al 'Imran: 99]. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter﴾ That is, they are disbelievers in the existence of the Hereafter.

The Exalted said: ﴿And between them is a veil﴾, meaning: between Paradise and the Fire there is a barrier, and it is the wall which God the Exalted mentioned in His saying: ﴿So a wall with a gate will be struck between them﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. This wall was named al-A'raf (the heights) because of its height. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-A'raf is the wall between Paradise and the Fire, having a crest like the crest of a rooster. Abu Hurayrah said: al-A'raf are mountains between Paradise and the Fire, and they are upon their heights, meaning: upon their peaks, and their form is like the form of a rooster's crest. The linguists said: al-A'raf, according to the Arabs, is everything that rises up from the earth and is high; every elevated thing is called 'urf, and its plural is a'raf. (p-205) The poet said:

Every thick one, its flesh firm, bright like a banner fastened upon the heights.

And another said:

I have inherited the building of noble fathers *** who rose by glory to the heights of the structure.

Regarding "the companions of the A'raf" there are two opinions.

The first: they are from the children of Adam, as the majority said. Muqatil claimed that they are from the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically. Regarding their deeds there are nine opinions.

The first: they are people who were killed in the way of God because of the disobedience of their fathers; the disobedience of their fathers prevented them from entering Paradise, and their being killed in the way of God prevented them from entering the Fire. This is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: they are people whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal, so their good deeds did not reach entry into Paradise, nor did their bad deeds reach entry into the Fire. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Hudhayfah, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, al-Sha'bi, and Qatadah.

The third: they are the children of fornication; Salih, the freed slave of al-Tawamah, narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: they are righteous people, jurists and scholars; this was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. According to this, their staying on the A'raf is for recreation. (p-206) The fifth: they are people whose fathers were pleased with them but not their mothers, or whose mothers were pleased with them but not their fathers; 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid narrated it from Ibrahim.

The sixth: they are those who died in the interval (between prophets) and did not change their religion; this was said by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya.

The seventh: they are prophets; Ibn al-Anbari related it.

The eighth: they are the children of polytheists; al-Manjufi mentioned it in his tafsir.

The ninth: they are people who did deeds for God but showed off in their deeds; some scholars mentioned it.

The second opinion: they are angels; this was said by Abu Mijlaz. He was objected to, and it was said: they are men, so how can you say angels? He said: they are males, not females. It was also said: the meaning of His saying ﴿and upon the A'raf are men﴾ is: upon recognition of the people of Paradise from the people of the Fire; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari. But in this there is remoteness and disagreement among the exegetes.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will recognize each by their mark﴾, meaning: the companions of the A'raf recognize the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. The mark of the people of Paradise is the whiteness of faces, and the mark of the people of the Fire is the blackness of faces and blueness of eyes. Al-simah means the sign. They recognized people because they were on a high place from which they overlooked the people of Paradise and the Fire, and they called out, meaning: the companions of the A'raf, ﴿to the companions of Paradise: Peace be upon you﴾. Regarding His saying: ﴿They have not entered it, while they aspire﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: it is an informing from God the Exalted to us that the companions of the A'raf had not entered Paradise while they hoped to enter it; this was said by the majority.

The second: it is an informing from God the Exalted to the people of the A'raf that when they see a group being taken to Paradise, these have not entered it while they aspire to enter it; this is the saying of al-Suddi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 47:

﴿When their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ (p-207) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When their eyes are turned﴾ means the companions of the Heights (al-A'raf). Al-tilqa' is the direction of meeting, which is the direction of facing. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Tilqa' the companions of the Fire" means opposite them (hiyalahum).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men they will recognize by their marks﴾. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They will call out, "O Walid ibn al-Mughira! O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham! O As ibn Wa'il! O Umayya ibn Khalaf! O Ubayy ibn Khalaf! O all the leaders of the disbelievers! Of what use to you was your gathering of wealth and children in the world?" ﴿And what you used to be arrogant about﴾, that is: what you used to magnify yourselves against, [refusing] faith.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir, *Zād al-Masīr*) on Surah 7, verse 49:**

Regarding His words, ﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them any mercy?﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: the people of the Fire swore that the people of al-A'raf (the Heights, the place between Paradise and Hell) would enter the Fire along with them, and that Allah would not admit them into Paradise. Then Allah says to the people of the Fire: "Are these, meaning the people of al-A'raf, ﴿the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them any mercy?﴾ ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾" This was narrated by Wahb ibn Munabbih from Ibn Abbas. Hudhayfah said: "While the people of al-A'raf were there, their Lord looked down upon them and said to them: 'Enter Paradise, for I have forgiven you.'"

The second: the people of al-A'raf see in Paradise the poor and the needy whom the disbelievers used to mock, such as Salman, Suhayb, and Khabbab. So they call out to the disbelievers: ﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore﴾ while you were in the world, ﴿that Allah would not grant them any mercy?﴾ This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. According to this view, the speech of the people of al-A'raf ends at His words ﴿mercy﴾, and the rest is Allah's address to the people of Paradise. The exegetes have mentioned three opinions regarding His words ﴿Enter Paradise﴾:

The first: that it is an address from Allah to the people of al-A'raf, which we have already mentioned.

The second: that it is an address from Allah to the people of Paradise.

The third: that it is an address from the people of al-A'raf to the people of Paradise. Al-Zajjaj mentioned both of the first two and this one. According to this last view, the meaning of the words of the people of al-A'raf to the people of Paradise, ﴿Enter Paradise﴾, is: "Ascend to the lofty palaces and rise to the exalted abodes, for they have seen them in Paradise."

Mujahid narrated from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, who said: "The people of al-A'raf are brought to a river called al-Hayah (the Life), over which are golden rods adorned with pearls. They are immersed in it and then brought out, and a white mark appears on their necks by which they are recognized. It is said to them: 'Wish for whatever you desire, and you shall have seventy times as much.' They are the poor of the people of Paradise."

The people of the Fire will call out to the people of Paradise. Ibn 'Abbas said: When the people of al-A'raf (the heights, the place between Paradise and Hell) entered Paradise, the people of the Fire began to hope for relief after despair. They said: "O Lord, we have relatives among the people of Paradise. Permit us to see them and speak with them." So they looked at them and at the bliss they were in, and they recognized them. The people of Paradise looked at their relatives among the people of Hell, and did not recognize them, for their faces had blackened and they had become a different kind of creation. The people of the Fire then called out to the people of Paradise by their names and told them of their relationships to them. A man would call to his brother: "O my brother, I am burning, so help me!" [p. 209] He would reply: ﴿Indeed, Allah has forbidden them both to the disbelievers﴾.

Al-Suddi said: By His words ﴿or from what Allah has provided you﴾ he meant food.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed us that the son of Adam is not free of need for food and drink, even if he is being punished.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 51:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the mockers (al-mustahzi'un). The meaning is that they toyed with their religion which He had prescribed for them. Abu Rawq said: "Their religion" means their festival (ʿid). Qatadah said: ﴿amusement and play﴾ means eating and drinking. Others said: it is what Satan made attractive to them of forbidding the baḥirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah, the ham, the mukaʾ, the tasdiyah, and similar practices of the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance).

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will forget them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, We will leave them in the punishment just as they left the action for the meeting of this day of theirs. The "ma" is coordinated with the "kama" and is in a position of genitive (jarr). The meaning is: and like their denial. Ibn al-Anbari said: it may also be that the meaning is: "So today We will leave them in the Fire, knowingly, as the leaving of a heedless forgetter, just as they engaged in turning away from Our signs while they were mindful of what one who forgets and is heedless engages in."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an. "We have detailed it" (faṣṣalnāhu), that is: We have made it clear, by clarifying the truth from falsehood. It is also said: We detailed it in sections, at one time by defining what is lawful (ḥalāl), at another by defining what is unlawful (ḥarām), at another by promise, at another by warning, and at another by the narratives of the nations.

Regarding His saying, ﴿with knowledge﴾, there are two opinions.

One: with knowledge from Us of what We have detailed. The second: with knowledge from Us of what benefits you among what We have sent down in it. Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, Ibn Muḥayṣin, ʿĀṣim, al-Jaḥdarī, and Muʿādh al-Qāriʾ recited it as "faḍḍalnāhu" with a dotted ḍād (ḍād muʿjama), meaning "We have favoured it" (faḍḍalnāhu).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they await anything but its fulfillment?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the confirmation of what they were promised in the Qur'an. ﴿On the day its fulfillment comes﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿those who had forgotten it will say﴾, that is, those who abandoned it "from before" in the world, ﴿Certainly the messengers of our Lord came with the truth﴾, that is, with the Resurrection after death.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or are we to be sent back﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "Or are we to be sent back?" And His saying: ﴿so that we may act﴾ is in the accusative as an answer to the interrogative particle "fa" (the fa of response following the question).

Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on Surah 7, verse 54:

The first opinion: that it was Saturday. Muslim narrated in his Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my hand and said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created the clay on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the trees on Monday, created the things that are disliked on Tuesday, created light on Wednesday, scattered the living creatures in it on Thursday, and created Adam after the afternoon prayer on Friday, at the last of creation, in the last hour of the hours of Friday, between the afternoon prayer and the night." This is the choice of Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is the consensus of the people of knowledge.

The second: Sunday. This was said by Abdullah ibn Salam, Ka'b, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid, and al-Tabari (Ibn Jarir al-Tabari) chose it, and the People of the Torah (Ahl al-Tawrah) hold this view.

The third: Monday. This was said by Ibn Ishaq, and the People of the Gospel (Ahl al-Injil) hold this view. The meaning of His words ﴿in six days﴾ is: in the measure of that, because the day is known by the rising and setting of the sun, and the sun did not yet exist at that time. Ibn Abbas said: the measure of each of those days is a thousand years, and Ka'b, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said the same. We know of no disagreement on this. If someone were to say that they were like the days of this world, his saying would be far-fetched for two reasons.

One: it contradicts the narrations. The other: what the one who imagines it takes as slowness over six thousand years, he would imagine over six days when reflecting on His words: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. If it is said: Why did He not create them in an instant, since He is able? Then there are five answers to this.

One: He intended to bring about in each day a matter that the angels and whoever witnesses it would greatly regard. Mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: deliberateness in preparing what He created for Adam and his offspring before their existence is more eloquent in magnifying Him in the sight of the angels.

The third: hastening is more eloquent in power, and deliberateness is more eloquent in wisdom, so He intended to manifest His wisdom in this, just as He manifests His power in His saying "Be, and it is."

The fourth: He taught His servants deliberateness, so that when one who never errs is deliberate, the one who errs is more in need of deliberateness.

The fifth: that this delay in creating one thing after another is further from the supposition that it happened by nature or by chance.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He istawa (rose) over the Throne﴾. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: The 'arsh (throne) is the couch, and every king's couch is called an 'arsh; the plural 'uroosh is rarely used except out of necessity. Know that the mention of the throne is well known among the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Glorify Allah, for He is worthy of glory; our Lord in the heavens has become great, by the lofty building that preceded the people, and He made above the heaven a couch, a canopy that the sight of the eye cannot reach, with the angels beneath it appearing as images."

Ka'b said: The heavens within the Throne are like a lamp suspended between heaven and earth. Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated from Sa'd al-Ta'i, who said: The Throne is a red ruby. The consensus of the Salaf is established that they did not go beyond the recitation of the verse. Some people deviated and said: 'arsh here means king (malik). This is a departure from the literal meaning toward metaphor, in opposition to the narration. Have they not heard His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and His throne was over the water﴾ [Hud: 7]? Was the kingdom over the water? And how could the kingdom be a red ruby? Some say: istawa means istawla (to take control), and they argue with the poet's verse:

"Until Bishr took control of Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

And the poet also says:

"The two of them took control together, by their merit, over the throne of kings without deceit."

This is rejected by the linguists. Ibn al-A'rabi said: The Arabs do not know istawa to mean istawla, and whoever says that has spoken a great error. They said: One says istawla fulan 'ala kadha only when he was far from it and not able to control it, then he became able to control it; but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has always been in control of things. The two verses have no known composer, as Ibn Faris the linguist said. Even if they were authentic, there would be no proof in them for what we have explained of taking control by one who was not already in control. We seek refuge in Allah from the denial of the atheists (ta'til) and the likening of the anthropomorphists (tashbih).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read "yughshi" with a sukun on the ghayn and lightly. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "yughshshi" with a fatha on the ghayn and with shaddah; and they read likewise in (al-Ra'd: 3). Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that the night comes upon the day and covers it. He did not say "and He covers the day with the night" because the speech contains an indication of it; and He said in another place: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ [al-Zumar: 5]. Abu 'Ali said: He did not say "yughshi al-nahar al-layl" because it is known from the sense of the speech, like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. The night and the day are in the accusative because each of them is an object. As for al-hathith, it means swift.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars, subjected﴾. Most readers read them in the accusative, and the meaning is: He created the heavens and the sun. Ibn 'Amir read "wal-shamsu wal-qamaru wal-nujumu musakhkharatun" in the nominative here and in (al-Nahl: 12), and Hafs followed him only in His saying in (al-Nahl: 12): ﴿and the stars subjected﴾. The nominative is by way of resumption (isti'naf). Al-musakhkharat means those made subservient to what is intended of them, of rising, setting, and motion, according to the will of the one who governs them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely to Him belongs the creation and the command﴾. Because they are His creation, He has the right to command whatever He wills. It is said: the command is the decree.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is Allah﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions.

One: tafa'ala from barakah (blessing). Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn Abbas, and al-Qutaybi and al-Zajjaj said the same. Abu Malik said: it is af'ala from barakah. Al-Hasan said: blessing comes from Him. Al-Farra' said: tabaraka is from barakah; in Arabic it is like His saying "taqaddasa Rabbuna" (our Lord is sanctified).

The second: tabaraka means ta'ala (exalted), narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Abu al-Abbas said likewise: tabaraka means irtafa'a (was raised high), and al-mutabarik is the one who is raised high.

The third: the meaning is that blessing is sought through His name in everything, said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: the meaning of "tabaraka" is taqaddasa, i.e., purified itself; Ibn al-Anbari also mentioned this.

(p-215) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾. At-tadarru' (humble supplication) means submissiveness and lowliness. Al-khifyah (secrecy) is the opposite of openness. Al-Hasan said: "They would strive in supplication, and you would hear nothing but a murmur." From this is the hadith of Abu Musa: "Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent."

As for the transgression (al-i'tida') mentioned here, there are two views.

The first: it is transgression in supplication. Within this there are three sayings. The first: that one invokes evil upon the believers, such as disgrace and curse; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. The second: that one asks for what one does not deserve of the ranks of the prophets; this was said by Abu Mijlaz. The third: that it is raising the voice in supplication; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: that it is exceeding what one has been commanded; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 56:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾. Concerning this there are six opinions.

The first: Do not corrupt it through disbelief after it has been reformed through faith. The second: Do not corrupt it through wrongdoing after it has been reformed through justice. The third: Do not corrupt it through disobedience after it has been reformed through obedience. The fourth: Do not disobey, so that Allah withholds the rain and destroys the crops because of your sins, after He had reformed it with rain and fertility. The fifth: Do not corrupt it by killing the believer after it has been reformed by his remaining alive. The sixth: Do not corrupt it by denying the Messengers after it has been reformed by the revelation.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾ there are two opinions. One: in fear of His punishment and in hope of His reward. The second: in fear of rejection and in hope of being answered.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾. Al-Farra' said: I have seen the Arabs feminize "qarib" when it refers to kinship, without any disagreement among them about this. But when they say "your house is near to us" or "so-and-so is near to us," in terms of nearness and distance, they use both the masculine and the feminine, because they treated "qarib" as a substitute for "place," as in His saying: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 83], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63]. And if one were to feminize it, that would be correct. 'Urwah said:

"On the evening when 'Afra' was not near to you, so as to draw close, nor was 'Afra' far from you."

Al-Zajjaj said: It was said "qarib" (masculine) because mercy, forgiveness and pardon have the same meaning, and likewise every feminine noun that is not a true feminine. Al-Akhfash said: It is permissible that "mercy" here means "rain."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 57:**

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends the winds﴾.** Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read *al-riyah* ("the winds") in the plural. Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *al-rih* ("the wind") in the singular. The singular form may be used while the plural is meant, as in the saying "the dirham has become abundant in people's hands," and similarly: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2].

**His saying, Exalted is He: *nashran* (﴿bringing good tidings﴾).** Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read *nushuran* with a *damma* on the *nun* and the *shin*, meaning the plural of *nushur*, which is a pleasant wind that blows from every direction and side. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-nashr* means "scattered from every side." Abu 'Ali said: *al-nushur* may mean "that which is spread out" (*al-munshar*), "that which spreads" (*al-muntashir*), or "that which revives" (*al-nashir*). It is said: "God *anshara* the wind," meaning He revived it, so it became *nushira*, that is, revived. The evidence that spreading the wind means reviving it is the words of al-Faqa'si:

*I blew the south wind for him, and for him Rayda was revived, whose breeze gives life to the waters.*

It is also evidenced by the fact that the wind has been described as dying. The poet said:

*Indeed I hope that the wind will die,*
*so that I may sit today and rest.*

*Al-rayda* and *al-raydana* mean "the wind." Ibn 'Amir, 'Abd al-Warith and al-Hasan al-Basri read *nushran* with a *damma* on the *nun* and a sukun on the *shin*, and it has the same meaning as *nashran*. It is said: *kutb* and *kutub*, *rusl* and *rusul*. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim (p-218) read *nashran* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a sukun on the *shin*. Al-Farra' said: *al-nashr* is the pleasant, gentle wind that produces the clouds. Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-nashr* is the spread-out, wide-blowing wind. Abu 'Ali said: *al-nashr* may be the opposite of *al-tayy* (folding), as if the wind, by ceasing, were folded up. It may also mean what Abu 'Ubayda said about *al-nashr*: that it is scattered in all directions. It may also mean *al-nashr* which is life, as in the saying of the poet:

*Until people say, seeing what they have seen:*
*"How strange, the dead one who is raised!"*

He said: this is the preferred meaning. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Masruq and Muwriq al-'Ijli read *nashara* with a *fatha* on both the *nun* and the *shin*. Ibn al-Qasim said: there are two possibilities regarding *al-nashr*.

The first: it is the plural of *al-nushur*, as they say *'amud* and *'umd*, *ihab* and *uhb*.

The second: it is a plural whose singular is *nashir*, following the pattern of *ghA'ib* and *ghayab*, and *hafid* and *hafad*. All the reciters read the *nun* of the word. The same difference occurs in (al-Furqan: 48) and (al-Naml: 63). These are the readings of those who read with *nun*.

Others read with *ba'* (﴿glad tidings﴾, *bushran*). 'Asim, except al-Mufaddal, read *bushra* with a *damma* on the *ba'* and a sukun on the *shin*, following the pattern *fa'la*. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the plural of *bashira*, which is the one that brings good tidings of rain. The original form has a *damma* on the *shin*, but they found the two *dammas* heavy. Ibn Khaythum and Ibn Jadhlam read like this, except that they gave the *ra'* nunation. Abu al-Jawza', Abu 'Imran and Ibn Abi 'Abla read with a *damma* on the *ba'* and the *shin*, and this is according to the view that it is the plural of *bashira*.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the mercy﴾.** The mercy here means the rain. He called it mercy because it came with mercy. ***Aqallat*** means "carried," as in "bore."

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-sahab* is the plural of *sahaba* (cloud). Ibn Faris said: the cloud was named *al-sahab* because it is drawn (*insihab*) through the air.

(p-219) **His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿heavy﴾.** That is, heavy with water.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We drove it﴾.** The pronoun returns to the word *al-sahab*, although its form is singular.

Regarding **His saying: ﴿to a dead land﴾** there are two views:

The first: "to a land." The second: "for the reviving of a land." *Al-mayyit* is the land in which nothing grows, so it is in need of rain.

Regarding **His saying: ﴿then We brought forth with it﴾** there are three views:

The first: the pronoun refers to the cloud. The second: it refers to the rain; both are mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The third: it refers to the land; this is mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. As for the *ha'* in ﴿then We brought forth with it﴾, it allows all three views.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus We bring out the dead﴾.** That is: just as We revived this land. Mujahid said: We will raise the dead by rain, just as We revived the dead land by it. Ibn 'Abbas said: God will send rain between the two blasts of the trumpet, like the semen of men, and people will grow in their graves just as they grew in the bellies of their mothers.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that you may remember﴾.** Al-Zajjaj said: *la'alla* expresses hope. The servants were addressed in terms of what some of them hope from others. The meaning is: so that you, by what We have made clear to you, may reason toward the oneness of God and that He resurrects the dead.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by its Lord's permission﴾. He means the land whose soil is good. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "yakhruju" with a damma on the yaa' and a kasra on the raa', and "nabatahu" with a fatha on the taa'. ﴿And that which is bad, it does not come forth except sparingly﴾ is likewise. Aban related from 'Asim: "la yakhruju" with a damma on the yaa' and a kasra on the raa'. What is meant by "that which is bad" is the salt-marsh land (al-sabkha, a salty, barren flat).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except sparingly﴾. The majority (al-jumhur) recited it with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the kaf. Abu Ja'far (p-220) recited "nakadan" with a fatha on the kaf. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Muhaysin recited "nakadan" with a sukun on the kaf. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Meagre, difficult, in hardship." He cited:

"Do not fulfil the promise if you make one, and if you give, you give only something paltry and meagre."

The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: This is a parable which Allah, may He be exalted, struck for the believer and the disbeliever. The believer, when he hears the Qur'an and understands it, benefits from it and its effect appears upon him. He is likened to the good land that yields abundant produce and becomes fertile, where the effect of rain is excellent. The disbeliever is the opposite.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Worship Allah﴾. Muqatil said: "Single Him out as One." The same applies throughout the stories that follow.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾. Al-Kisa'i read "ghayruhu" (other than Him) in the genitive case (bi-l-khafd). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: he treated "ghayr" (other than) as a qualifier (sifah, an attributive adjective) of "ilah" (god), according to its literal wording (ʿala al-lafz).

His saying, Exalted is He: "U-ballighukum" (I convey to you). Abu 'Amr read "Ublighukum," with the ba' unvowelled (sakinah) and the lam light (khafifah). The rest read "Aballaghukum," with the ba' vowelled with a fatha and the lam doubled (mushaddadah).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I give you sincere counsel﴾. It is said: "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu" (both mean "I advised him"), just as "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu" (both mean "I thanked him").

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾. That is, of His forgiveness for whoever repents, and His punishment (p-221) for whoever persists. Muqatil said: "I know of the descent of the punishment what you do not know, for the people of Noah had not heard of any people who were punished before them."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Worship Allah﴾. Muqatil said: "Single Him out as One." The same applies throughout the stories that follow.

Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: he treated "ghayr" (other than) as a qualifier (sifah, an attributive adjective) of "ilah" (god), according to its literal wording (ʿala al-lafz).

His saying, Exalted is He: "U-ballighukum" (I convey to you). Abu 'Amr read "Ublighukum," with the ba' unvowelled (sakinah) and the lam light (khafifah). The rest read "Aballaghukum," with the ba' vowelled with a fatha and the lam doubled (mushaddadah).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I give you sincere counsel﴾. It is said: "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu" (both mean "I advised him"), just as "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu" (both mean "I thanked him").

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾. That is, of His forgiveness for whoever repents, and His punishment (p-221) for whoever persists. Muqatil said: "I know of the descent of the punishment what you do not know, for the people of Noah had not heard of any people who were punished before them."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 63–64:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you wonder﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: This is the waw of conjunction, to which the interrogative alif (alif al-istifham) was added, so it remained with a fatḥah. Regarding the word al-dhikr (the reminder) there are two opinions. One: it is the admonition (al-mawʿiza). The second: it is the clarification (al-bayan).

Regarding His saying: ﴿upon a man from among you﴾ there are two opinions. One: that "ʿala" here means "maʿa" (with), as said by al-Farra'. The second: that the meaning is "upon the tongue of a man from among you," as said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a blind people﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: their hearts became blind to the knowledge of Allah, His power, and the severity of His seizing.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 65–70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-safahah (foolishness) is ignorance. Al-Zajjaj said: al-safahah is lightness of forbearance and opinion; it is said: "a garment is safih (safih, flimsy)" when it is thin. ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾. So they disbelieved in him, suspecting, not being certain. ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no foolishness in me"﴾. This is a place of etiquette for creation in good speech, for he only repelled what they had called him of foolishness by negating it alone.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I am to you a sincere, trustworthy adviser﴾. Al-Dahhak said: trustworthy regarding the message. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: I was trustworthy among you before today.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember when He made you successors﴾. Their mention of the blessing is that He destroyed those who were before them and settled them in their dwellings. ﴿And He increased you in creation in stature (bastah)﴾, that is: in height and strength. Ibn Abbas said: the tallest of them was one hundred cubits, and the shortest sixty cubits. Al-Zajjaj said: the ala' of Allah (ala', blessings) are His bounties; its singular is ilay (ilay, a bounty). The poet said:

A white one who does not fear poverty, nor cuts off kinship, nor betrays a bounty (ilay).

It is also permissible that its singular be "ilya" and "ilay".

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So bring us what you promise us﴾, that is: of the descent of the punishment, ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in that the punishment is descending upon us. Ata said: in your prophethood and your being sent to us.

(p-223) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Indeed there has fallen upon you from your Lord abomination (rijs) and wrath (ghadab)﴾. That is: it has become obligatory. Ibn ʿAbbas said: punishment (ʿadhab) and anger (sukhṭ). Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ said: al-rijz, with a zay, and al-rijs, with a sin, have one meaning; they interchanged the sin with a zay.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you dispute with me concerning names which you have named, you and your fathers?﴾ He means: the idols.

And al-sultan means the proof (ḥujjah). ﴿So wait﴾ for the descent of the punishment; ﴿indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ for the punishment that will come upon you because of your denial of me.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 73–74:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Thamud﴾. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: Thamud was named for the scarcity of its water. Ibn Faris said: al-thamd (a small amount of water that has no source replenishing it).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah﴾. Regarding its attribution to Him there are two opinions. The first: that this is for specification and honour, as one says "the House of Allah." The second: that it was created by His command without a (natural) cause.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a sign for you﴾, i.e., a sign indicating the power of Allah. He said "for you" because they were the ones who proposed it, although it was a sign for them and for others.

Regarding the manner in which it was a sign there are two opinions.

The first: that it emerged from a smooth rock, and it writhed as a pregnant woman writhes, then the rock split open to produce it in the form they had requested.

The second: that it used to drink the whole water of the valley in one day, and would give them milk in its place.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So leave her to eat in the earth of Allah﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is not incumbent upon you to bear her expenses and her fodder. "Ta'kul" (she eats) is in the jussive mood as a response to an implied condition, i.e., "if you leave her, she will eat."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾, i.e., do not strike her to hamstring her.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He settled you in the earth﴾, i.e., He made you dwell. One says: "Ta'accha fulan manzilan" (so-and-so occupied a dwelling) when he dwells in it; and "baww'atuhu" (I caused him to dwell): I lodged him. The poet said:

"And I was settled in the midst of her people... and those who settle among her people have been completed"

i.e., I was lodged from among the noble in the core of lineage; said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾. Al-sahl (the plain) is the opposite of the rugged land. And al-qasr (the palace): that which is built up and raised of dwellings. Ibn 'Abbas said: They took palaces in the plains of the land for summer, and they hewed out (dwellings) in the mountains for winter. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: A man among them would build a structure, and a hundred years would pass over it, and it would fall into ruin, so he would rebuild it, and a hundred years would pass over it, and it would fall into ruin, and a hundred years would pass over it, and it would fall into ruin; this wearied them, so they took houses from the mountains.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 75–76:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The eminent ones among his people who were arrogant said﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir recited (wa-qāla al-mala'u) with an added waw, and so it is in their codices (maṣāḥif). The meaning of the verse: they were arrogant toward the worship of Allah. ﴿To those who were oppressed﴾ means: the humble (al-masākīn). ﴿To those of them who believed﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿to those who were oppressed﴾, because they are the believers. ﴿Do you know that Ṣāliḥ is one sent (mursal)?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial (istifhām inkār).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 77–78:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾, meaning: they killed her. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-ʿaqr (hamstringing) can carry the meaning of killing, and from it is his saying, peace be upon him, when mentioning the martyrs: "Whoever hamstrings his steed..." Ibn Ishaq said: Her killer lay in wait for her at the root of a tree and shot her with an arrow, which struck the muscle of her leg. Then he attacked her with the sword, cut her hamstring, and then slaughtered her. Al-Azhari said: al-ʿuqr (hamstringing), according to the Arabs, is cutting the hamstring of a camel; then ʿaqr was applied to slaughtering (nahr), because the one who slaughters a camel hamstrings it and then slaughters it.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And they defied" (ʿutuwwan). Al-Zajjaj said: they exceeded the measure in disbelief. Abu Sulayman said: they rebelled against obeying the command of their Lord.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with what you threaten us﴾, meaning: of the punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: ar-rajfah (the earthquake) is a violent quaking.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they became in their home﴾, meaning: in their city. If it is asked: why did he use the singular "dar" (home) here, while in another place he used the plural, saying ﴿in their homes﴾ [Hud: 67]? There are two answers to this, which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned.

The first: he meant by "dar" the encampment, i.e., they became in their camp. And by his saying "in their homes" he meant the dwellings, each of which is a separate residence.

The second: he meant by "dar" the dwellings, and he suffices with the singular for the whole, as in the saying of the poet:

"Eat within the half of your belly, you will live."

Examples of this are numerous in this book.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿prostrate (jathimin)﴾. Al-Farra' said: they became ashes lying prostrate. Abu ʿUbaydah said: meaning some of them lying upon others; al-judhum (crouching) for people and birds is like al-buruk (kneeling) for camels. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-judhum is kneeling upon the knees. Others said: as if they became dead in this state. Al-Zajjaj said: they became bodies cast upon the earth like crouched ashes. The exegetes said: the meaning of "jathimin" is that some of them lie upon others, i.e., some of them fell upon others at the descent of the punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And they defied" (ʿutuwwan). Al-Zajjaj said: they exceeded the measure in disbelief. Abu Sulayman said: they rebelled against obeying the command of their Lord.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with what you threaten us﴾, meaning: of the punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: ar-rajfah (the earthquake) is a violent quaking.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they became in their home﴾, meaning: in their city. If it is asked: why did he use the singular "dar" (home) here, while in another place he used the plural, saying ﴿in their homes﴾ [Hud: 67]? There are two answers to this, which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned.

The first: he meant by "dar" the encampment, i.e., they became in their camp. And by his saying "in their homes" he meant the dwellings, each of which is a separate residence.

The second: he meant by "dar" the dwellings, and he suffices with the singular for the whole, as in the saying of the poet:

"Eat within the half of your belly, you will live."

Examples of this are numerous in this book.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿prostrate (jathimin)﴾. Al-Farra' said: they became ashes lying prostrate. Abu ʿUbaydah said: meaning some of them lying upon others; al-judhum (crouching) for people and birds is like al-buruk (kneeling) for camels. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-judhum is kneeling upon the knees. Others said: as if they became dead in this state. Al-Zajjaj said: they became bodies cast upon the earth like crouched ashes. The exegetes said: the meaning of "jathimin" is that some of them lie upon others, i.e., some of them fell upon others at the descent of the punishment.

(p-227) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he turned away from them﴾. He says: Salih departed from them after the slaughter of the she-camel, because Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Leave from among them, for I am going to destroy them." Qatadah said: It has been related to us that Salih made his people hear [his message] just as your Prophet (ﷺ) made his people hear it, meaning: after their death.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾, meaning the coming of men [to men]. ﴿That no one in the worlds has preceded you in it.﴾ 'Amr ibn Dinar said: "Male mounting upon male (dhikr 'ala dhikr) did not occur in the world until the people of Lut appeared."

Some of the philologists (lughawiyyun) said: Lut is derived from "latta al-hawd," meaning when you smooth the basin with mud. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: This is an error, because it is a non-Arabic name like Ishaq (Isaac), and it cannot be said to be derived from "al-sahq," which means distance.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, you approach men lustfully﴾. This is a rhetorical question of denunciation. "Al-musrif" (the transgressor) means one who exceeds what he has been commanded. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Expel them from your town﴾, meaning Lut and his believing followers. ﴿Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They keep themselves clear of the anuses of men and the anuses of women.

"One of them: his two daughters. And the second: the believers in him. ﴿Except his wife; she was among those who remained behind﴾, i.e., those who remained in the punishment of Allah the Exalted. Abu 'Ubayda said: He said "among those who remained behind" because the description of the women is mentioned together with the description of the men when they are joined together.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning: stones. Mujahid said: Jibril descended, placed his wing beneath the cities of the people of Lut, lifted them, then overturned them so that their upper part became their lower part, and then they were pursued with stones."

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning: stones. Mujahid said: Jibril descended, placed his wing beneath the cities of the people of Lut, lifted them, then overturned them so that their upper part became their lower part, and then they were pursued with stones."

And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. (Qur'an 7:85 begins with this clause; the passage here comments on it.)

Qatadah said: Madyan is a water that the people of Shu'ayb lived beside, and al-Zajjaj said likewise, and he said: it is not declined, because it is the name of a place. Muqatil said: Madyan is the son of Ibrahim the Friend (al-Khalil) from his loins. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: Madyan is the son of Midyan ibn Ibrahim, and the meaning is: We sent to the descendants of Madyan; according to this, it is the name of a tribe. Some of them said: it is the name of a city, so the meaning is: and to the people of Madyan. Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: Madyan is a non-Arabic name; but if it is Arabic, then the ya' is extra, from their saying: madana bi-l-makan, meaning he resided in the place.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not diminish from people their things﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-bakhs (diminishing) is reduction and lessening; it is said: bakhastu abkhasu, with the sin (س), and bakhastu ʿaynahu, with the sad (ص), and not otherwise.

(p-229) ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾, that is: do not act in it with acts of disobedience after Allah has set it right by commanding justice and sending the messengers.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If you are believers﴾, that is: if you are ones who affirm what I have informed you of from Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 86:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not sit on every path﴾, meaning: on every road, threatening those who believed in Shu'ayb with evil, and frightening them with punishment and killing. If it is said: Why did He use the verb in the singular and leave it without an object? Why did He not say: "you threaten them with such-and-such"? The answer: when the Arabs leave this verb (awʿada, "to threaten") without an object, it signifies only evil; they say: "awʿadtu fulānan" (I threatened so-and-so). Likewise, when they use it in the form waʿadtu with an object, it signifies only good news. Al-Farra' said: they say "waʿadtuhu khayran" (I promised him good) and "awʿadtuhu sharran" (I threatened him with evil). When they drop both the good and the evil, they say: "waʿadtuhu" for good and "awʿadtuhu" for evil. When they bring the preposition bi (with), they say: "waʿadtuhu wa-sharran" (I promised him, and [with] evil). The rajiz (reciter of verse) said:

؎ He threatened me with prison and shackles

The author said: I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: when they want to mention what they threaten with alongside awʿidat, they bring the preposition bi, and say: "awʿadatahu bi-l-darb" (she threatened him with beating), and they do not say "awʿadtuhu al-darb" (I threatened him the beating). Al-Suddi said: they were tax collectors. Ibn Zayd said: they used to cut off the road.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you bar from the way of Allah﴾, meaning: you turn away from the religion of Allah those who believe in it. ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ is explained in (Al 'Imran: 99).

(p-230) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember when you were few, and He multiplied you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that the meaning is that He made you wealthy after you were poor; and it is permissible that the meaning is that your number increased after you were few; and it is permissible that you were not people of power and status, so He multiplied them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 87–88:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent, and a group who have not believed﴾ — meaning: if you differ regarding my message, so that you become two groups, believers and deniers ﴿then be patient until Allah judges between us﴾ — by punishing the deniers and saving the believers ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾ — because He is the Just who does not oppress.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or you will return to our religion﴾ — they mean our religion, which is polytheism. Al-Farra' said: In His saying "latu'udunna" (you will return), He placed a lam (la) as in the answer to an oath, and it has the meaning of a condition. Its equivalent in speech is: "By Allah, I will strike you unless you confess to me," so its meaning is the meaning of "illa" (unless) or the meaning of "hatta" (until). ﴿He said: Even though we were unwilling?﴾ — meaning: will you compel us into your religion if we dislike it? The alif is for interrogation.

If it is said: how did they say "you will return," when Shu'ayb had never been in disbelief at all, so that he could return to it? On this there are two answers.

The first: when they grouped together, in their address to him, those who had been disbelievers and then believed, they addressed Shu'ayb with the address of his followers, and gave precedence to their wording over his wording, because of their large number and his being alone.

The second: the meaning is "you will be transformed into our religion," so the "return" was used in the sense of "beginning," as one says: "harm has returned upon me from so-and-so," meaning that such harm reached me from him, even if no harm had previously come from him. The poet said:

*If the days were once kind to me, a single time, then indeed their misdeeds have returned to them.*

We have explained this in His saying: ﴿And to Allah are all matters returned﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah (2:210). Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari also mentioned the meaning of both answers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 89–93:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We would be fabricating a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion﴾. This was because the people claimed that Allah had commanded them to what they were upon, so they called it a millah (religion/creed). ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the millah, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., unless it has already preceded in the knowledge and will of Allah that we would return to it. ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He knows what will be before it comes to be.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., regarding what you threaten us with, and regarding our protection from misguidance. ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth﴾. Abu Ubayda said: judge between us. He recited:

Ala ubligh Bani Asam rasulan, bi-anni ʿan futahatikum ghaniyyun
("Notify the Banu Asam with a messenger that I am independent of your judgment.")

Al-Farra said: The people of Oman call the judge "al-fatih" and "al-fattah." Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is: make our matter manifest until what is between us is opened and revealed. So it is possible that they asked for this, the descent of punishment upon their people, so that it would show that the truth was with them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As if they had never flourished therein﴾. In this there are four opinions.

The first: as if they had never lived in their homes. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Akhfash. The poet Hatim al-Ta'i said:

Ghaniyna zamanan bi-l-tasaʿlluki wa-l-ghina / fa-kullan saqanahu bi-kasayhima al-dahr
Fa-ma zadana baghyan ʿala dhi qarabatin / ghinana wa-la azra bi-ahsabina al-faqr
("We lived for a time with poverty and wealth, and time gave each of us a drink from its two cups. Our wealth did not increase us in insolence toward a kinsman, nor did poverty diminish our lineage.")

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ghinina is "we lived." Al-tasaʿluk means poverty, and the Arabs call the poor man "al-saʿluk."

The second: as if they had never enjoyed comfort therein. This was said by Qatada.

The third: as if they had never existed therein. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

The fourth: as if they had never dwelt therein. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Asmaʿi said: al-maghani means dwellings; it is said "ghinina bi-makan kadha," meaning "we dwelt at such a place." Ibn Qutayba said: as if they had never resided therein; and the meaning of "ghinina bi-makan kadha" is "we resided." Ibn al-Anbari said: He repeated His saying, ﴿Those who denied Shuʿayb﴾, for emphasis in condemning them, just as you say: "Your brother who took our wealth, your brother who insulted our honor."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he turned away from them﴾. In this there are two opinions.

One: he turned away. The second: he departed. ﴿And he said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord."﴾ Qatada said: Shuʿayb made his people hear, and Salih made his people hear, just as your Prophet (ﷺ) made his people hear on the Day of Badr; meaning, he addressed them after their destruction. ﴿So how should I grieve﴾, i.e., how should I be sorrowful. Ibn Ishaq said: Shuʿayb was overcome with severe grief over his people, then he reproached himself, saying: "How should I grieve over a disbelieving people?"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We would be fabricating a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion﴾. This was because the people claimed that Allah had commanded them to what they were upon, so they called it a millah (religion/creed). ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the millah, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., unless it has already preceded in the knowledge and will of Allah that we would return to it. ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He knows what will be before it comes to be.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., regarding what you threaten us with, and regarding our protection from misguidance. ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth﴾. Abu Ubayda said: judge between us. He recited:

Ala ubligh Bani Asam rasulan, bi-anni ʿan futahatikum ghaniyyun
("Notify the Banu Asam with a messenger that I am independent of your judgment.")

Al-Farra said: The people of Oman call the judge "al-fatih" and "al-fattah." Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is: make our matter manifest until what is between us is opened and revealed. So it is possible that they asked for this, the descent of punishment upon their people, so that it would show that the truth was with them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As if they had never flourished therein﴾. In this there are four opinions.

The first: as if they had never lived in their homes. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Akhfash. The poet Hatim al-Ta'i said:

Ghaniyna zamanan bi-l-tasaʿlluki wa-l-ghina / fa-kullan saqanahu bi-kasayhima al-dahr
Fa-ma zadana baghyan ʿala dhi qarabatin / ghinana wa-la azra bi-ahsabina al-faqr
("We lived for a time with poverty and wealth, and time gave each of us a drink from its two cups. Our wealth did not increase us in insolence toward a kinsman, nor did poverty diminish our lineage.")

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ghinina is "we lived." Al-tasaʿluk means poverty, and the Arabs call the poor man "al-saʿluk."

The second: as if they had never enjoyed comfort therein. This was said by Qatada.

The third: as if they had never existed therein. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

The fourth: as if they had never dwelt therein. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Asmaʿi said: al-maghani means dwellings; it is said "ghinina bi-makan kadha," meaning "we dwelt at such a place." Ibn Qutayba said: as if they had never resided therein; and the meaning of "ghinina bi-makan kadha" is "we resided." Ibn al-Anbari said: He repeated His saying, ﴿Those who denied Shuʿayb﴾, for emphasis in condemning them, just as you say: "Your brother who took our wealth, your brother who insulted our honor."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he turned away from them﴾. In this there are two opinions.

One: he turned away. The second: he departed. ﴿And he said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord."﴾ Qatada said: Shuʿayb made his people hear, and Salih made his people hear, just as your Prophet (ﷺ) made his people hear on the Day of Badr; meaning, he addressed them after their destruction. ﴿So how should I grieve﴾, i.e., how should I be sorrowful. Ibn Ishaq said: Shuʿayb was overcome with severe grief over his people, then he reproached himself, saying: "How should I grieve over a disbelieving people?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send into any town⦅qaryah⦆﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Every city is called a qaryah (town), because people gather in it. Others said: there is an ellipsis (ikhtisar) in the verse, its estimated meaning being: "so they denied him." ﴿Except that We seized its people with adversity and hardship﴾. The explanation of al-ba'sa' and al-darra' has already been given in (al-An'am: 42), and the explanation of humbling oneself (al-tadarru') in this surah [al-A'raf: 55]. The purpose of the verse is to inform the Prophet (ﷺ) of God's way (sunnah) regarding those who deny, and to warn Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 95–97:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We replaced the bad condition with good⁠﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: the "bad" (sayyi'ah) is hardship, and the "good" (hasanah) is ease. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the "bad" is evil, and the "good" is goodness. This was said by Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until they multiplied⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they increased in number, and their wealth increased. ﴿And they said: Hardship and ease have already touched our fathers⁠﴾, so we are like them, and what befell them befalls us too, meaning: they intended that this is the custom of time, and not a punishment. ﴿So We seized them suddenly⁠﴾, that is, unexpectedly, with the descent of the punishment ﴿while they did not perceive⁠﴾ its descent, until Allah destroyed them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had We opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth⁠﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that rain came to them from the sky and plants from the earth, and He made that abundant and plentiful.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 98–99:

His saying, Most High: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Nafi' read ﴿Awa-amina ahlu﴾ with the waw (و) sukun (silent, without vowel). 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Aw a-mina" with the waw vocalized (with a fatha-like movement). Warsh related from Nafi': "Awamana", assimilating the hamzah (idgham) and transferring its vowel onto the preceding unvowelled letter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 100–101:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Did it not become clear to those who﴾. Ya'qub read "نَهْدِ" (nahdi, with the nun). The same is the case in [Ta-Ha 128] and [as-Sajdah 26]. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads with the ya' (yahdi), the meaning is: "Did Allah not make it clear to them?" Whoever reads with the nun, the meaning is: "Did We not make it clear?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We seal﴾ is not governed by "أصبناهم" (asabnahum, "We would have struck them"), because if it were governed by "asabnahum," it would read: "and We would have sealed." Rather, the meaning is: "and We seal upon their hearts." It is also permissible that it be governed by the past tense while its wording is that of the future, as He said: ﴿That if We willed﴾, meaning: "if We had willed." Ibn al-Anbari said: it is permissible that it be conjoined to "asabna" (we struck), since it carries the sense of "nasib" (to befall); so the past tense is placed in the position of the future when the sense of futurity is clear, as He said: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾ [al-Furqan 10], meaning: "if He wills," and His saying ﴿and will give you palaces﴾ indicates it. The poet said:

"If they hear a suspicion, they fly with it, joyful at my expense; and what good they hear, they bury."

Meaning: "they are buried" (yudfanu).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they do not hear﴾, meaning: they do not accept, and from this is the saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." The poet said:

"I called upon Allah until I feared that Allah would not hear what I say."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they would not have believed in what they had denied before﴾. In it there are five opinions.

The first: "So they would not have believed upon the coming of the messengers in what had already been known in Allah's knowledge, that they would deny it, on the day they acknowledged it in the covenant when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam." This is the saying of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

The second: "So they would not have believed upon the sending of the messengers in what they had denied on the day He took their covenant when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam; so they believed under compulsion, as they acknowledged with their tongues while concealing denial." This was said by Ibn Abbas and as-Suddi.

The third: "So they would not, even if We returned them to the world after their death, have believed in what they had denied before their destruction." This is the saying of Mujahid.

The fourth: "So they would not have believed in what their predecessors among the bygone nations had denied, but rather they joined them in denial." This was said by Yaman ibn Rabab.

The fifth: "So they would not have believed after seeing the miracles and wonders in what they had denied before seeing them."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 102:

Allah's statement: ﴿And We found not for most of them any covenant﴾. Mujahid said: "It means: the earlier generations." (min ʿahd) Abu ʿUbayda said: "That is, fidelity (wafaʾ)." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He means fidelity to the covenant which He made with them when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam." Al-Hasan said: "The covenant here is what He enjoined upon them through the prophets, that they should not associate anything with Him."

Allah's statement: ﴿And indeed, We found﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: "And We did not find most of them except defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)."

(p-237) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then after them We sent﴾ — meaning: the prophets mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they wronged themselves by them﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbas said: they denied them (fakadhdhabū bihā). Others said: they rejected them (fajaḥadū bihā).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is fitting for me that I should not say of Allah except the truth﴾ — "ʿalā" here carries the meaning of "bāʾ" (i.e., "on" is used in the sense of "concerning/regarding"). Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs put "bāʾ" in the place of "ʿalā"; they say: "I shot with the bow" (ramaytu bi-l-qaws) and "ʿalā al-qaws," and "I came with a good condition" (jiʾtu bi-ḥālin ḥasanatin) and "ʿalā ḥālin ḥasanatin." Abū ʿUbayda said: "ḥaqīq" means "eager/keen" (ḥarīṣ). Nāfiʿ and Abān, from ʿĀṣim, read ﴿ḥaqīqun ʿalayya﴾ with the yāʾ doubled and vowelled with a fatḥa, as an idāfa (construction). The meaning is: "obligated upon me."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed I have come to you with a clear sign﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means the staff. ﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾ — i.e., release them; he had been employing them in hard labour. ﴿And behold, it became a manifest serpent﴾ — Abū ʿUbayda said: i.e., a clearly visible snake. Al-Farrāʾ said: "thuʿbān" is the largest of snakes, and it is the male. Likewise al-Ḍaḥḥāk related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "thuʿbān" is the male snake.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs put "bāʾ" in the place of "ʿalā"; they say: "I shot with the bow" (ramaytu bi-l-qaws) and "ʿalā al-qaws," and "I came with a good condition" (jiʾtu bi-ḥālin ḥasanatin) and "ʿalā ḥālin ḥasanatin." Abū ʿUbayda said: "ḥaqīq" means "eager/keen" (ḥarīṣ). Nāfiʿ and Abān, from ʿĀṣim, read ﴿ḥaqīqun ʿalayya﴾ with the yāʾ doubled and vowelled with a fatḥa, as an idāfa (construction). The meaning is: "obligated upon me."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed I have come to you with a clear sign﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means the staff. ﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾ — i.e., release them; he had been employing them in hard labour. ﴿And behold, it became a manifest serpent﴾ — Abū ʿUbayda said: i.e., a clearly visible snake. Al-Farrāʾ said: "thuʿbān" is the largest of snakes, and it is the male. Likewise al-Ḍaḥḥāk related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "thuʿbān" is the male snake.

(p-238) His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he put his hand into his collar (jayb), then took it out, and behold, it was shining like lightning, having a radiance that overpowered the light of the sun. So they fell on their faces. Then he put it back into his collar, and it returned to what it had been. Mujahid said: white, without leprosy.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So what do you command?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: What do you advise me? This indicates that it is the speech of Pharaoh, and that the speech of the council (al-mala') ended at His words: ﴿from your land﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that it is from the speech of the council, as if they addressed Pharaoh and those close to him, or they addressed him alone, since it is said to a leader: "The one obeyed, what do you see?"

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Put him off﴾ (arjihhu). Ibn Kathir recited "arjihhu" with hamza, with a waw after the ha' in pronunciation. Abu ʿAmr recited similarly, except that he gives the ha' a damma without extending it into a waw; and both of them used hamza in (muranjawn) [al-Tawba: 106] and (turji') [al-Ahzab: 51]. (p-239) Qalun and al-Musayyabi from Nafi' recited "arjihi" with a kasra on the ha', without extending it into a ya', and without hamza. Warsh narrated from him "arjihi" with a ya' connecting it, without hamza between the jim and the ha'. Ismaʿil ibn Jaʿfar also said this from Nafiʿ, and it is the recitation of al-Kisa'i. Hamza recited "arjih" with the ha' sukun, without hamza, and ʿAsim likewise, except in the narration of al-Mufaddal; al-Mufaddal narrated from him a kasra on the ha' without elongation or hamza, and this is the recitation of Abu Jaʿfar. Their difference is similar in (al-Shuʿara': 36). Ibn Qutayba said: arrijhu means: delay him; and it may be with hamza: it is said "arjaʾtu al-shayʾ" and "arjaytuhu." From it is His saying: ﴿You may put off whom you will of them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 51]. Al-Farra' said: the Banu Asad say "arjaytu al-amr" without hamza, and so do most of Qays; while some of the Banu Tamim say "arjaʾtu al-amr" with hamza. The reciters are fond of hamzing it, and leaving out the hamza is better.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And send into the cities﴾, meaning the cities of Egypt, (ḥāshirīn), i.e., those who will gather the sorcerers to you and assemble them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the police (al-shurta).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿That they bring you every sorcerer﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, and Ibn ʿAmir recited (sāḥir) here, and in (Yunus: 79) (bi-kulli sāḥir); Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited (sahhār) in both places; and there is no disagreement that in (al-Shuʿara': 37) it is (sahhār).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed for us there will surely be a reward﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Hafs from ʿAsim recited ﴿inna lanā la-ajran﴾ with a kasra on the alif as a statement; and in (al-Shuʿara': 41) (āyin) with an elongated, fatha-ed alif, except that Hafs narrated from ʿAsim in (al-Shuʿara': 41) (a-in) with two hamzas. Abu ʿAmr recited (āyin lanā) elongated in both surahs. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim recited with two hamzas in both places. (p-240) Abu ʿAli said: the interrogative is more fitting in this place, because they did not affirm that they would have the reward, but rather they asked about it.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed you will be among those brought near﴾, meaning: and for you, along with the reward, is a lofty rank with me.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: they clouded the eyes of the people and seized them. (wa-istarhabūhum): meaning they frightened them. Al-Zajjaj said: they sought to elicit their dread until the people feared them.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then behold, it swallowed﴾ (talqafu). ʿAsim recited taləqquf with the lam quiescent and the qaf light, here and in (Ta Ha: 69) and (al-Shuʿara': 45). Al-Bazzi and Ibn Fulayh narrated from Ibn Kathir: (talaqqafa) with the ta' doubled. Al-Farra' said: it is said "laqafa al-shayʾ," so "I laqufu it, laqfan and luqfanan"; and the meaning is: it swallows.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿What they falsely fabricate﴾, meaning: they lie, because they claimed that they were snakes.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So the truth took place﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it became manifest. ﴿And what they had been doing was nullified﴾ of the sorcery.

Indication of their story

They differed on the number of the sorcerers, giving thirteen opinions. The first: seventy-two, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: seventy-two thousand, also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muqatil said so. The third: seventy, also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The fourth: twelve thousand, said by Kaʿb. The fifth: seventy thousand, said by ʿAta', (p-241) and Wahb said likewise in one narration, except that he said: he chose from them seven thousand. The sixth: seven hundred. ʿAbd al-Munʿim ibn Idris narrated from his father from Wahb that he said: the number of the sorcerers who opposed Moses was seventy thousand, selected from seven hundred thousand; then Pharaoh chose from the seventy thousand seven hundred. The seventh: twenty-five thousand, said by al-Hasan. The eighth: nine hundred, said by ʿIkrima. The ninth: eighty thousand, said by Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir. The tenth: some thirty thousand, said by al-Suddi. The eleventh: fifteen thousand, said by Ibn Ishaq. The twelfth: nineteen thousand, narrated by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The thirteenth: four hundred, related by al-Tha'labi.

As for the names of their leaders: Ibn Ishaq said: the heads of the sorcerers were Sanur, ʿAzur, Hatahat, and Musaffa, and they are the ones who believed; thus Ibn Makula related it. I have seen from other than Ibn Ishaq: Sabura and ʿAzura. Muqatil said: the name of the eldest of them was Shamʿun.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they cast down ropes, thick, and long sticks, and they were a mile upon a mile; then Moses cast his staff, and behold, it was greater than their ropes and staffs, filling the horizon; then it opened its mouth eighty cubits, and swallowed what they had cast of their ropes and staffs, and began eating everything it could reach of rock or tree, while the people looked on, and Pharaoh laughed, feigning composure. Then the serpent came toward Pharaoh, and he cried: "O Moses, O Moses!" So Moses seized it, and the sorcerers knew that this was from heaven and not sorcery, so they fell prostrate and said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾. Pharaoh said: "Do you believe in me before I permit it?" They said: "The Lord of Moses and Aaron." So they became sorcerers in the morning and martyrs in the evening.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: when it became a serpent, it charged at the people, who fled from it, and some of them trampled others, so twenty-five thousand of them died.

Al-Suddi said: Moses met the chief of the sorcerers and said: "Tell me, if I defeat you tomorrow, will you believe in me?" (p-242) The sorcerer said: "I will surely come tomorrow with a sorcery that sorcery cannot overcome. By God, if you overcome me, I will certainly believe in you."

If it is asked: how was it permissible for Moses to command them to cast, when performing sorcery is disbelief? The answer to this has three responses. The first: the implication of his command is: if you are truthful, then cast. The second: cast upon what is sound, not upon what corrupts and changes; both were mentioned by al-Mawardi. The third: he commanded them to cast only so that his miracle would be more manifest, because when they cast and he cast his staff, it swallowed that; this was mentioned by al-Wahidi.

If it is asked: how did He say: ﴿And the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate﴾, when they prostrated by their own choice? The answer is that when every doubt was removed by what God Exalted showed of His affair, the magnitude of what they witnessed compelled them to hasten to prostration, so they became passive in the casting, affirming and magnifying the matter of the signs they had seen; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: when the sorcerers believed, Moses was followed by six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel.

Indication of their story

They differed on the number of the sorcerers, giving thirteen opinions. The first: seventy-two, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The seventh: twenty-five thousand, said by al-Hasan. The eighth: nine hundred, said by ʿIkrima. The ninth: eighty thousand, said by Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir. The tenth: some thirty thousand, said by al-Suddi. The eleventh: fifteen thousand, said by Ibn Ishaq. The twelfth: nineteen thousand, narrated by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The thirteenth: four hundred, related by al-Tha'labi.

As for the names of their leaders: Ibn Ishaq said: the heads of the sorcerers were Sanur, ʿAzur, Hatahat, and Musaffa, and they are the ones who believed; thus Ibn Makula related it. I have seen from other than Ibn Ishaq: Sabura and ʿAzura. Muqatil said: the name of the eldest of them was Shamʿun.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they cast down ropes, thick, and long sticks, and they were a mile upon a mile; then Moses cast his staff, and behold, it was greater than their ropes and staffs, filling the horizon; then it opened its mouth eighty cubits, and swallowed what they had cast of their ropes and staffs, and began eating everything it could reach of rock or tree, while the people looked on, and Pharaoh laughed, feigning composure. Then the serpent came toward Pharaoh, and he cried: "O Moses, O Moses!" So Moses seized it, and the sorcerers knew that this was from heaven and not sorcery, so they fell prostrate and said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾. Pharaoh said: "Do you believe in me before I permit it?" They said: "The Lord of Moses and Aaron." So they became sorcerers in the morning and martyrs in the evening.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: when it became a serpent, it charged at the people, who fled from it, and some of them trampled others, so twenty-five thousand of them died.

Al-Suddi said: Moses met the chief of the sorcerers and said: "Tell me, if I defeat you tomorrow, will you believe in me?" (p-242) The sorcerer said: "I will surely come tomorrow with a sorcery that sorcery cannot overcome. By God, if you overcome me, I will certainly believe in you."

The third: he commanded them to cast only so that his miracle would be more manifest, because when they cast and he cast his staff, it swallowed that; this was mentioned by al-Wahidi.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: when the sorcerers believed, Moses was followed by six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel.

Qunbul related from al-Qawwas the same as Ibn al-Ikhrit's reading, except that he pronounced a hamza after the waw. Abu 'Ali said: the hamza after the waw is pronounced, because this waw has been converted from the interrogative hamza, and after the interrogative hamza comes ﴿أفَعَلْتُمْ﴾ (af'altum), so he made it fully articulated and did not lighten it.

God's words, ﴿Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: it is a scheme you devised between yourselves and Moses in Egypt before your departure to this place, so that you might seize Egypt and expel its people from it. ﴿So you will come to know﴾ the outcome of what you have done. ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on alternate sides﴾, which means cutting off the right hand and the left foot. Ibn 'Abbas said: the first to do that, and the first to crucify, was Pharaoh.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read ﴿أآَمَنتُمْ﴾ (a-ā-amantum) with two hamzas, the second elongated, also as an interrogative. Hafs, from 'Asim, read ﴿آَمَنتُمْ بِهِ﴾ as a statement. Qunbul related from al-Qawwas the same as Ibn al-Ikhrit's reading, except that he pronounced a hamza after the waw.
