Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 126–128:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you do not resent us﴾ meaning: you do not disapprove of anything in us, and you do not hold us in contempt except because we have believed. ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾. Mujahid said: "[Meaning] upon [the threat of] cutting off and crucifixion, so that we do not return to disbelief." ﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾, meaning: sincere in the religion of Musa.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you leave Musa and his people﴾. This is an incitement by the chieftains (al-mala') to Pharaoh. Regarding what they meant by "corruption in the land," there are two opinions. The first: the killing of the sons of the Copts and the sparing of their women, as they had done to the Children of Israel; this was said by Muqatil. The second: their calling people to oppose Pharaoh and to abandon his worship.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [will he leave] you﴾. The majority of the reciters read it with a fatha on the ra'; al-Hasan read it with a damma. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "wa-yadharaka" with a fatha has put it in the subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative with the waw; the meaning being: Is it possible for you to leave Musa and for him to leave you? Whoever reads it with a damma has made it a new (resumed) clause, so the meaning is: Will you leave Musa and his people, while he leaves you and your gods? The better reading is that it is conjoined to "a-tadhar" (will you leave), so the meaning is: Will you leave Musa, and will Musa leave you? That is: Will you allow him this?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your gods﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Pharaoh had made small idols for his people and commanded them to worship them, and he said, "I am your lord and the lord of these idols." This is His saying: ﴿I am your most high lord﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. Others said: his people worshipped those idols seeking nearness to him. Al-Hasan said: he worshipped a male goat in secret. It was said: he worshipped a cow in secret. It was said: he would put something around his neck and worship it. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya, and Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa-ilahataka" with a kasra on the hamza, shortened, with a fatha on the lam and an alif after it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "and [will he leave] you and your lordship." Ibn al-Anbari said: the linguists said: al-ilaha (worship) means worship; so the meaning is: "and [will he leave] you and people's worship of you." Ibn Qutayba said: whoever reads "wa-ilahataka" intends: "and [will he leave] you and the sun which is worshipped," for among the Arabs there were people who worshipped the sun and called it gods. al-A'sha said:

"So I do not recall the dread until it turned,
Just before the gods, near to us."

He means the sun. Al-Rahab: his she-camel. He says: I have been occupied with this woman away from my she-camel until this time.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will kill their sons﴾. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "sa-nuqattilu" and "yuqattiluna abnaakum" [al-A'raf: 141] with doubling (tashdid); Nafi' read them with a lightened form. Ibn Kathir read "sa-naqtulu" lightly and "yuqattilun" doubled. He turned from killing Musa to killing the sons only because he knew that he could not prevail over him. ﴿And indeed we are above them, dominant﴾, meaning: exalted through kingship and authority. The Children of Israel complained of the renewal of killing their sons, so Musa said: ﴿Seek help through Allah and be patient﴾ against what they do to you, ﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He causes whom He wills of His servants to inherit it﴾. Al-Hasan, and Hubayra from Hafs from 'Asim, read "yuwarithuha" with doubling. Musa thus gave them the hope that Allah would give them the land of Pharaoh and his people after their destruction.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the final outcome is for the God-fearing﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions. The first: Paradise. The second: victory and triumph.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 129–130:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us."﴾ Regarding this harm there are six opinions.

The first: the first harm and the second harm was the imposition of the jizya (poll tax). This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri).

The second: the first was the slaughter of their sons, and the second was Pharaoh overtaking them on the day they were pursued. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: the first was that they were conscripted for labour until midday, and then sent off during the rest of the day to earn their living; the second was their being conscripted for the whole day without food or drink. This was said by Juwaybir.

The fourth: the first was their being conscripted to make bricks, and they were given the straw which they mixed into the clay; the second was that they were ordered to make bricks and to place the straw upon them. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fifth: the first was the killing of the sons and the sparing of the daughters; the second was Pharaoh's imposition on them of what they could not bear. This was said by Muqatil.

The sixth: the first was their subjugation and the killing of their sons and the sparing of their women; the second was the return of that torment.

Regarding His saying: ﴿before you came to us﴾ there are two opinions.

One: "before you came to us with the message" and "after we came with it" (i.e., after you came to us with it). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "before you came to us with the covenant of Allah that He would deliver us," and "after you came to us with it." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "'Asa" (it may be) expresses hope and apprehension, except that what Allah is hoped for is necessarily fulfilled.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and make you successors in the land﴾. Regarding this succession there are two opinions.

One: that it is succession from Pharaoh and his people. The second: that it is succession on behalf of Allah, Exalted is He, because the believers are the vicegerents of Allah on His earth. Regarding "in the land" there are two opinions.

One: the land of Egypt, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the land of Syria, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and see how you act﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, He sees it by its occurrence from you, for He only recompenses them for what has occurred from them, not for what He knew would occur.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is: We tested them with barrenness. "The people of Pharaoh" (Al Fir'awn): the people of his religion and his folk. Muqatil said: they are the people of Egypt.

(p-247) Al-Farra' said: "bil-sinin" means: with drought and barrenness, year after year. Al-Zajjaj said: al-sunun in the speech of the Arabs means barrenness; it is said: "the year (sanah) afflicted them," meaning the barrenness of the year and the severity of the year. He only seized them with adversity because states of hardship soften hearts and encourage turning to what is with Allah and returning to Him. Qatada said: as for the years of drought, they were in their deserts and among their livestock; as for the loss of fruits, it was in their cities and villages. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: everything dried up for them and their livestock perished, until the Nile of Egypt dried up. So they gathered before Pharaoh and said to him: "If you are a lord as you claim, then fill the Nile of Egypt for us." He said: "In the morning the water will reach you." When they had left his presence, he said: "What have I done? I am able to bring water into the Nile of Egypt by morning, and they will call me a liar?" When it was the middle of the night, he bathed, then put on a woollen garment, then went out barefoot until he reached the bed of the Nile of Egypt, stood in its bed, and said: "O Allah, You know that I know that You are able to fill the Nile of Egypt with water, so fill it." He knew nothing except by the rushing of water, when Allah willed for him what was destruction.

I say: this report is far from sound, for the man was a materialist who did not affirm a god. And even if it were sound, his acknowledgement of that would be like the acknowledgement of Iblis, and his opposition would remain out of obstinacy.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 131:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But when good came to them﴾, and it is the rain, fertility, abundance of provision and well-being, (they said, "This is due to us"). That is: we deserve it, according to the customary course of abundant provision that has befallen us, and they did not know that it was from Allah, so that they would give thanks for it. ﴿But if an evil befalls them﴾, and it is drought, dearth and calamity, ﴿they ascribe it as an omen to Musa and those with him﴾, that is: they consider them a bad omen. The Arabs used to scare away birds (zajr al-tayr, the practice of augury by birds), and they would take a bad omen from the ba'ih (al-barih, that which comes from the north side), and seek blessing from the sanih (al-sanih, that which comes from the right side).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly, their omen is with Allah﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Ala" (ألا, "Indeed/Behold") is an alert, an emphasis, and a figurative usage. "Ta'iruhum" (طائرهم, their omen) means their share and portion. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Certainly, their omen is with Allah" means: what has befallen them is from Allah. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Certainly, the ill omen that overtakes them is that which they were promised in the Hereafter, not what they receive in this world.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 132–133:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The grammarians claim that the original form of "mahma" (whatever) was "mama", but the first alif was replaced by a haa' so that the wording would differ. The first "ma" is the "ma" of conditionality (al-jaza'), and the second "ma" is the one that is added for emphasis to the conditional particle. The grammarians' evidence for this is that there is no conditional particle (huruf al-jaza') except that "ma" is added to it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So if you encounter them﴾ [al-Anfal: 57], like your saying: "in tathqafannahum"; and He said: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ [al-Isra': 28]. The second "ma" serves as the conditional and conditioned, and the first explanation is the one spoken, and it is the usage of people. Ibn al-Anbari said: According to the view of those who say that the meaning of "mah" is "restraint" (al-kaff), it is good to pause on "mah", but the preferred view is not to pause on it without "ma", because in the Mushaf it is one letter.

As for the flood (al-tufan), there are three views.

The first: that it is water. Ibn 'Abbas said: He sent upon them rain that continued day and night for eight days. This meaning was adopted by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Malik, and Muqatil, and al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah chose it. (p-249)

The second: that it is death. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Mujahid, 'Ata', Wahb ibn Munabbih, and Ibn Kathir said likewise.

The third: that it is plague (al-ta'un). This was transmitted from Mujahid and Wahb as well.

As for the lice (al-qaml), there are seven views.

The first: that it is the weevil (al-suss) that infests wheat. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas and said it.

The second: that it is locusts in their early stage (al-dabaa). al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid and 'Ata' said it. Qatadah said: "al-qaml" are the offspring of locusts. Ibn Faris said: al-dabaa is the locust when it moves before its wings have grown.

The third: that they are small black creatures. This was said by al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also said: these creatures are the weevils.

The fourth: that they are dung beetles (al-ju'lan). Habib ibn Abi Thabit said this.

The fifth: that they are lice. 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Zayd ibn Aslam mentioned it.

The sixth: that they are fleas. Ibn Zayd related it.

The seventh: that they are ticks (al-hamnan), singular hamnanah, a kind of tick. Abu 'Ubaydah said this. al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Ya'mur read "al-qaml" with a raised qaf and a sukun on the mim. (p-250)

As for the blood, there are two views. The first: that their water turned into blood; the majority said this. The second: that it was a nosebleed that afflicted them; Zayd ibn Aslam said this.

Explanation of the story

Ibn 'Abbas said: The flood came upon them, so that a man could not go out to his land until they feared drowning. They said: "O Musa, pray to your Lord to remove it from us, and we will believe in you and send the Children of Israel with you." He prayed for them, and Allah removed it from them, and caused to grow for them something that had not grown before. They said: "This is what we used to wish for." So Allah sent upon them locusts, which ate what the earth had produced. They said: "Pray to your Lord for us," and he prayed, and Allah removed it from them. They then stored their crops in their houses, so Allah sent upon them lice, and a man would bring the flour of ten sacks to the mill but would see from it no more than three qafizah. They asked him, and he prayed for them, and He removed it from them, but they did not believe. So Allah sent upon them frogs, and there was nothing more severe than them: they would come to the cooking pots while boiling and seething and throw themselves into them, spoiling their food and extinguishing their fires. The frogs were terrestrial, but Allah made them inherit cold water and moist earth until the Day of Resurrection. They asked him, and he prayed for them, but they did not believe. So Allah sent upon them blood, and their rivers and their wells ran with blood, so they could not find sweet water, while the Children of Israel had sweet water. Whenever a man of them entered the streams of the Children of Israel to draw water, what he entered became blood, while water before him and behind him was clear and sweet, and he could not reach it. Pharaoh said: "I swear by my God, O Musa, if you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe in you and surely send the Children of Israel with you." Musa prayed, and the blood departed and their water became sweet. They said: "By Allah, we will not believe in you, nor send the Children of Israel with you." (p-251)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when the punishment (al-rijz) befell them﴾, meaning: the torment descended upon them. Regarding this punishment there are two views.

The first: that it was a plague (ṭāʿūn) which destroyed seventy thousand of them. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: that it was the punishment which God imposed upon them through locusts, lice, and other things. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The meaning of rijz as punishment is that it is that which shakes (al-muqallqil) with its severity, a severe and successive quaking. The original meaning of rijz in the language is the succession of movements; from this is the saying of the Arabs: a rajzāʾ she-camel, when her legs tremble (p-252) as she stands. And from it is rajz poetry (rajz al-shiʿr), because it is the shortest of verse lines and the transition from one line to another is swift, such as the saying:

"Would that I were in it as a young camel, I would move about in it and dwell."

Al-Khalīl (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) claimed that rajz is not poetry, but rather half-lines and thirds of lines.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿by what He has promised you (bi-mā ʿahida ʿindaka)﴾, regarding which there are four views.

The first: that its meaning is: by what He charged you to call upon Him with. The second: by what He conveyed to you that you should call upon Him, and He would answer you. The third: by what He promised you concerning the removal of punishment from those who believe. The fourth: that this from them is in the sense of an oath, as though they swore by it, by what He promised Him, that He would supplicate on their behalf.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until a term which they must reach﴾, meaning: until the time of their drowning. ﴿Then behold, they break their word﴾, meaning: they violate the covenant.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾. Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī said: We gained victory over them by bringing down Our vengeance upon them, and that vengeance was Our drowning them in the sea (al-yamm). Ibn Qutayba said: al-yamm means the sea in Syriac.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they were heedless of them﴾, regarding which there are two views.

The first: of the signs, and their heedlessness is their neglect of taking heed from them. The second: of the vengeance.

The eastern and western parts of the Levant (al-Sham). This is the view of al-Hasan. The second view: the eastern parts of the land of al-Sham and Egypt. The third: that it is in its unrestricted sense, the east and west of the earth.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah?"﴾ That is: "Shall I seek for you (abghi) a god?" This is a rhetorical question of denunciation (istifham inkar). The commentators, among them Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, said: "The worlds (al-'alamin) here means: the people of their own time."

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 7, verse 141:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [recall] when We delivered you﴾. Ibn ʿAmir recited: "wa-idh anjākum" (﴿and when He delivered you﴾), in the form of the third-person singular masculine (ghaʾib mufrad), i.e., "anjākum" with the subject being Allah in the third person rather than the first-person plural "anjaynākum."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 142:

If it is asked: what is the meaning of ﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾, since it was already known that this was the case when the ten were joined to the thirty?

The answer has several aspects. The first is that it is for emphasis (ta'kid). The second is that it indicates the ten are nights, not hours. The third is that it negates that the completion of the thirty by the ten might be understood as the ten being part of the thirty, because it is possible that it would occur to the mind that they had been twenty nights and were then completed by ten. We have explained in surah al-Baqarah (2:51) why this promise was made.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And set things right﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: command them to reform (al-islah). Muqatil said: be gentle (irfuq).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 143–144:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "You will not see Me"﴾. The deniers of the vision (of Allah) (nufat al-ru'yah) cling to this and say that *an* (أنْ) is for the permanent negation of the future (nafy al-abad). This is a mistake, because it has been used where the meaning is not permanence, in His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:95]. Then He reports of them that they will wish (for death) in the Fire, saying: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:77]. Also, Ibn 'Abbas said in its explanation: "You will not see Me in this world." Others said: this is an answer to Musa's saying "Show me (Yourself)," and he did not mean "Show me in the Hereafter," but in this world, so he was answered concerning what he asked. Some of them said: "You will not see Me by your asking."

In this verse there is evidence that the vision is permissible, because Musa, with his knowledge of Allah the Exalted, asked for it. Had it been impossible, it would not have been permissible for Musa to ask for it. It is not permissible that Musa be ignorant of such a thing, because the knowledge of the prophets of Allah contains no deficiency. Also, Allah the Exalted did not reject his request; He only prevented him from seeing (Him). Had it been impossible for Him, He would have said, "I am not seen." Do you not see that when Nuh said: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hud 11:45], He rejected him saying: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family﴾ [Hud 11:46].

Among what indicates the permissibility of the vision is that He made it conditional on the mountain remaining firm in its place, and that is possible, not impossible, so this shows it is permissible. Do you not see that when the entry of the disbelievers into Paradise was impossible, He tied it to something impossible, saying: ﴿Until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf 7:40].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if it remains firm in its place﴾, i.e., it stays and does not collapse.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: (*tajalla*) means it appeared and became clear.

﴿He made it crumble to dust (dakkan)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *dakkan* (دَكًّا) with tanwin and without the long vowel, here and in (al-Kahf 18:98). 'Asim read *dakkan* here with tanwin and without the long vowel, and in *dakka'* (دَكّاءَ) with the long vowel and without tanwin. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *dakka'* (دَكّاءَ) with the long vowel and without tanwin in both places.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *ja'alahu dakkan* means *mundakkan*, i.e., leveled. *Al-Dakk* means level, and the meaning is: level with the surface of the earth. It is said: a she-camel *dakka'* (دَكّاءُ), meaning one whose hump has gone, with a level back.

Ibn Qutaybah said: as if its hump was *dukka*, i.e., pressed flat. He said: it is said that the original root of *dakakt* is *daqaqt* (I pounded), and the qaf was changed to kaf because the two articulation points are close.

Anas ibn Malik, regarding His saying "made it crumble to dust," said: the mountain sank (into the earth).

Ibn 'Abbas said: the name of the mountain was Zubayr, and it was the greatest mountain in Madyan. The mountains had raised themselves so that He would manifest Himself to them, but Zubayr humbled itself, so He manifested Himself to it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious (sa'iqan)﴾. There are two views concerning it.

The first: he was unconscious (maghshiyyan 'alayhi). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

The second: he was dead. This was said by Qatadah and Muqatil. The first is more correct, because of His saying: ﴿Then when he regained consciousness﴾, and that is not said of a dead person. It was also said: he remained in his swoon for a day and a night.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Glory be to You! I have repented to You"﴾. Concerning what he repented of there are three views.

The first: his asking for the vision. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The second: (repenting of) advancing to ask before being given permission to ask. The third: the belief that His vision is permissible in this world.

Concerning His saying: ﴿"And I am the first of the believers"﴾ there are two views.

The first: that you will not be seen in this world. Abu Salih narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the first of the believers from the Children of Israel. Ikrimah narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Indeed, I have chosen you"﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the *ya'* of *inni* (إنِّي) with a fatha. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read *bi-risalati* (بِرِسالَتِي) (in the singular). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "I have taken you as the elite over the people by My messages and by My speech." If he had heard only the speech of other than Allah, He would not have said "by My messages and My speech," because the angels descend to the prophets with the speech of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 143–144:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "You will not see Me"﴾. The deniers of the vision (of Allah) (nufat al-ru'yah) cling to this and say that *an* (أنْ) is for the permanent negation of the future (nafy al-abad). This is a mistake, because it has been used where the meaning is not permanence, in His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:95]. Then He reports of them that they will wish (for death) in the Fire, saying: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:77]. Also, Ibn 'Abbas said in its explanation: "You will not see Me in this world." Others said: this is an answer to Musa's saying "Show me (Yourself)," and he did not mean "Show me in the Hereafter," but in this world, so he was answered concerning what he asked. Some of them said: "You will not see Me by your asking."

In this verse there is evidence that the vision is permissible, because Musa, with his knowledge of Allah the Exalted, asked for it. Had it been impossible, it would not have been permissible for Musa to ask for it. It is not permissible that Musa be ignorant of such a thing, because the knowledge of the prophets of Allah contains no deficiency. Also, Allah the Exalted did not reject his request; He only prevented him from seeing (Him). Had it been impossible for Him, He would have said, "I am not seen." Do you not see that when Nuh said: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hud 11:45], He rejected him saying: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family﴾ [Hud 11:46].

Among what indicates the permissibility of the vision is that He made it conditional on the mountain remaining firm in its place, and that is possible, not impossible, so this shows it is permissible. Do you not see that when the entry of the disbelievers into Paradise was impossible, He tied it to something impossible, saying: ﴿Until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf 7:40].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if it remains firm in its place﴾, i.e., it stays and does not collapse.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: (*tajalla*) means it appeared and became clear.

﴿He made it crumble to dust (dakkan)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *dakkan* (دَكًّا) with tanwin and without the long vowel, here and in (al-Kahf 18:98). 'Asim read *dakkan* here with tanwin and without the long vowel, and in *dakka'* (دَكّاءَ) with the long vowel and without tanwin. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *dakka'* (دَكّاءَ) with the long vowel and without tanwin in both places.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *ja'alahu dakkan* means *mundakkan*, i.e., leveled. *Al-Dakk* means level, and the meaning is: level with the surface of the earth. It is said: a she-camel *dakka'* (دَكّاءُ), meaning one whose hump has gone, with a level back.

Ibn Qutaybah said: as if its hump was *dukka*, i.e., pressed flat. He said: it is said that the original root of *dakakt* is *daqaqt* (I pounded), and the qaf was changed to kaf because the two articulation points are close.

Anas ibn Malik, regarding His saying "made it crumble to dust," said: the mountain sank (into the earth).

Ibn 'Abbas said: the name of the mountain was Zubayr, and it was the greatest mountain in Madyan. The mountains had raised themselves so that He would manifest Himself to them, but Zubayr humbled itself, so He manifested Himself to it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious (sa'iqan)﴾. There are two views concerning it.

The first: he was unconscious (maghshiyyan 'alayhi). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

The second: he was dead. This was said by Qatadah and Muqatil. The first is more correct, because of His saying: ﴿Then when he regained consciousness﴾, and that is not said of a dead person. It was also said: he remained in his swoon for a day and a night.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Glory be to You! I have repented to You"﴾. Concerning what he repented of there are three views.

The first: his asking for the vision. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The second: (repenting of) advancing to ask before being given permission to ask. The third: the belief that His vision is permissible in this world.

Concerning His saying: ﴿"And I am the first of the believers"﴾ there are two views.

The first: that you will not be seen in this world. Abu Salih narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the first of the believers from the Children of Israel. Ikrimah narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Indeed, I have chosen you"﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the *ya'* of *inni* (إنِّي) with a fatha. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read *bi-risalati* (بِرِسالَتِي) (in the singular). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "I have taken you as the elite over the people by My messages and by My speech." If he had heard only the speech of other than Allah, He would not have said "by My messages and My speech," because the angels descend to the prophets with the speech of Allah.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 145:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything﴾. Regarding the substance of the tablets there are seven opinions.

The first: they were emerald (zabarjad, topaz or chrysolite), related by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they were ruby (yaqut), related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The third: they were green emerald (zumurrud akhdar), related by Mujahid. The fourth: they were hail (barad), related by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fifth: they were wood, related by al-Hasan. The sixth: they were rock, related by Wahb ibn Munabbih. The seventh: they were emerald and ruby, related by Muqatil. Regarding their number there are four opinions.

The first: they were seven, narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they were two tablets, related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and preferred by al-Farra'. He said: God, the Exalted, called them "tablets" (in the plural) according to the Arab usage of applying the plural to the dual, as in His saying: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78], meaning Dawud and Sulayman, and His saying: ﴿Your hearts have certainly inclined﴾. The third: they were ten, related by Wahb. The fourth: they were nine, related by Muqatil.

Regarding His saying ﴿concerning everything﴾ there are two opinions. The first: concerning everything a person needs in his religion, of what is lawful and unlawful, obligatory and otherwise. The second: concerning the wisdoms and lessons.

(p-259) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿admonition﴾, meaning a prohibition of ignorance. And ﴿detailed explanation﴾, meaning a clarification of everything concerning the commands, the prohibitions, the limits and the rulings.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So take hold of it with strength﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first: with determination and resolve, related by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: with obedience, related by Abu al-'Aliyah. The third: with gratitude, related by Juwaybir.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And command your people to take the best of it﴾. If it is said: Does it not contain what is not good? Then there are two answers.

The first: the meaning is "they should take its goodness, and all of it is good," related by Qutrub. Ibn al-Anbari said: "the best" (ahsan) stands in place of "good" (hasan), as al-Farazdaq said:

"Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mighty and lofty."

That is, "mighty and lofty." Others said: "the best" here is a silah (a particle that is grammatically superfluous), and the meaning is: they should take it.

The second: some of what is in it is better than other parts. Regarding this there are five opinions.

The first: they were commanded in it to do good and forbidden from evil, so doing good is the best.

The second: it contained good things, some better than others, such as retaliation (qisas), pardon, self-defence and patience, so they were commanded to take the best of them. Al-Zajjaj mentioned these two opinions.

According to this opinion, the meaning is that they follow the resolute (ʿaza'im) and the virtuous acts. According to the preceding one, the meaning is that they follow what is described as good, which is obedience, and avoid what is described as ugly, which is disobedience.

The third: the best of them are the obligatory acts (fara'id) and the supererogatory acts (nawafil), and the lowest in goodness is the permissible (mubah).

(p-260) The fourth: a word may have two or three meanings, and it is turned to the one most fitting to the truth.

The fifth: the best of them is combining the obligatory acts with the supererogatory acts.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions.

The first: it is Hell, related by al-Hasan and Mujahid. The second: it is the abode of Pharaoh and his people, which is Egypt, related by 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi. The third: it is the dwellings of those among the tyrants and the 'Amalaqah who perished, which He showed them when they entered Syria, related by Qatadah. The fourth: it is the places where the defiantly disobedient fell, related by al-Suddi. The meaning of the statement is: I will show you the outcome of whoever opposes My command. This is a threat to the one who opposes, and a warning to the one who complies.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 146–147:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾. Regarding this verse there are two opinions.

One of them: it is specific to the people of Egypt concerning the signs they saw. The second: it is general, and this is the more sound (ashahh). Regarding the signs there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the signs of the recited Books. Then, concerning the meaning of the statement, there are three opinions. The first: I will prevent them from understanding them. The second: I will prevent them from believing in them. The third: I will turn them away from objecting to them by way of nullification. (p-261) The second: they are the signs of created things, such as the heaven, the earth, the sun, the moon and others, so the meaning is: I will turn them away from reflecting and taking lesson from what I have created. Regarding the meaning of "they are arrogant" (yatakabbarun) there are two opinions.

One of them: they are arrogant about faith and following the Messenger.

The second: they belittle people and regard themselves as superior to them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "sabila al-rushd" (سَبِيلَ الرُّشْدِ) with a dammah on the ra' and lightened. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sabila al-rashad" (سَبِيلَ الرَّشَدِ) with a fathah on the ra' and the shin, emphasized (muthaqqalah).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is because they﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: God did that to them because ﴿they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾, meaning: in their abandoning of faith in them and of reflecting upon them, they were in the position of the heedless. It is also permissible that the meaning is: and they were heedless of their consequence (jaza'ihā).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 146–147:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾. Regarding this verse there are two opinions.

One of them: it is specific to the people of Egypt concerning the signs they saw. The second: it is general, and this is the more sound (ashahh). Regarding the signs there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the signs of the recited Books. Then, concerning the meaning of the statement, there are three opinions. The first: I will prevent them from understanding them. The second: I will prevent them from believing in them. The third: I will turn them away from objecting to them by way of nullification. (p-261) The second: they are the signs of created things, such as the heaven, the earth, the sun, the moon and others, so the meaning is: I will turn them away from reflecting and taking lesson from what I have created. Regarding the meaning of "they are arrogant" (yatakabbarun) there are two opinions.

One of them: they are arrogant about faith and following the Messenger.

The second: they belittle people and regard themselves as superior to them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "sabila al-rushd" (سَبِيلَ الرُّشْدِ) with a dammah on the ra' and lightened. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sabila al-rashad" (سَبِيلَ الرَّشَدِ) with a fathah on the ra' and the shin, emphasized (muthaqqalah).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is because they﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: God did that to them because ﴿they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾, meaning: in their abandoning of faith in them and of reflecting upon them, they were in the position of the heedless. It is also permissible that the meaning is: and they were heedless of their consequence (jaza'ihā).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 148:

His saying, Exalted is He: لِلْمِقَاتِ (for Our appointed time). ﴿مِن حُلِيِّهِمْ﴾ (from their ornaments). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "مِن حُلِيِّهِمْ" with a ḍammah on the ḥā'. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "حِلِيِّهِمْ" with a kasrah on the ḥā'. Ya'qub read it with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a sukun on the lām, and a light (unstressed) yā'. Al-ḥulī is the plural of ḥulī, like thady and thudī, and it is a name for what one adorns oneself with of gold and silver. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads the ḥā' with a kasrah in "حُلِيِّهِمْ" has made the ḥā' follow the kasrah of the lām. Al-jasad is that which does not understand or discern; it means only the body (juththah). Ibn al-Anbari said: mentioning "al-jasad" indicates that it had no spirit in it, and that its form was a mere image and likeness, with no spirit or soul joined to it. As for al-khuwar, it is the lowing of a cow; it is said: the cow khārat yakhūru, and jaʾarat yajʾaru. It has been transmitted from the Arabs that they use, for the sound of animals resembling the human voice: raghā the camel, jarjara, hadara, and qabqaba; ṣahala and ḥamḥama for the horse; shahiqa and nahaqa for the donkey; shaḥaja for the mule; thaghat and ya'arat for the sheep; tha'ajat for the ewe; baghama and nazaba for the gazelle; za'ara and nahata and na'ata for the lion; wa'wa'a for the wolf; nahama for the elephant; zaqaḥa for the monkey; ḍabaḥa for the fox; 'awā and nabaḥa for the dog; mā'at for the tomcat; ṣa'at for the mouse; naghaqa (with a ghayn marked with a dot) for the raven; zaqa'a and saqa'a for the rooster; ṣafara for the vulture; hadara for the pigeon; hadala; naqaḍat and naqqat for the frogs; and 'azafat for the jinn. Ibn 'Abbas said: whenever the calf lowed, they prostrated, and whenever it fell silent, they raised their heads. In the narration of Abu Salih from him: it lowed one single lowing and did not follow it with another like it. Wahb and Muqatil said the same. Mujahid used to say: its lowing was the rustling of the wind within it; and this indicates that there was no breath of life in it. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli and Abu Mijlaz read: "لَهُ جِوَارٌ" with a raised jīm.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿أَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّهُ لَا يُكَلِّمُهُمْ﴾ (Did they not see that it does not speak to them?), i.e., it cannot speak to them. ﴿وَلَا يَهْدِيهِمْ سَبِيلًا﴾ (nor guide them to a path), i.e., it does not show them a way to any proof. "اتَّخَذُوهُ" (They took it), meaning they took it as a god. ﴿وَكَانُوا ظَالِمِينَ﴾ (and they were wrongdoers). Ibn 'Abbas said: polytheists.

(p-263) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they were overcome with remorse﴾ meaning: they regretted. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said of a man who regrets what he has done and grieves over what he has neglected: "He has been struck in his hand (saqata fi yadihi)," and "It has been struck in his hand (usqita fi yadihi)."

Ibn al-Sumayfa and Abu Imran al-Jawni read "suqita" with a fatha on the sin. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "When regret fell into their hands," likening what occurs in the heart and soul to what is seen with the eye. The exegetes said: this regret of theirs came only after Musa had returned.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy upon us﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read ﴿yarhamna rabbuna﴾ and ﴿wa yaghfir lana﴾ with the ya' and the raf' (nominative). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "tarhamuna" and "taghfiru lana" with the ta' and "rabbana" with the nasb (accusative).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿angry and grieved﴾ Regarding "asaf" there are three opinions.

The first: that it means sorrowful; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi. The second: distress, said by Mujahid. The third: that it means very intense anger, said by Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj. Abu al-Darda' said: "Asaf" is a station beyond anger, more intense than it.

(p-264) His saying, the Exalted: He said, i.e., to his people: ﴿Evil is what you did as my successors after me﴾ The people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read the ya' of "ba'di" with a fatha; the meaning: evil is what you did after my departure, by worshipping the calf. ﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾ Al-Farra' said: It is said: "ajiltu al-amr wa al-shay'" meaning I preceded it, and this verse is an instance of it. And "a'jaltuhu" means I urged it. Ibn 'Abbas said: Did you hasten the appointment of your Lord, so that you did not wait for it? Al-Hasan said: He means the promise of forty nights.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾ those in which was the Torah. Regarding the cause of his throwing them down there are two opinions.

The first: it was anger when he saw them worshipping the calf; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: when he saw the virtues of a nation other than his own, the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), it weighed heavily upon him, so he threw them down; this was said by Qatada, though this view is far-fetched. Ibn 'Abbas said: When he threw down the tablets, they shattered; six-sevenths of them were lifted up, and one-seventh remained.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he seized his brother by the head﴾ Regarding what he seized of his head there are three opinions.

The first: his beard and forelock. The second: the hair of his head. The third: his ear. It was said: he did this because he suspected that he had disobeyed God by staying among them and not following him, and by informing him of what they had introduced after him, so that he would return to them and set them right and bring them back to the truth; and this is his saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Son of my mother﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read "qala ibna umma" with a fatha (nasb). Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read it with a kasra on the mim, and likewise in [Ta-Ha: 94]. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads with a fatha on the mim does so because of the frequent use of this name; whoever reads with a kasra makes it an annexation to himself after having made it a single name. Among the Arabs there are those who say "ya ibna ummi" with the ya' retained. The poet said:

(p-265)

Oh son of my mother, and oh twin of my soul, you are my successor in a severe age.

Abu 'Ali said: It may be that whoever reads "ya ibna umma" with a fatha intends the alif to be elided, and whoever reads "ibni ummi" with a kasra elides the ya'. If it is asked: why did he say "ya ibna umma" and not "ya ibna abb" (son of my father)? The answer is that Ibn 'Abbas said: he was his brother from his father and mother, and he said this to him only to soften him toward him. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: A person is more tender when the mother is mentioned than when the father is mentioned. It was also said that he was a brother only on his mother's side, not his father's; this was related by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the people﴾ meaning the worshippers of the calf. ﴿Deemed me weak﴾ i.e., they made me abject. ﴿So do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾ Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, Malik ibn Dinar and Ibn 'Asim read "fa la tushmit" with a ta' with a fatha and a mim with a fatha, and "al-a'da'" with the raf'. Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Dahhak and Abu Raja' read "fa la tashmit" with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the mim, and "al-a'da'" with the nasb. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Abi 'Abla read the same, except that they put "al-a'da'" in the raf'. By "the enemies" is meant the worshippers of the calf. ﴿And do not place me﴾ in Your wrath and Your punishment of me ﴿among the wrongdoing people﴾, who are the worshippers of the calf. When his excuse for his brother became clear to him, ﴿he said: My Lord, forgive me.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And humiliation in the life of this world﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions.

The first: that it is the jizya (poll tax); this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: what they were commanded to do, namely killing themselves; this was said by al-Zajjaj. According to the first view, what is attributed to them of the jizya is in regard to their children, because (p-266) those people were killed and did not pay the jizya. 'Atiyya said: This verse refers to what befell the Banu Qurayza and the Nadir of killing and expulsion, because they turned away from the worshippers of the calf and approved of it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: Thus do I punish whoever takes a god other than Me. Malik ibn Anas said: There is no innovator except that he finds abasement above his head, and he recited this verse. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: There is no possessor of innovation on earth except that he finds an abasement covering him, and he said: It is in the Book of God, the Exalted. They said: Where is it? He said: Did you not hear His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world﴾? They said: O Abu Muhammad, this is specific to the people of the calf. He said: No, recite what follows it: ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾, so it applies to every fabricator and innovator until the Day of Resurrection.

(p-263) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they were overcome with remorse﴾ meaning: they regretted. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said of a man who regrets what he has done and grieves over what he has neglected: "He has been struck in his hand (saqata fi yadihi)," and "It has been struck in his hand (usqita fi yadihi)."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 153:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who committed evil deeds﴾, regarding which there are two opinions.

One of them: they are shirk (associating partners with God). The second: shirk and other sins besides it. ﴿Then repented after them﴾, meaning after the evil deeds. Regarding His saying "and believed" there are two opinions.

One of them: they believed in God, and this fits with the view of the one who said that the evil deeds are shirk.

The second: they believed that God, may He be exalted, accepts repentance. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after them﴾, meaning after the evil deeds.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 154:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu ʿImran recited "sakata" (سَكَتَ) with a fatha on the sin and a shadda on the kaf, and with a taa' after it, and "al-ghadaba" (الغَضَبَ) in the accusative. Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibn Yaʿmur and al-Jahdari recited "sakata" with a damma on the sin and a shadda on the kaf with a kasra. Ibn Masʿud, ʿIkrima and Talha recited "sakana" (سَكَنَ) with a nun. Al-Zajjaj said: "Sakata" is in the sense of "sakana," as one says: sakata yaskutu sakتan, meaning it became still; and sakata yaskutu sakتan and sukutan, meaning he ceased speaking. He said: Some of them said the meaning is: "When Moses was silent from the anger," by inversion (ʿala al-qalb), as they say: "I put the qalansuwa (cap) on my head," and the meaning is: "I put my head into the cap." The first view is the view of the people of Arabic grammar.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿took up the tablets﴾, meaning those which he had cast down. Regarding His saying: ﴿and in their inscription﴾ there are two views.

One: and in what remained of them; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: and in what was abrogated in them; this is the view of Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for those who fear their Lord﴾. Concerning them there are two views.

One: that it is general to those who fear Allah; this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that they are specifically the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ); this is the meaning of the saying of Qatada.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 155:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾. The meaning is: he chose from among his people, so "min" (from) was omitted. The Arabs say: "I chose you the people," meaning: "I chose you from the people." And they recited:

"From us is the one who was chosen among men for generosity and bounty, when the stormy winds blow violently."

This is the statement of Ibn Qutayba, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Regarding this appointed time (miqat) there are four opinions.

The first: it is the appointed time that Allah set for Musa to receive the Torah, and He commanded him to come with seventy men. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Nawf al-Bakali also said this.

The second: it is an appointed time that Allah set for Musa, and He commanded him to choose seventy men from his people to supplicate to their Lord. They supplicated and said: "O Allah, give us what You have not given anyone before us, and do not give it to anyone after us." Allah disliked that, and the quaking (al-rajfa) seized them. This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is an appointed time that Allah set for Musa, because the Children of Israel said to him: "A group claims that Allah does not speak to you, so take with you a group of us that they may hear His speech and believe, and the accusation will be removed." Allah revealed to him: "Choose from their best seventy, then ascend the mountain with them, you and Harun, and appoint Yusha' ibn Nun as your successor." He did so. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The fourth: it is an appointed time that Allah set for Musa to meet him with some of the Children of Israel, so that he might apologize to Him for the act of the worshippers of the calf. This was said by al-Suddi. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: Musa would not come except with His permission.

As for the quaking (al-rajfa), it is intense movement. Regarding the cause of its seizing them there are four opinions.

The first: their claim against Musa that he had killed Harun. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The second: their transgression in supplication, which we have mentioned in the narration of Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that they did not forbid the worshippers of the calf and did not disapprove. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas. Qatada and Ibn Juraij said: they did not enjoin good, did not forbid evil, and did not separate from them.

The fourth: that they asked to hear the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, and when they heard it they said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ [al-Baqara: 55]. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: "My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me [as well]."﴾ al-Suddi said: Musa stood weeping and saying: "My Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel when I come to them, after You have destroyed their best?" ﴿Had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me.﴾ al-Zajjaj said: Had You willed, You would have caused them to die before You tested them with what caused the quaking upon them. It was also said: Had You willed, You would have destroyed them before our departure and me, so the Children of Israel would have witnessed that and would not have accused me.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ al-Mubarrad said: this is a question of entreaty, meaning: do not destroy us. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is a question carrying the sense of denial, meaning: You are not doing that. And "the foolish" (al-sufaha') here refers to the worshippers of the calf. al-Farra' said: Musa thought they had been destroyed because of their companions' taking of the calf, but they were only destroyed because of their saying: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is only Your trial﴾. Regarding it there are two statements.

One: it is the testing (ibtila'), narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-'Aliya said this too.

The second: it is the punishment, narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatada said this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 160–162:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We divided them﴾ — meaning the people of Musa — He says: We separated them ﴿into twelve tribes﴾ — meaning the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob). They were twelve sons, and each one of them became the forefather of a tribe (sibt). Al-Farra' said: He said ﴿twelve﴾ [in the feminine form, ithnatay 'ashrata] although the word sibt is masculine, because after it comes ﴿ummam﴾ (nations), so he gave it the feminine gender in reference to the nations. Had he said ithnay 'ashar, agreeing with sibt in the masculine, it would have been permissible. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: We divided them into twelve groups (firqa). ﴿Asbatan﴾ is an adjective of firqa, as if he were saying: We made them asbat and divided them into asbat. So asbatan is a substitute (badal) for ﴿twelve﴾, and ummaman is an adjective of asbat. The asbat among the offspring of Ishaq hold the position of tribes (qaba'il), in order to distinguish between the offspring of Isma'il and the offspring of Ishaq. Abu 'Ubayda said: The asbat are the tribes of the Children of Israel; the singular is sibt. It is said: "Of which sibt are you?" That is: of which tribe and kind?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 163:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ask them﴾ meaning the descendants of the Jews. This is a question of confirmation and rebuke, confirming them upon their ancient disbelief and their opposition to their forefathers, the Prophets, and informing them of what none knows except through revelation. Regarding "the town" there are five opinions.

The first: that it is Ayla. This was related by Murrah from Ibn Mas'ud, and by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and al-Suddi also said so.

The second: that it is Madyan. This was related by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that it is the shore of Madyan. This was narrated from Qatada.

The fourth: that it is Tiberias. This was said by al-Zuhri.

The fifth: that it is a village called Muqna, between Madyan and 'Aynuna. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The meaning of ﴿situated by the sea﴾ is: adjacent to the sea, near it, and on its shore. ﴿When they transgressed﴾: al-Zajjaj said: that is, they wronged. It is said: "So-and-so transgressed (ʿadā yaʿdū ʿudwānan, ʿaddāʾan, ʿadwan, ʿudūwan) when he wronged." The position of "idh" (when) is in the accusative; the meaning is: ask them about the time of their transgression on the Sabbath. ﴿When their fish came to them﴾ is also in the accusative position, governed by "yaʿdūna" (they transgress). The meaning is: ask them about the time when they transgressed, at the time of the coming. "Shurra'an" means "shurraʿan" (openly), i.e., visible. ﴿Thus We test them﴾: that is, like this severe trial, We test them for their wickedness. It is possible, though remote, that the meaning of ﴿and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them﴾ is thus, i.e., they did not come to them openly; and "nabluhum" (We test them) would then be a new independent sentence. Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Aban, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "yasbatun" with a dammah on the ya' (yusbituna).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 164:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when a community among them said﴾. The exegetes said: The people of the town split into three groups: one group hunted and ate; one group forbade and admonished; and one group refrained from the hunting and said to the group that forbade: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?﴾ They blamed them for admonishing a people who they knew would not desist. Then the forbidding group said: ﴿As a excuse before your Lord﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read مَعْذِرَةٌ (ma'dhiratun) in the nominative, meaning: our admonition of them is an excuse (ma'dhirah), and the sense is that enjoining good is obligatory upon us, so admonishing these people is an excuse before Allah. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read مَعْذِرَةً (ma'dhiratan) in the accusative, which is according to the meaning "we offer an excuse, an excuse." ﴿And perhaps they will fear Allah﴾: that is, it is possible that they will benefit from the admonition and abandon disobedience.

[(p-٢٧٨)] Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, meaning: they abandoned what they had been admonished with. ﴿We saved those who forbade evil﴾, and they were the ones who forbade the wrong. ﴿And those who did wrong﴾ were the transgressors regarding the Sabbath.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿with a wretched punishment﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited بَئِيس on the pattern of فَعِيل, so the hamzah is between the ba' and the ya'. Nafi' recited "بَيْسَ" with a kasrah on the ba' and without hamzah. Ibn 'Amir recited likewise, except that he used hamzah. Khárijah related from Nafi': "بَيْسٍ" with a fathah on the ba' and without hamzah, on the pattern of فَعْل. Abu Bakr related from 'Asim: "بَيَأْس" on the pattern of فَيْعَل. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, and Ayyub recited: "بَيْآَس" on the pattern of فَيْعال. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Mu'adh al-Qari recited: "بِئْس" with a fathah on the ba' and a kasrah on the hamzah, without ya', on the pattern of نَعِس. al-Dahhak and 'Ikrimah recited: "بَيِّس" with a shaddah on the ya', like قَيِّم. Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu Mijlaz recited: "بَئِس" with a fathah on the ba' and the sin, and a kasrah on the hamzah, without ya' or alif, on the pattern of فِعْل. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu Raja' recited: "بائِس" with an alif and a long vowel after the ba', and a kasrah on the hamzah, on the pattern of فاعِل. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-Ba'is means the severe. He recited:

"Enraged against me, and you do not see in them any trace of severity (ba'isan)."

al-Zajjaj said: It is said بَئِسَ يَبْأَسُ بَأْسًا. al-'Ati means the one who persists strongly in corruption, the rebellious one who does not accept admonition. Ibn Jarir said: ﴿When they became insolent﴾ means they rebelled against what they had been forbidden. We have already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah [2:65] the story of their transformation. al-Hasan al-Basri used to say: By Allah, the flesh of these fish is not greater in the sight of Allah than the blood of a Muslim people.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when your Lord declared﴾. There are four opinions regarding (تَأَذَّنَ):

First: it means "made known" (a'lama), said by al-Hasan and Ibn Qutaybah, and he said: it is from آذَنْتُكَ بِالأمْرِ (I informed you of the matter). Ibn al-Anbari said: تَأْذَنَ here means أذِنَ, just as one says تَعْلَمُ أنَّ فُلانًا قائِمٌ, meaning اعْلَمْ (know that so-and-so is standing). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: meaning "He made known to the prophets of the Children of Israel."

Second: it means "decreed" (hatama), said by 'Ata'.

Third: it means "promised" (wa'd), said by Qutrub.

Fourth: it means "swore" (ta'alla), said by al-Zajjaj.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He will surely send against them﴾, meaning against the Jews. Mujahid said: against the Jews and the Christians for their disobedience. ﴿Those who will afflict them with the worst torment﴾, meaning: who will put them in charge of ﴿the worst torment﴾. Regarding who is meant by those sent against them, there are two opinions. One: it is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Two: it is the Arabs, who used to impose the kharaj tax on them, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: No prophet ever imposed the kharaj except Musa, who collected it for thirteen years, then it ceased until the Prophet (ﷺ). al-Suddi said: Allah sent the Arabs against them, who took the jizyah from them and killed them.

First: the taking of the jizyah, related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Second: poverty and the jizyah, related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.
