Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 168:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We divided them into communities upon the earth﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "We scattered them into groups." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are the Jews; there is no city without a group of them in it." Muqatil said: "They are the Children of Israel." It was also said: its meaning is the dispersal of their affairs and the scattering of their word. ﴿Among them are the righteous ones﴾, and they are the believers in 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. ﴿And among them are those who are other than that﴾, and they are the disbelievers. Ibn Jarir said: "They were in this state before 'Isa was sent, and before their apostasy."

(p-280) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We tested them﴾, that is: We tried them with good things, which are goodness, fertility, and well-being, and with bad things, which are drought, evil, and hardships. Good things and bad things both urge toward obedience: as for blessings, there is the seeking of their increase and fear of their loss; and as for afflictions, there is the seeking of their removal and safety from them. ﴿That perhaps they might return﴾, that is: so that they might repent.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 169:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then there succeeded them﴾, meaning: after those whom We have described. "Khalf" (khalf), and al-Jawni and al-Jahdari read "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam. Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-khalf" and "al-khalaf" are one and the same; but some people make the vowelled form (with fatha) for the righteous and the sukun form for the non-righteous. Ibn Qutayba said: "al-khalf" is the inferior among people and among speech; it is said: "this is khalf of speech." Ibn al-Anbari said: The Arabs most often use "al-khalf," with the lam silent, for the inferior and blameworthy, and the lam is vowelled with fatha for the excellent and praiseworthy. It may be that "al-khalf" is applied to the praiseworthy and "al-khalaf" to the blameworthy; however, what we have mentioned is the preferred view. Regarding who is meant by this khalf there are three opinions.

The first: they are the Jews, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd. The second: the Christians. The third: that the khalf is from the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), and both opinions are reported from Mujahid.

If it is said: "khalf" is singular, so how did He say: ﴿they take﴾? Similarly He said in [Maryam 59]: ﴿they wasted [prayer]﴾. Ibn al-Anbari reported from him two answers.

(p-281) One of them: that "khalf" is the plural of "khalif," just as "rakb" is the plural of "rakib" and "shurb" is the plural of "sharib."

The second: that "khalf" is a verbal noun which can be used for the dual and the plural, and for the masculine and the feminine.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They inherited the Book﴾, meaning: it passed to them by way of inheritance from predecessor to successor. Thus there are three opinions regarding "the Book."

The first: that it is the Torah. The second: the Gospel. The third: the Qur'an.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They take the goods of this lower life﴾, meaning: this world, and what of it comes to them. It was said: He called it "'aradh" (goods) because of the brevity of its duration. Ibn 'Abbas said: they take whatever they love, of lawful or unlawful things. It was said: it refers to bribery in judgment. Regarding describing it as "al-adna" (the lower) there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is from "dunuww" (nearness). The second: that it is from "dana'a" (baseness).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It will be forgiven us﴾, there are two opinions regarding this.

One of them: the meaning is: "We will not be held accountable," presumptuously desiring falsehood from Allah.

The second: that it is a sin which Allah will forgive us, hoping for the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And if there comes to them goods like it, they will take it﴾ there are two opinions.

One of them: the meaning is that nothing satisfies them; they take without need, as said by al-Hasan.

The second: that they are people persisting in sins, as said by Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they would not say about Allah except the truth?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah emphasized upon them in the Torah that they should not say about Allah except the truth, but they said falsehood, which is what they asserted about Allah of forgiveness for their sins which they did not repent of; and there is no promise of forgiveness in the Torah along with persistence.

(p-282) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they studied what is in it﴾ is conjoined to "inherited," and the meaning of "they studied what is in it" is that they read it; it is as if He said: they opposed it knowingly. ﴿And the Last Abode﴾, meaning: what is in it of reward, ﴿is better for those who are righteous. Will you not then reason?﴾ that what remains is better than what perishes. Ibn 'Amir, Nafi', and Hafs from 'Asim read with the "ta" (you will not reason), and the rest with the "ya".

The Exalted said: ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read "yumassikūna" with a doubled sīn (shaddah). They read ﴿And do not hold fast to the marriage ties of disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:10] with a single sīn. Abu 'Amr read both with the doubled sīn. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim that he read both with a single sīn. It is said: "masaktu bi-l-shay'" (I held onto the thing), "tamassaktu bihi," "istamsaktu bihi," and "imtasaktu bihi" (all meaning I held fast to it).

This verse was revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book who preserved its limits and did not distort it, among them [ʿAbd Allah] ibn Salam and his companions.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The predicate of "alladhīna" is "innā" and what follows it, and it has an implied pronoun (ḍamīr) after "al-muslihīn." Its interpretation is: "And those who hold fast to the Book, indeed We do not waste the reward of the righteous among them." For this reason He promised them the preservation of their reward on a condition, since some of them were not righteous.

He said: Some of the grammarians said: "al-muslihūn" refers back to "alladhīna." The summarized meaning according to them is: "And those who hold fast to the Book and establish the prayer, indeed We do not waste their reward." Their pronominal reference (kināya) was made explicit as "al-muslihīn," just as one says: "ʿAlī, I met al-Kisa'ī," and "Abu Saʿīd, I narrated from al-Khudrī," meaning: "I met him and narrated from him." The poet said:

"O my Lord, Layla is with You in every place,
and You are the One in whose mercy of Allah I hope."

He meant "in His mercy," and so he made the pronoun of the hā' explicit.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 171:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when We raised the mountain over them﴾, meaning: and remember for them when We lifted (nataqna) the mountain, i.e., We raised it up. Mujahid said: The mountain was uprooted from the earth and raised above them like a canopy (zullah), and it was said to them: "You will either believe, or it will fall upon you."

Qatadah said: They had descended to the foot of the mountain, so it was raised above them, and He said: "You will either take hold of My command, or I will drop it upon you."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they thought that it was going to fall upon them﴾ — concerning this there are two views.

One of them: it is the well-known meaning of ẓann (thought/supposition). The second: it is in the sense of yaqin (certainty). The rest of the verse has been explained in Surat al-Baqarah [2:63].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 172:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah took the covenant from the back of Adam at Nuʿman" — and Nuʿman is near ʿArafah — as mentioned by Ibn Qutaybah. So He brought forth from his loins every offspring He had created, and scattered them before Him like specks (dharr), then spoke to them directly, and said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes, we testify﴾ — ﴿lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: Indeed, we were unaware of this﴾ (p-284).

The meaning of the verse is: "And when your Lord took from the backs of the Children of Adam." So His saying ﴿from their backs﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the Children of Adam." It was said: He said ﴿from their backs﴾ and did not say "from the back of Adam" because He brought some of them out from the backs of others, so He dispensed with mentioning the back of Adam, since it is known that they are his children and they were brought out from his back.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿their offspring (dhurriyyatihim)﴾, Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisai read ﴿dhurriyyatahum﴾ in the singular. Nafi`, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿dhurriyyatihim﴾ in the plural. Abu ʿAli said: the word dhurriyyah may be a plural and may be a singular.

As for His saying: ﴿and made them testify concerning themselves﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: He made them testify against themselves by their own acknowledgment; this is the view of Muqatil.

The second: He guided them, through His creation, to His Oneness; this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: He made some of them testify against others by their acknowledgment of that; this is the view of Ibn Jarir.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ The meaning is: He said to them, "Am I not your Lord?" This is a question of affirmation. They said: "Yes, we testify that You are our Lord." al-Suddi said: His saying "we testify" is a report from Allah, the Exalted, about Himself and His angels, that they bore witness to the acknowledgment of the Children of Adam (p-285). It is good to pause at His saying "Yes," because the speech of the offspring has ended. Al-Kalbi claimed that when the offspring said "Yes," Allah said to the angels, "Bear witness," and they said, "We bear witness." Abu al-ʿAliyah narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: He gathered them all together, made them into pairs, then shaped them, then questioned them, then said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said, "Yes, we testify," that You are our God. He said: "Then I call the seven heavens and the seven earths to witness against you, and I call your father Adam to witness against you, lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: Indeed, we were unaware of this." Al-Suddi said: a group answered Him willingly, and a group answered Him unwillingly out of taqiyyah (dissimulation).

As for His saying, the Exalted: (lest they say) — Abu ʿAmr read ﴿an yaqulu﴾ and ﴿aw yaqulu﴾ with the ya in both. The rest read with the ta in both. Abu ʿAli said: The proof for Abu ʿAmr is His saying ﴿And when your Lord took﴾ and His saying ﴿They said: Yes﴾; the proof for those who read with the ta is that address has occurred in the speech: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we testify.﴾ The meaning of His saying "yaqulu" is "lest they say," like His saying "lest the earth shake with you" (an tamida bikum).

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were﴾ there are two views.

One: it refers to the covenant and the acknowledgment.

The second: it refers to the knowledge that He is the Creator. The exegetes said: this verse is a reminder from Allah, the Exalted, of the covenant He took from all the accountable, and an argument against them, lest the disbelievers say: "Indeed, we were unaware of this covenant; we did not remember it." Their forgetfulness does not nullify the argument, once Allah, the Exalted, has informed of it through the tongue of the truthful Prophet (ﷺ). When this is established by the word of the truthful one, it stands in the souls in the place of remembrance, so the argument based on it is established.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 173:

﴿Or you should say, "It was only that our fathers associated partners with Allah before us, and we were descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ (p-286) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or you should say, "It was only that our fathers associated partners with Allah before us, and we were descendants after them"﴾, meaning: so we followed their path in ignorance on our part of Your divinity, ﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾, in their claim that there is a god with You. Allah cut off their argument with this, by reminding them of the covenant taken from each one of them. The body of the people of knowledge, according to what we have explained, hold that He questioned the atoms (al-dharr), and placed in them intellects and understandings by which they recognised what was presented to them. Some have mentioned that the meaning of taking the descendants is bringing them out into the world after they had been drops of seed, and the meaning of making them testify against themselves is compelling them to know that He is their Creator through the signs and proofs He manifested to them. When they knew that, and everything they saw and witnessed called them to affirmation, they were in the position of those who bear witness and cause witness against themselves to its soundness, as He said: ﴿testifying against themselves to disbelief﴾ [al-Tawba: 17], meaning: they are in the position of the two witnesses, even if they did not say, "We are disbelievers," just as a man says, "My limbs have testified to your truthfulness," meaning: I have known it. From this category is His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 19], meaning: He made clear and informed. Ibn al-Anbari has related something like this view, but the first is more correct, because it agrees with the reports (al-athar).

"And thus We detail the signs" — that is, just as We made clear the signs concerning the taking of the covenant, so that the servants might reflect upon them and act in accordance with what they require. "So that they may return" — that is, and in order that they might turn back from the disbelief they are upon to monotheism (al-tawhid).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 175:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: This is a continuation of what came before, and the meaning is: recite to them when your Lord took (the covenant). ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾. There are six opinions concerning him.

The first: He is a man from the Children of Israel called Bal'am ibn Ba'ur (Bal'am ibn Abar). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn 'Abbas said: Bal'am ibn Ba'ura. It is also reported from him that he was Bil'am ibn Ba'ur, and this was the view of Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Suddi. Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that Balam was from the people of Yemen. Ibn Abi Talha related from him that he was from the city of the giants (al-Jabbarin).

The second: He is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. This was said by 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Abu Rawq and Zayd ibn Aslam. Umayya had read the scriptures and knew that God would send a messenger, and he hoped that he himself would be that messenger. When the Prophet ﷺ was sent, he envied him and disbelieved.

The third: He is Abu 'Amir the monk. al-Sha'bi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Ansar say: He is the monk for whom the Mosque of Opposition (masjid al-shiqaq) was built. A similar report came from Ibn al-Musayyib.

The fourth: He was a man among the Children of Israel who was given three supplications, each of which would be answered. He had a wife by whom he had a child, and she was ugly and misshapen. She said: Pray to God that He make me the most beautiful woman among the Children of Israel. He prayed to God for her, and when she learned that there was no one among the Children of Israel like her, she turned away from her husband and wanted someone else. When she turned away from him, he prayed to God that she become a barking dog. Two of his three supplications were thus used up. Her sons came and said: We cannot bear this, that our mother has become a barking dog, and people shame us with her. Pray to God that He return her to the state she was in at first. He prayed to God, and she returned as she had been, and so the three supplications were used up. This was related by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. What has come down to us in this hadith is "wa kanat samijatan" with a kasra on the mim. Sibawayh, however, related from the Arabs that they say: rajulun samijun (with the mim sukun), and they did not say samijun (with the mim kasra).

The fifth: He is the hypocrite. This was said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: He is anyone who has departed from the truth after being given it, from among the Jews, Christians and Hanifs. This was said by Ikrimah.

Concerning the verse there are five opinions.

The first: It is the Greatest Name of God. This was related by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr said likewise.

The second: They are a book from the books of God, Mighty and Majestic. Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: He is Bil'am, who was given a book and departed from it.

The third: He was given prophethood, but his people bribed him to keep silent, and he did so and left them as they were. This was said by Mujahid, but it is far-fetched, because God, Exalted is He, does not choose for His message anyone who is not protected from such a state.

The fourth: They are the proofs of monotheism and understanding its evidences.

The fifth: They are knowledge of the books of God, Mighty and Majestic. The well-known view in tafsir is that he was Bil'am. According to what the exegetes mention, the matter was this: Musa, peace be upon him, attacked the city in which he was, and its people were disbelievers. He was one whose supplication was answered. Their king said: Pray against Musa. He said: He is of my religion, and it is not fitting for me to pray against him. So the king ordered a piece of wood to be carved for his crucifixion. When he saw this, he went out on his donkey to pray against Musa. When he came in sight of their army, the donkey stopped, and he struck it. It said: Why do you strike me? Here is a fire blazing that has prevented me from walking. Turn back. So he returned to the king and told him. The king said: Either you pray against them, or I will crucify you. So he prayed against Musa by the Greatest Name of God that he should not enter the city, and God answered him. Musa and his people then fell into the wilderness (al-tih) because of his supplication. Musa said: O Lord, for what sin have we fallen into the wilderness? He said: Because of the supplication of Bal'am. He said: O Lord, just as You heard his prayer against me, hear my prayer against him. So he prayed to God that the Greatest Name be taken from him, and it was taken from him. It is also said that Bil'am ordered his people to adorn the women and send them into the army so that they would spread fornication among them, and thus they would be made victorious over them. It is also said that Musa killed him after that. al-Suddi related from his shaykhs that Bal'am came to his people voluntarily and said: Do not fear the Children of Israel, for if you go out to fight them, I will pray against them and they will perish. He was given what he wished of worldly things among them. This was after the passage of the forty years in which they wandered, and their prophet was Yusha', not Musa.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he withdrew from them﴾, i.e., he went out from knowledge of them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So Satan overtook him﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: He caught up with him. It is said: "ittaba'tu al-qawm" when I overtake them, and "tabi'tuhum" when I walk in their trail. Talha ibn Musarrif read "fattaba'ahu" with the shadda. Al-Yazidi said: atba'ahu and ittaba'ahu are two dialects. It seems that "ittaba'ahu" (light form) means: followed him from behind, and "ittaba'ahu" (with shadda) means: followed his example. One may not say atba'naka meaning ittaba'naka, because its meaning would be "we followed you as a model." Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: taba'a al-rajulu al-shay' and ittaba'ahu with one meaning. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾ [al-Baqara 38], and He said: ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he was among the misguided﴾. In this there are two opinions.

One is: among the astray, said by Muqatil. The second is: among the lost and corrupt, said by al-Zajjaj.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾.** Scholars differ over whom the pronoun in "raised him" ("رَفَعْناهُ") refers to, and there are two views.

The first is that it refers to the person already mentioned. This is the view of the majority, and the meaning is: *Had We willed, We would have raised this person's rank by what We had taught him.*

The second is that it refers to rejecting the signs (al-kufr bil-ayat). The meaning is: *Had We willed, We would have removed disbelief in Our signs from him.* This meaning is related from Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: *Had We willed, We would have placed a barrier between him and disobedience.*

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But he clung to the earth﴾.** That is, he inclined towards this world and settled in it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *akhlada* and *khullida*, and the first is more common in the language. "The earth" here is an expression for this world, because the world is the earth together with what is upon it. There are two views on the meaning of this statement.

The first is that he inclined towards the people of this world. It is said that he pleased his wife with this, for she had urged him to it. It was also said that he pleased his paternal cousins and his people.

The second is that he inclined towards the desires of this world. This is clarified by His saying: ﴿and followed his desire﴾. The meaning is that he yielded to what his desire called him to. Ibn Zayd said: his desire was with his people. This verse is among the most severe verses for the people of knowledge, when they turned away from knowledge towards desire.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So his likeness is like the likeness of a dog: if you chase it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾.** Its meaning is that this disbeliever, if you rebuke him, he will not be restrained, and if you leave him, he will not be guided. So both conditions are the same for him, like the two conditions of the dog: if it is driven away and chased, it pants, and if it is left and lies down, it also pants. The comparison is with the panting dog specifically. So the meaning is: *his likeness is like the likeness of a dog panting.* He was compared to the panting dog because it is the basest of examples, in the basest and most repulsive of states.

Ibn Qutayba said: every panting creature pants only from exhaustion or thirst, except the dog, for it pants both when it is at rest and when it is tired. So Allah struck this as an example for the one who denies His signs, and said: if you admonish him, he is astray, and if you do not admonish him, he is astray, like the dog: if you drive it away and rebuke it, it runs and pants, or if you leave it in its state, lying down, it pants.

The exegetes said: he (Balaam) was rebuked in his dream for invoking (a curse) against the Children of Israel, but he was not restrained, and his she-ass addressed him but he did not desist. So He struck this example for him and for the rest of the disbelievers. This is His saying: ﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs﴾, because the disbeliever, if you admonish him, he is astray, and if you leave him, he is astray. And he, despite the sending of messengers to him, is like one to whom no messenger came and no clear proof.

**Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So relate the stories﴾.** Ata said: the stories of those who disbelieved and denied their prophets.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 177–178:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Evil is the example﴾. It is said: "sā'a al-shay'" (ساء الشيء) means "yasū'u," when a thing becomes ugly. The meaning is: evil is the example of the people, so the word "muḍāf" (the governed noun, "the example of") is omitted, and "mathalan" (example) is put in the accusative as a specifying noun (tamyīz).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they were wronging themselves﴾, meaning: they were harming themselves through disobedience.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 177–178:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Evil is the example﴾. It is said: "sā'a al-shay'" (ساء الشيء) means "yasū'u," when a thing becomes ugly. The meaning is: evil is the example of the people, so the word "muḍāf" (the governed noun, "the example of") is omitted, and "mathalan" (example) is put in the accusative as a specifying noun (tamyīz).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they were wronging themselves﴾, meaning: they were harming themselves through disobedience.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 179:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have certainly created﴾, meaning: We created. Ibn Qutayba said: From this comes "dhurriyyat al-rajul" (the offspring of a man). It is only from "al-khalq" (creation), but most of the Arabs drop its hamza (the glottal stop, i.e., they say "durriyya" rather than "dhur'iyya").

(p-292) His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿for Hell﴾. This lam (the preposition "li-") is called by some scholars of meanings "lam al-'aqiba" (the lam of consequence, i.e., the lam indicating the eventual outcome), as in His statement: ﴿so that it may become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Similar to it is the statement of the poet:

"Our wealth we gather for the heirs,
and our houses we build for the ruin of time."

A man entered upon Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz to console him on the death of his son, and he said:

"Be consoled, Commander of the Believers, for indeed
in what you see, the young one is nourished and born."

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has informed in this verse of the pervasiveness of His knowledge concerning them, that they will arrive at it (Hell) because of their disbelief.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾. When these people turned away from the truth and from reflecting upon it, they were in the position of one who does not understand, does not see, and does not hear. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Nahwi said: He intended by all of this the matter of the Hereafter, for they understand the matter of this world.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are like livestock﴾. He compared them to livestock because they hear and see but do not take heed. Then He said: ﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾, because livestock perceive their benefits and harms, so they keep to some of what they perceive, whereas most of these people know that they are obstinate, yet they advance toward the Fire. ﴿Those are the heedless﴾ regarding the matter of the Hereafter.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on Surah 7 (al-A'raf), verse 180:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾. The occasion of its revelation: a man supplicated to Allah in his prayer and called upon "al-Rahman." Abu Jahl said: "Does Muhammad and his companions not claim that they worship one Lord? So what is this man doing calling upon two?" Then Allah revealed this verse. This was related by Muqatil.

As for *al-husna* (the most beautiful), it is the feminine form of *al-ahsan* (the most beautiful). The meaning of the verse is that the names of Allah are beautiful, and it is not intended that there is among them what is not beautiful (p. 293). Al-Mawardi mentioned that what is meant by this is that toward which souls incline in mentioning Him, with pardon and mercy, rather than wrath and vengeance. His saying, ﴿so call upon Him by them﴾, means: call out to Him by them, as in your saying: "O Allah, O Rahman."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited *yulhidun* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, and likewise in [al-Nahl: 103] and [al-Sajdah: 40 / Fussilat: 40]. Hamzah recited *yalhadun* with a *fatha* on the *ha'* and the *ya'* in these places, and al-Kisa'i and Khalaf agreed with him in [al-Nahl: 103]. Al-Akhfash said: *alhada* and *lahada* are two dialects; whoever recites with both intends to take both dialects, and it is as if *al-ilhad* is turning away from uprightness. Ibn Qutaybah said: they stray from the truth and deviate, and from this comes *lahd al-qabr* (the niche in the side of a grave), because it is in a side. Al-Zajjaj said: No one should call upon Him by what He has not named Himself with. So one says, "O Generous (ya Jawad)," and does not say, "O Liberal (ya Sakhiy)"; one says, "O Strong (ya Qawiy)," and does not say, "O Sturdy (ya Jald)"; one says, "O Merciful (ya Rahim)," and does not say, "O Kind (ya Rafiq)," because He has not described Himself by that. Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: The evidence of this verse is that error concerning His names and deviation from them is *ilhad* (deviation). Among what is heard on the tongues of the common people is their saying, "O Subhan (Glory)," "O Burhan (Proof)," and this is abandoned and repugnant, with no precedent for it. Some of them may say, "O Lord, Ta Ha and Ya Sin," and Ibn 'Abbas denounced a man who said, "O Lord of the Qur'an." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that their deviation concerning His names was that they named their idols with them, and added to them and subtracted from them: they derived *al-Lat* from *Allah*, *al-'Uzza* from *al-'Aziz*, and *Manat* from *al-Mannan*.

**Section**

The majority hold that this verse is *muhkam* (a clear, unabrogated ruling), because it is stated in the manner of a warning, like His saying: ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]. Some have held that it is *mansukh* (abrogated) by the verse of fighting, because His saying, ﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾, requires turning away from the disbelievers. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 181:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among those whom We have created is a community who guide by the truth﴾, meaning: they act by it. ﴿And by it they do justice﴾, meaning: and by acting upon it they do justice. Regarding those intended by this verse there are four opinions.

The first: they are the Muhajirun (Emigrants) and the Ansar (Helpers) and those who followed them in goodness from this Ummah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Jurayj used to say: It has been mentioned to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is my Ummah; they take by the truth, they give by the truth, and they judge by the truth." Qatadah said: "It has reached us that when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse he said: 'This is for you, and the people [of Musa] were given the like of it,'" then he would recite: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 159].

The second: they are from all of creation. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: they are the Prophets. The fourth: they are the scholars; al-Mawardi mentioned both of these opinions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verses 182–183:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾. Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas: they are the people of Makkah. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the mockers from Quraysh.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We will lead them step by step﴾. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: We will fold up their lives while they are deluded about them. Abu Ubayda said: Istidraj (gradual leading on, a drawing near by degrees) is that one progresses towards a thing secretly, little by little, and does not rush upon it. Its root is from ad-daraja (degree, step), because the one who ascends and the one who descends go up and down step by step. From it comes: "daraja al-kitab" (the book was rolled up), when one folds it piece after piece; and "daraja al-qawm" (the people passed away), when they die one after another. Al-Yazidi said: Istidraj is that it comes to him from where he does not know. Ibn Qutayba said: it is that He makes them taste a little of His punishment, little by little, from where they do not know, without seizing them suddenly or confronting them openly. Al-Azhari said: We will take them little by little, from where they do not expect; that is because God the Exalted opens for them of blessings what delights them and they incline to it, then He seizes them in their heedlessness when they are most unaware. Al-Dahhak said: Whenever they renew a disobedience for Us, We renew a blessing for them.

Regarding His saying: ﴿from where they do not know﴾, there are two views.

One: from where they are not made aware by the istidraj. The second: by destruction.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And I will give them respite﴾. Al-Imla' is granting time and delay.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾. Ibn Abbas said: indeed My scheme is severe. Ibn Faris said: al-kayd is makr (scheming); so everything you work at, you are plotting it. The exegetes said: the makr (plotting) and kayd (plan) of God is requiting the people of scheming and plotting in the manner we explained in surah al-Baqarah [2:15] and Al 'Imran [3:54], concerning the mention of mockery, deception and scheming.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 184–186:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And have they not considered that there is no madness in their companion? He is not but a clear warner.﴾ Wait, the verse as given in the passage is: ﴿And what has Allah created of things, and that it may be that their term has drawn near?﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy and al-Jahdari read: ājālahum (their terms, in the plural). The meaning of the verse: Have they not looked into the dominion (al-malakut) and into all the things that Allah has created, and into the possibility that their terms have drawn near, so that they die upon disbelief and go to the Fire? ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ That is, the Qur'an and the clarity it contains. Then he mentioned the reason for their turning away from faith, saying: ﴿Whoever Allah leaves astray, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn Amir read: "wa-nadharuhum" with the nun and the raf' (nominative). Abu 'Amr read: with the ya' and the raf'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "wa-yadharuhum" with the ya' and a light jazm (jussive). Whoever reads with the raf' has begun a new clause (isti'naf). Whoever reads the jazm in "wa-yadharhum" has conjoined it to the position of the fa' (fa' al-jaza', the response particle). Sibawayh said: its position is jazm; so the meaning is: whomever Allah leads astray, He leaves him. The meaning of al-tughyan (transgression) and al-'amah (blindness) has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah [2:15].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 187:

(p-297) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ — concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

One: that some Jews said, "O Muhammad, tell us when the Hour will come?" So this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that the Quraysh said, "O Muhammad, there is kinship between us and you, so make clear to us when the Hour will come." So this verse was revealed. This was said by Qatadah. 'Urwah said: the one who asked him about the Hour was 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. The meaning of "the Hour" here is that in which all creation dies.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When will be its landing?﴾ Abu 'Ubaydah said: that is, "When is its landing?" i.e., its termination. And "marsa" of the ship means where it comes to rest. Ibn Qutaybah said: "ayyan" has the sense of "mata" (when), and "mata" has the sense of "ay hina" (at what time). We consider its origin to be "ayyu awan," so the hamza [and the waw] were dropped and the two particles were made into one. The meaning of the verse is: when will it take place (thubut)? One says "rasa fi al-ard," meaning it became firmly fixed, and from this the mountains are called "rawasi." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the statement is: when will its occurrence be?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ — that is, He has kept its knowledge exclusively to Himself. ﴿None will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ — that is, none will make it manifest at its time except Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It has become heavy upon the heavens and the earth﴾ — concerning this there are four views. (p-298) First: its occurrence has become heavy upon the people of the heavens and the earth. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and its reasoning is that all of them fear it, the righteous among them and the sinners.

Second: its matter has become great in the heavens and the earth. This was said by 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, and Ibn Jurayj.

Third: its matter is hidden, so none knows when it will occur. This was said by al-Suddi.

Fourth: "fi" here has the sense of "ala," so the meaning is: it has become heavy upon the heavens and the earth. This was said by Qatadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ — that is, unexpectedly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you as if you were informed about it﴾ — concerning this there are four views.

First: it is from the inverted order (muqaddam wa mu'akhkhar), its intended sense being: "They ask you about it as if you were ḥafiyy," i.e., kind to them, as in their saying: ﴿Indeed, He has been ḥafiyy to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Asbat reported from al-Suddi: "as if you were a friend to them."

Second: "as if you were ḥafiyy in regard to their questioning," i.e., responsive to them. Ibn Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "as if their questioning pleases you." Khasif reported from Mujahid: "as if you love that they would ask you about it." Al-Zajjaj said: "as if you are glad at their questioning."

Third: "as if you know it." This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of Ibn Zayd and al-Farra'. (p-299) Fourth: "as if you have made the asking about it insistent until you came to know it." This was said by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. 'Ikrimah said: "as if you are one who is much questioned about it." Ibn Qutaybah said: "as if you are concerned with seeking its knowledge." Ibn al-Anbari said: there is inversion of order here; its intended sense is: "They ask you about it as if you were ḥafiyy concerning it," and ḥafiyy in the speech of the Arabs means "concerned with" (ma'ndiyy).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with God﴾ — that is, none knows it except Him. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾. Muqatil, along with others, said: the intended "people" here are the people of Makkah. Regarding His saying "do not know," there are two views. One: they do not know that it will occur; this was said by Muqatil. The second: they do not know that this is among what God has kept exclusively to His knowledge; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 188:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: I possess not for myself any benefit or any harm﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "The people of Makkah said: O Muhammad, will your Lord not inform you of cheap goods before they become expensive, so that you may buy and profit, and of the land that you fear will become barren, so that you may move from it to somewhere that has become fertile?" So this verse was revealed. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Regarding what is meant by benefit and harm there are two opinions.

The first: it is general, covering everything that benefits and harms. This is the view of the majority.

The second: benefit is guidance and harm is misguidance. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except what Allah wills﴾, meaning: except what He wills to grant me possession of by His making me possess it. And one who is described by this attribute, how could he know the knowledge of the Hour?!

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if I had known the unseen﴾, concerning which there are four opinions. (p-300) The first: if I had known of the barrenness of the land and the failure of rain before it occurred, I would have prepared for the year of drought what would suffice for it. This is the view of Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: if I had known what I would profit from when I bought it, I would have acquired much of the good. This is the view of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: if I had known when I would die, I would have acquired much righteous deed. This is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: if I had known the answers to what I was asked of the unseen, I would have answered it. ﴿And harm would not have touched me﴾, meaning: denial would not have reached me. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. As for the unseen, it is everything that is hidden from you. Regarding what is meant by good here, there are three opinions.

The first: it is righteous deed. The second: wealth. The third: provision.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And harm would not have touched me﴾, concerning which there are four opinions.

The first: it is poverty, this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is everything that causes distress, this is the view of Ibn Zayd. The third: it is madness, this is the view of al-Hasan. The fourth: it is denial, this is the view of al-Zajjaj. According to the view of al-Hasan, this statement is a new beginning, and the meaning is: there is no madness in me; I am only a warner. According to the rest of the opinions, it is connected to what precedes it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 189–190:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul﴾. By "the soul" is meant Adam, and by "its mate" is meant Hawwa' (Eve). The meaning of ﴿that he might find rest in her﴾ is that he might feel at ease with her and take refuge in her. ﴿When he covered her﴾ means he had intercourse with her. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the most beautiful euphemism for intercourse. Al-Haml, with a fatha on the ha', is what is in the womb, or what a tree bears; al-Haml, with a kasra on the ha', is what is carried. By "the light burden" is meant the water (of the seed).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿she carried it about [marrat bihi]﴾, meaning she continued with it; she sat and stood and it did not weigh her down. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak recited fastamarrat bihi. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Jawni recited istamarrat bihi with an added alif. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr and al-Jahdari recited famarat bihi with an alif and a shadda on the ra'. Abu al-'Aliya, Ayyub, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur recited famarrat bihi with a light ra', meaning she doubted and was uncertain: had she conceived or not? ﴿When it became heavy﴾ means her burden became heavy. Al-Akhfash said: she became one with heaviness, as one says "athmarna," meaning we became people with fruit.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they called upon Allah, their Lord﴾, meaning Adam and Hawwa', ﴿saying: If You give us a righteous one﴾. Regarding what is meant by "righteous," there are two views.

The first: it is a human being resembling them, and they feared it would be an animal. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is a boy, as said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Explanation of the cause of their supplication

The people of tafsir mentioned that Iblis came to Hawwa' and said: "How do you know what is in your belly? Perhaps it is a dog, a pig, or a donkey. And how do you know from where it will come out? Will it split your belly, or come out from your mouth, or from your nostrils?" This grieved her, so they called upon Allah at that time. Then Iblis came and said: "How do you find yourself?" She said: "I cannot stand when I sit down." He said: "What do you think if you call upon Allah and He makes it a human like you and like Adam; will you name it after me?" She said: "Yes." When she bore it healthy, Iblis came to her and said: "Why do you not name it after me, as you promised me?" She said: "What is your name?" He said: "al-Harith." Iblis's name among the angels was al-Harith, so she named him 'Abd al-Harith. It was also said: 'Abd Shams, with Adam's consent. This is His saying: ﴿So when He gave them a righteous one, they made for Him partners in what He had given them.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim recited shuraka' with a damma on the shin and a mad, the plural of shariek. Nafi' and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited shirkan with a kasra on the shin, as a verbal noun, not as a plural. Abu 'Ali said: whoever recites shirkan has elided the genitive; it is as if he meant: they made for Him one who has a share, and those who have a partner; so the meaning is: they made for another a share, because if the estimate is "they made for Him those who have a share," the meaning is "they made for another a share." This reading in meaning is like the reading of the one who recites shurakа'. Others said: the meaning of shurakа' is shariikan (a partner), so the plural is placed in the position of the singular, as in His saying: ﴿those to whom people said: Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]. The partner intended is Iblis, because they obeyed him regarding the name, so the association was in obedience, not in worship. They did not intend that al-Harith was their lord, but they intended that he was the cause of their child's deliverance. The word 'abd is sometimes applied to one who is not a slave. The poet said:

I am the servant of the guest as long as he stays, and there is in me nothing but that trait of the servant.

Mujahid said: no child of Adam survived, so Satan said: when a child is born to you, name him 'Abd al-Harith; they obeyed him regarding the name, and this is His saying: ﴿they made for Him partners in what He had given them.﴾ This is the view of the majority. There is a second view, transmitted by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Adam did not commit shirk; the beginning of the verse is gratitude, and its end is an example Allah struck for those who worship others, in His saying: ﴿they made for Him partners in what He had given them.﴾ Qatadah narrated from al-Hasan, who said: they are the Jews and Christians, whom Allah gave children, and they made them Jews and Christians. It is also narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah that they said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿they made for Him partners﴾ refers to the soul and its mate from among the children of Adam, not to Adam and Hawwa'. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the righteous child, namely the one sound in creation; so the meaning is: that child made partners for Him. It is said "they made" because Hawwa' used to bear, in every pregnancy, a male and a female. Ibn al-Anbari said: those who made partners for Him are the Jews, Christians, and other disbelievers who are the children of Adam and Hawwa'. So the interpretation of the verse is: when He gave them a righteous one, their children made partners for Him; the children were elided and the two parents were put in their place, as He said: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. al-Suddi held that His saying ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate﴾ refers specifically to the idolaters of the Arabs, and that it is separated from the story of Adam and Hawwa'.

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿Do they associate with Him that which creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾

Ibn Zayd said: This refers to Adam and Eve, when they named their child ʿAbd Shams (the servant of the sun), and the sun creates nothing. Others said: This refers to the disbelievers, who associated idols with God, and idols create nothing.

His words ﴿and they are created﴾ mean: and they (the idols) are created.

Ibn al-Anbari said: He said "mā" (ما, "that which," a neuter form), then said ﴿and they are created﴾ (وَهُمْ يُخْلَقُونَ, *wa-hum yukhlaqūn*, with the masculine plural *hum*) because "mā" can refer to the singular, the dual and the plural. He said *wa-hum* (وَهُمْ, "and they," masculine plural), meaning the idols, because their worshippers claimed that they reason and discern, so they were treated as humans. This is like His words: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf 12:4], His words: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [An-Naml 27:18], and His words: ﴿and each is swimming in an orbit﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:40]. The poet said:

*I drank it while the rooster was calling its dawn, when the Banū Naʿsh (the stars of the Big Dipper) drew near and turned.*

Tha'lab recited for ʿAbdah ibn al-Tabib:

*When the rooster rose up calling some of its family at the break of dawn, and they are a people without weapons (maʿāzīl).*

When he (the poet) made it (the rooster) call, he made the roosters a people, and described them as *maʿāzīl*, which means those who have no weapons with them. He also made them a family (usrah). The *usrah* of a man is his kin and his people.

(p-305)

Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir): On His words, the Exalted: ﴿And they cannot help them﴾ (wa-la yastati'una lahum nasran). He says: Indeed the idols are unable to help those who worship them, and they cannot defend themselves.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 193:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you call them﴾, there are two opinions concerning it.

The first: it refers to the idols. The meaning: "And if you, O polytheists, call your idols to the path of guidance, they will not follow you, because they do not understand."

The second: it refers to the disbelievers. The meaning: "And if you, O Muhammad (ﷺ), call these polytheists to guidance, they will not follow you. So your calling them and your silence about them are equal, because they do not submit to the truth." Nafi' recited ﴿they will not follow you﴾ with the letter ta' (ت) of لا يَتَّبِعُوكم pronounced with a sukun (silent).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 7, verses 194–196:**

His saying, ﴿So let them answer you﴾, means: let them respond to you, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ that they have benefit and reward.

﴿Do they have feet with which they walk﴾ in pursuit of their interests? ﴿Or do they have hands with which they strike﴾ to ward off what harms? Abu Ja'far recited "يَبْطِشُونَ" (yabtishuna, "they strike") with a ḍamma on the ṭā' here, and in [al-Qasas 19] and [al-Dukhan 16] as well.

﴿Or do they have eyes with which they see﴾ the benefits and avoid the harms? ﴿Or do they have ears with which they hear﴾ your supplication and your calling out?

In this there is an alert to the superiority of those who worship over those who are worshipped, and a rebuke to them for worshipping one who is inferior to them.

﴿Say: Call upon your partners﴾. Al-Hasan said: They used to frighten him with their gods, so Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Call upon your partners﴾, ﴿then plot against me﴾, you and they, ﴿and give me no respite﴾, meaning: do not delay that.

Ibn Kathir, Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i used to read "ثُمَّ كيدون" (thumma kīdūni, "then plot against me") without a yā' in both continuous recitation (al-waṣl, connecting the words) and pause (al-waqf, stopping). Abu 'Amr and Nafi', in the transmission of Ibn Hammad, read it with the yā' in continuous recitation. Warsh, Qalun and al-Musayyibi transmitted it without a yā' in continuous recitation and in pause. As for "تَنْظُرُونَ" (tanẓurūna, "you give respite"), Ya'qub read it with the yā' in both continuous recitation and pause.

﴿Indeed my protector is Allah, who has sent down the Book﴾, which is the Qur'an, meaning: just as He strengthened me by sending down the Book, He will give me victory.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 197:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those you invoke besides Him﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿cannot help you﴾, that is: they are not able to protect you from whoever intends you harm, nor can they protect themselves from any harm intended for them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 198:

(p-307) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not hear﴾. Regarding who is meant by "them," there are two opinions.

The first: they are the idols. Then, regarding His saying ﴿and you see them looking at you﴾, there are two opinions. The first: they face you; the Arabs say, "My house looks toward your house" (tanzuru, "faces/looks toward"). ﴿Yet they do not see﴾, because there are no spirits in them. The second: "and you see them" means "as if they were looking at you," because they have made eyes, so the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih, "the kaf of comparison") is dropped, as in His saying: ﴿And you see people as drunk﴾ [al-Hajj: 2], meaning "as if they were drunk." ﴿Yet they do not see﴾ in reality. He referred to them with the ha' and the mim (the pronoun "hum," used for rational beings) because they are in the form of the children of Adam,

The second opinion: they are the polytheists. The meaning then is: "and you see them looking at you with their eyes, but they do not see with their hearts."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 199:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Take what is easy (al-'afw)﴾. Al-'afw means what is easy (al-maysur), and its explanation has already been given in surah al-Baqarah [2:219]. Concerning the one to whom the command to take al-'afw is addressed, there are three opinions.

The first: it refers to the dispositions of people. This was said by Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan and Mujahid. So the meaning is: accept what is easy from people's dispositions, and do not scrutinize them, lest hatred appear between them. (p-308)

The second: it refers to wealth, and concerning this there are two views. One is that what is meant by the "easy" of wealth is zakat; this was said by Mujahid in a narration from al-Dahhak. The other is that it was a voluntary charity that used to be taken before zakat was made obligatory, and then it was abrogated by zakat; this was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: what is meant is leniency toward the polytheists and pardoning them, and then it was abrogated by the verse of the sword. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And enjoin what is customary (al-'urf)﴾, that is, what is good (al-ma'ruf).

Concerning His saying: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾, there are two views.

One is that they are the polytheists, and he was commanded to turn away from them, and then this was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

The second is that it is general, concerning whoever is ignorant. He was commanded to keep himself from confronting them over their foolishness, even though it was obligatory for him to denounce them. According to the majority, this verse is entirely muhkam (definitive, not abrogated); according to some, its middle part is muhkam while its two ends are mansukh (abrogated), as we have explained.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 7, verses 200–201:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When a phantom from [Satan] touches them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "طَيْفٌ" (*tayf*) without an alif. Nafi', Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "طائِفٌ" (*ta'if*) with a long alif and a hamza. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Jahdari and al-Dahhak read "طَيَّفٌ" (*tayyaf*) with a shaddah on the ya' and no alif. Do "al-ta'if" and "al-tayf" have the same meaning, or do they differ? On this there are two views.

The first: they have the same meaning, namely that which is like a phantom or a passing thing that comes upon you. This is related from al-Farra'. Al-Akhfash said: "al-tayf" is more common in the speech of the Arabs than "al-ta'if". A poet said:

*Ala bil-qawmi latayfu al-khayali araqqu min nazihin dhi dalali*
(Truly, the phantom of the people's visitor is more delicate than a distant one who holds his coquetry.)

The second: "al-ta'if" is that which goes around a thing, while "al-tayf" is the fleeting impulse, the whisper and the passing thought. This is related from Abu 'Amr, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-ta'if" is a fleeting impulse from Satan, and "al-tayf" is anger. Ibn al-Anbari said: "al-ta'if" is the active participle from "al-tayf", and "al-tayf" according to the lexicographers is the lamam (a brief touch or passing temptation) from Satan. Mujahid claimed that it is anger.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remember﴾. On this there are three views.

The first: they remember God when they intend acts of disobedience, so they abandon them. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: they reflect upon the proof that God has made clear to them. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: they remember the anger of God. The meaning is: when Satan emboldens them to do what is not permitted, they remember the anger of God and refrain; then they are seeing clearly the places of error through reflection.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 202:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their brothers﴾ regarding this pronoun (hā' and mīm, "them"), there are two opinions.

The first: it refers back to the polytheists (al-mushrikīn). In that case this verse is placed before the one preceding it, and the sense is: "Turn away from the ignorant, and the brothers of the ignorant, who are the devils (al-shayāṭīn), ﴿keep them spiraling in error﴾." Nafi' read: "yamuddūnahum" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm. The rest read it with a fatḥa on the yā' and a ḍamma on the mīm. Abu 'Ali said: Most of what comes in the revelation concerning what is praised and recommended is ummidtu (in the form of af'alta, "to supply"), as in His saying: ﴿Will you supply me with wealth?﴾ [al-Naml: 36], ﴿We supply them with it of wealth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55], ﴿And We supplied them with fruit﴾ [al-Tur: 22]. And what is contrary to that comes as madadtu (in the form of fa'altu), as in His saying: ﴿and He lets them continue in their transgression﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. This indicates that the preferred form is with a fatḥa on the yā'. However, the reading of Nafi' is like ﴿So give them the tidings of a painful punishment﴾. The exegetes said: "yamuddūnahum fi al-ghayy" means: they make it appealing to them, and they desire from them that they adhere to it. So the meaning of the statement is: when the devils drag those who fear God into a sin, they repent from it. And the brothers of the ignorant, who are the devils, keep them in error. This is the view of the majority of scholars. Some of them said: the hā' and mīm refer back to the devils, since they were mentioned in His saying: "from the devil," so the meaning is: the brothers of the devils keep them (the devils) spiraling.

The second: the hā' and mīm refer back to the God-fearing (al-muttaqūn). Thus the meaning is: and the brothers of the God-fearing from among the polytheists; and it was said: from among the devils, keep them in error, that is, they want from the Muslims that they enter into disbelief with them. A group of scholars mentioned this view, including Ibn al-Anbari. If it is asked: how does He say "and their brothers" when they are not of their religion? The answer: if we say they are the polytheists, it is permissible that they be their brothers by lineage, or by being of the children of Adam, or because they show sincere counsel like brothers. And if we say they are the devils, it is permissible that they be so because they accompany them. The first view is more sound.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then they do not refrain﴾. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "lā yaqṣurūn" with shadda. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: aqṣara yuqṣiru and qaṣara yuqaṣṣiru. Ibn 'Abbas said: neither do humans refrain from the evil deeds they commit, nor do the devils cease from them. Accordingly, His saying "yuqṣirūn" is from the act of both groups. This is according to the well-known view; and according to the second view, it would be a description of the brothers alone.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 203:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign﴾, meaning the polytheists. Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two views.

One: "When you do not bring them a sign," they asked for it out of obstinacy. This is what Ibn al-Sa'ib said. (p-٣١٢) The second: "When you do not bring them a sign," due to the delay of the revelation. This is what Muqatil said.

Regarding His saying: ﴿Why did you not invent it?﴾ there are two views.

One: "Why did you not fabricate it on your own account?" This is what Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutayba, among others, said. It is related from al-Farra' that he said: The Arabs say, "I chose the speech (ijtabaytu al-kalam), I fabricated it (ikhtalaqtuhu), and I improvised it (irtajaltuhu)," when you invent it on your own account.

The second: "Why did you not seek it for us before your request?" This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The first view is more sound.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord﴾, meaning: the matter is not up to me.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is insights from your Lord﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Basa'ir" means proofs, evidence, and clarification; its singular is "basira." Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "basa'ir" is the manifestation of a thing and its clarification.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 204:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it⌋ — the scholars differed concerning its occasion of revelation, and there are five opinions.

The first: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the obligatory prayer, and his companions recited behind him, raising their voices, so this verse was revealed." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "The polytheists used to come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he prayed, and some of them would say to others: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, so this verse was revealed." This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. (p-313)

The third: "A young man from the Ansar used to recite whatever the Prophet (ﷺ) recited, reciting it himself along with him, so this verse was revealed." This was said by al-Zuhri.

The fourth: They used to speak during their prayer when it was first enjoined. A man would come and say to his companion: How many [rak'ahs] did you pray? And he would say: Such-and-such. So this verse was revealed. This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: It was revealed to command listening silently to the imam during the sermon on Friday. This is narrated from 'A'ishah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', Mujahid, 'Amr ibn Dinar, and others.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 205:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself⦅﻿⦆﻿...﻿ There are four opinions regarding this remembrance.

The first: that it is the recitation in the prayer. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. According to this, he was commanded to recite inwardly during the silent prayer (ṣalat al-isrār).

The second: that it is the recitation behind the imam, silently within oneself. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: that it is the remembrance of God with the tongue.

The fourth: that it is the remembrance of God by sustaining reflection, not being heedless of God, Exalted is He. Al-Mawardi mentioned these two opinions. Regarding the one addressed by this remembrance, there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is the listener to the Qur'an, either in the prayer or from the preacher (khatib). This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), though its meaning is general for all the obligated (mukallafun).

(p-314) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿humbly and with fear⦅﻿⦆﻿...﻿ Tadarru˓ (humble supplication) is submissiveness with humility; khifah is fear of His punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and without loudness in speech⦅﻿⦆﻿...﻿ Al-jahr (loudness) is the public declaration of a matter; a man is called jahir al-sawt when his voice is raised. Here it is explicitly stated that this refers to remembrance with the tongue, and it allows two possibilities.

One: the recitation of the Qur'an. The second: supplication (du'a'). Both are recommended to be performed quietly, except that the etiquette of the loud prayer has been specified in His saying: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent in it⦅﻿⦆﻿...﻿ [al-Isra' 110].

As for al-ghuduww, it is the plural of ghudwah (morning), and al-asal is the plural of asil, so al-asal is the plural of the plural, and al-asal means the evenings. Abu ʿUbaydah said: they are the times between ʿasr and maghrib. He recited:

"By my life, you are the House; I honor its people, and I sit in its shade in the evenings (al-asa'il)."

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: by al-ghuduww he means the dawn prayer (salat al-fajr), and by al-asal the afternoon prayer (salat al-ʿasr).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 7, verse 206:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ means the angels. ﴿do not disdain﴾ meaning they do not act arrogantly or consider themselves too great (to worship Him). Regarding this worship there are two views. One is obedience; the second is prayer and humble submission within it.

Regarding His saying ﴿and they exalt Him﴾ there are two views. One is that they declare Him free of any imperfection. The second is that they say: "Glory be to Allah."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾ means they pray. It was said: the occasion of revelation of this verse is that the disbelievers of Makkah said: "Shall we prostrate to what you command us?" So this verse was revealed informing them that the angels, who are greater in station than you, do not act arrogantly toward the worship of Allah. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, the Satan withdraws weeping and says: 'Woe to him! This one was commanded to prostrate, he prostrated, so for him is Paradise; and I was commanded to prostrate, but I disobeyed, so for me is the Fire.'"
